def time_travel_test(build_features, cutoff):
    """True if features are unchanged when all data from the cutoff onward is deleted."""
    cutoff = pd.Timestamp(cutoff)
    everything = build_features(sales, returns, cutoff)
    past_only = build_features(sales[sales["invoice_date"] < cutoff], returns[returns["invoice_date"] < cutoff], cutoff)
    return everything.equals(past_only)

def course_features(s, r, c):
    return retail.make_snapshot(s, r, c, features="full").drop(columns="y")       # the label is allowed to differ; features are not

print("course features pass the time-travel test:", time_travel_test(course_features, cut))

Now prove the test can fail. Here is a plausible-looking feature with a one-line bug: "orders in the next 30 days", perhaps written by someone who meant the last 30 days.

def buggy_features(s, r, c):
    f = course_features(s, r, c)
    inv_ = retail.invoices(s)
    nxt = inv_[(inv_["date"] >= c) & (inv_["date"] < c + 30 * day)].groupby("customer_id").size()     # BUG: looks forward, not back

Make this a permanent test

The time-travel test is cheap, general, and catches the most expensive class of bug. Run it on every feature set, on a few cutoffs, in your test suite. This course's own feature code has exactly such a unit test.

Reading the result. Adding five groups of carefully reasoned features raises AUC by about nine thousandths, and the paired interval says that gain is real in direction (it stays above zero). In money the story is weaker: the revenue protected moves by roughly a percentage point, and its paired interval includes zero (the full set comes out ahead in only about three resamples in five). So the honest summary is a small, real gain in ranking and no demonstrable gain in money. Both are tiny next to the decision-rule effect on the baselines page, which was worth tens of points. Statistically detectable is not the same as practically important, and here the money effect is not even detectable.

This is a real and common outcome, and it is worth saying plainly:

Effort is not value

The three basic numbers already carried nearly all the usable signal. Every additional feature is something to compute, test for leakage, monitor for drift and explain, forever. A feature has to earn its keep. "It seemed sensible" is a hypothesis, and here the data mostly said "not much".

Our decision. We keep the full set for the modelling page, because it is harmless, slightly better at ranking, and lets us test models that exploit it. But we record the honest value of the engineering (small, and unproven in money) and we know that if the pipeline ever needs simplifying, the basics-only model is nearly as good.

1. State the time-travel test in one sentence, and say why it catches leakage.

A feature built for cutoff c must be unchanged if all data from c onward is deleted. A feature that uses the future depends on that deleted data, so its value changes and the test fails; a legitimately past-only feature cannot change.

2. 36% of customers have no average gap. Why is it better to keep that missingness than to fill it with the average gap?

Missing here means "ordered once", which is itself predictive (new and occasional customers behave differently). Filling in an average hides that fact and invents a rhythm that does not exist. Tree models use the missing pattern directly; linear models should get a separate "has rhythm" indicator alongside any filled value.

3. The extra features gave a tiny gain. Is the feature work wasted?

Not wasted: it produced a measured answer (small), a leakage test we will reuse, and a feature set whose behaviour we understand. The mistake would be to assume it helped without measuring, or to keep adding features because effort felt like progress. Report the gain honestly, and weigh it against the cost of maintaining each feature.

Add spend_per_day_of_tenure = monetary / tenure_days. Guard against dividing by zero, run the time-travel test, and check whether it changes the validation AUC. 
def with_new_feature(s, r, c):
    f = course_features(s, r, c)
    f["spend_per_day"] = f["monetary"] / f["tenure_days"].clip(lower=1)     # clip: a customer first seen today has tenure ~ 0
    return f

print("passes time-travel:", time_travel_test(with_new_feature, cut))      # True: both ingredients are past-only

ratio = lambda d: d["monetary"] / d["tenure_days"].clip(lower=1)           # same formula on the ready-made tables
cols = [c for c in train.columns if c not in ("customer_id", "cutoff", "y")]
for name, extra in [("without", []), ("with", ["spend_per_day"])]:
    tr, va = train.assign(spend_per_day=ratio(train)), valid.assign(spend_per_day=ratio(valid))
    p = make_model().fit(tr[cols + extra], tr["y"]).predict_proba(va[cols + extra])[:, 1]
    print(name, round(at_risk_report(va["y"], p, va["monetary"])["AUC"], 4))

It passes the time-travel test (both ingredients only use the past), and the validation AUC does not improve: it moves by about three thousandths, in the wrong direction. A ratio of two features the model already has adds nothing a tree cannot already learn. A good outcome for an exercise is not "the feature helped", it is "I tested it properly and know".

docs.title: Feature Engineering¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Turn domain hypotheses into features and build one by hand.
  • Recognise ratio blow-ups and informative missingness in real data.
  • Write and run a time-travel test that catches features using the future.
  • Measure what each feature group adds, with a paired interval, and report it honestly.

Prerequisites: Baselines. Dataset: Online Retail II. Time: about 40 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
On the baselines page, one lesson was loud: the decision rule mattered far more than the model. A fair next question is whether better inputs help. Feature engineering is where domain knowledge enters a model, and it is also where the most dangerous bugs live, because a feature that accidentally contains the future makes everything look wonderful.

This page does three things: builds features from hypotheses, builds a test that catches future-peeking, and then measures honestly how much the extra features are worth. The answer is humbling, and worth knowing.

docs.title: Features are hypotheses¶
docs.text:
Each feature should be a sentence that begins "customers who ...". The set in mlp_data.retail (the features="full" option) comes from such sentences:

Group Features Hypothesis Basics recency, frequency, past-year spend recent, frequent, big buyers come back (Page 4) Windows and trend orders in the last 30 / 90 / 180 days, previous 90 days, 90-day change, 90-day spend recent behaviour matters more than the whole year; slowing down is a warning Rhythm average gap between orders, recency divided by that gap a customer who orders monthly is "overdue" after 60 days; one who orders yearly is not Basket average order value, items per order, distinct products big-basket wholesalers behave differently from occasional shoppers Returns number of returns, share of spend returned returns signal engagement or dissatisfaction Tenure, country days since first order, UK or not new customers are different; location may matter

docs.title: Build one by hand: "overdue"¶
docs.text: The most interesting is the overdue ratio: how long the customer has been silent, compared with how often they normally buy. Build it step by step for the validation snapshot, then confirm it matches the tested module.

docs.title: The test that catches future-peeking¶
docs.text:
A feature is point-in-time correct if it could have been computed on the snapshot date. That has a precise, testable consequence: if we delete every record from the cutoff onward, the feature must not change. If it does, it was using the future.

We can turn that into a function and run it on any feature builder.

docs.title: How much are the features worth? Measure it¶
docs.text: Add the groups one at a time and watch the validation scores. We use one fixed, modest gradient-boosted model for every row, so the only thing that changes is the inputs. For the revenue column we rank customers by value at risk (the winning rule from the baselines page).

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Write each feature as a hypothesis ("customers who ..."), then test it. Plausible is not proven.
  • Real data breaks ratios (division by near-zero) and carries information in what is missing.
  • The time-travel test (delete everything from the cutoff on; the features must not change) is a cheap, general guard against the costliest bug. Prove it can fail, then keep it in your test suite.
  • Measure what each group adds, on the same customers, with an interval. Here five groups added very little: effort is not value.
  • Keep features that earn their keep, and remember each one has an ongoing cost.

Next: Modelling, where we compare model families fairly on these features.

mlp_data.models reproduces the logistic regression exactly and the boosted model to three decimals

Reading the table.

  • Logistic regression, forest and boosting land within 0.004 AUC of each other, and even the depth-4 tree is only about 0.015 behind. A plain linear model is nearly indistinguishable from boosted trees at ranking. This is the same message as the feature page: we are near what these inputs can support, and a fancier algorithm cannot create information that is not there.
  • The unlimited tree is a disaster, and a useful one. It scores a perfect 1.000 on the data it trained on and far worse on validation. It has memorised the training rows. Its log loss is huge because it makes confident wrong predictions (it says 0% or 100% when the truth is in between). A model that is overconfident is dangerous precisely when you multiply its probability by money.
  • "Overfit gap" (train minus validation AUC) is the number to watch. The forest's gap (about 0.09) is twice boosting's (about 0.04); the logistic regression and the shallow tree have none (a slightly negative gap simply means validation scored a little higher than training, which can happen when periods differ in difficulty).
  • Cost is not equal. The logistic regression fits in a fraction of a second; the forest takes far longer, for no gain in AUC.

Reading the chart. Training AUC rises steadily with depth, because a deeper tree can carve out ever finer pockets of the training rows. Validation AUC rises at first (the tree is learning real structure), peaks at a shallow depth, and then falls: from there on the tree is memorising noise. The gap between the two lines is overfitting. The remedy is not a cleverer algorithm but constraints: limit depth, require a minimum number of rows per leaf, or average many trees. That is exactly what the forest and boosting do.

Reading the diagrams. The three sensible models follow the diagonal, with a mild and consistent tilt: they under-predict, so customers they score at 50% to 55% actually return nearer 60%. That is what you would expect when the validation period has a higher repurchase rate than the training period (36.6% against 34.4%), and it is an early taste of the drift problem. The unlimited tree only ever says about 0% or 100%, so its middle is empty, and both of its extremes are wrong: customers it gives 0% return about 27% of the time, and those it gives 100% only about 55%. That is why its log loss was so bad. If a model's probabilities are off, a calibration step (fit on data the model has not seen) can repair them, but it is better to start with a model that is already honest.

Reading the curve. The two models behave very differently. Logistic regression is already close to its ceiling with a tenth of the customers (a few thousandths of AUC are gained from there to the full data), because a handful of coefficients are learned quickly. Boosting starts far lower and climbs steadily, drawing level at roughly 80 to 90% of the data and only just ahead at 100%, with the curve not yet fully flat. A flexible model needs more data to find its structure; a simple one saturates early. Two lessons: with a smaller dataset, the simple model would win outright; and with these features the best either can do is close to 0.80 AUC, so the next real gains must come from better information (new features, new data sources) or a better question, not from a fancier algorithm.

Reading the comparison.

  • Boosting vs logistic regression: boosting has higher point estimates, but the 90% interval for the AUC difference (about −0.002 to +0.010) and for the revenue difference (about −£15k to +£37k) both include zero. We cannot claim it is better.
  • Forest vs logistic regression: indistinguishable.
  • Boosting vs forest: the AUC difference is borderline (the interval just touches zero) and the revenue difference includes zero. On money, no model is distinguishable from any other. The forest is also more than ten times slower to fit than the logistic regression, for no demonstrable gain.
1. The unlimited tree scores 1.000 on training data. Why is that a warning and not good news?

A score on the data the model learned from only measures memory. A tree grown until every leaf is pure has simply stored the training rows, noise included. The score that matters is on data the model has not seen, where it collapses. The gap between the two is overfitting.

2. Why did we put the log transforms, imputers and scalers inside the logistic regression's pipeline instead of transforming the whole table first?

Because those steps learn from data (medians, means, standard deviations). Fitting them on the whole table would leak validation information into training. Inside a pipeline they are fitted on the training rows only, then applied unchanged to validation, exactly as they will be in production.

3. Four models score almost the same. How should you choose between them?

Prefer the simplest model whose performance is within the noise of the best, unless the extra performance is large enough, on the metric that matters, to justify its costs (speed, maintenance, explainability). Report the comparison with intervals so the choice is defensible.

Refit the random forest with min_samples_leaf=1 instead of 20. Predict whether the overfit gap grows or shrinks, then check. 
rf1 = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=1, n_jobs=-1, random_state=0).fit(tree_input(train), train["y"])
print("train AUC     :", round(roc_auc_score(train["y"], rf1.predict_proba(tree_input(train))[:, 1]), 3))
print("validation AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(valid["y"], rf1.predict_proba(tree_input(valid))[:, 1]), 3))

The training AUC reaches 1.000 (each tree can now memorise its rows) while validation AUC actually drops, from about 0.796 to about 0.774, so the gap grows from roughly 0.09 to over 0.22. min_samples_leaf is a dial between memorising and generalising; a larger value forces each leaf to summarise many customers, which is a form of regularisation.

docs.title: Modelling¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Compare model families fairly on the same data, split and yardstick.
  • Read an overfitting gap and recognise overconfident probabilities.
  • Use a reliability diagram and a learning curve to decide where improvement must come from.
  • Choose the simplest model within noise of the best, with paired evidence.

Prerequisites: Feature Engineering. Dataset: Online Retail II. Time: about 45 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
We have a bar to beat (the baselines), a split we trust, and a feature table. Now the question every course eventually reaches: which model? The honest way to answer is to give every candidate the same data, the same split and the same yardstick, and to look at more than one number: how well it ranks, how trustworthy its probabilities are (our value-at-risk rule multiplies them by money, so a probability of 0.9 had better mean 90%), how badly it overfits, and what it costs to run.

We compare five candidates:

Candidate Why it is here Logistic regression simple, fast, interpretable: the benchmark that must be beaten to justify anything fancier Decision tree, unlimited depth the textbook overfitter, as a warning Decision tree, depth 4 a tree that cannot memorise: readable rules Random forest many de-correlated trees, averaged Gradient boosting trees built one after another, each correcting the last

docs.title: Different families need different preparation¶
docs.text: Tree models only compare orders, so they take the features as they are and handle missing values natively. A linear model assumes a roughly linear, well-scaled input, so it needs the heavy tails (Page 4), missing values and the broken ratio (Page 7) handled inside its pipeline, so that every fit learns its medians and scales from the training rows only.

docs.title: Watching overfitting happen¶
docs.text: Let a tree grow deeper one level at a time, and track both scores.

docs.title: Can we trust the probabilities?¶
docs.text: Our decision multiplies a probability by money, so we need probabilities that mean what they say. A reliability diagram groups customers by predicted probability and compares it with how often they actually returned. A trustworthy model hugs the diagonal.

docs.title: Would more data help?¶
docs.text: A learning curve answers a practical question: if we collected twice the customers, would the model improve? Train on growing slices of the training customers and watch validation AUC.

docs.title: Is the apparent winner really better?¶
docs.text: Boosting is nominally first. Paired bootstrap against the simple logistic regression, on the same validation customers:

docs.title: Our choice¶
docs.text:
We apply the rule from the check-yourself box: prefer the simplest model whose performance is within noise of the best. That makes the logistic regression our champion: it is as good as anything at ranking, well behaved on probabilities, has no overfit gap, fits instantly, and can be explained to a non-specialist.

We keep gradient boosting as the challenger. It has the best point estimates, the learning curve says it is still gaining from more data, and it is the model most likely to improve with tuning. The next page tunes both fairly and settles it with the same paired test.

A decision made on validation is a small bet, not a verdict

We have now compared several models on the validation set. With only a handful of candidates the optimism from "picking the winner" is small, but it is not zero, and it grows with every extra model and setting we try. That is exactly why the test set stays locked until the very end: it is the only number not touched by our choices.

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Compare candidates on the same data, split and yardstick, and read more than one column: validation score, overfit gap, probability quality, cost.
  • Different families need different preparation. Put anything that learns from data inside the pipeline.
  • Overfitting is a gap between training and validation. It grows with model freedom, and the cure is constraint, not cleverness.
  • Probabilities that feed a money calculation must be calibrated; check with a reliability diagram.
  • A learning curve tells you whether more data or better information is the bottleneck.
  • Choose the simplest model that is within noise of the best, and back the choice with paired intervals.

Next: Evaluation and error analysis, where we look beyond the headline number to where the chosen model is right, wrong, and unfair to certain customers.

def profit_curve(cost, save_rate, margin, ks=np.arange(0, 1601, 10)):
    """Expected net gain of calling the top-K by value at risk: what the model EXPECTS, and what actually HAPPENED."""
    order = np.argsort(-risk, kind="stable")
    value = v["monetary"].to_numpy()[order]
    expected = save_rate * margin * np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum((1 - p[order]) * value)])[ks] - cost * ks     # uses the model's probabilities
    realised = save_rate * margin * np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(lapse_revenue[order])])[ks] - cost * ks       # uses what really happened
    return ks, expected, realised

ASSUME = dict(cost=25.0, save_rate=0.10, margin=0.25)
ks_, expected, realised = profit_curve(**ASSUME)
best_exp, best_real = ks_[expected.argmax()], ks_[realised.argmax()]

ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)

best K: model expects 640 calls (gain £11,098); in hindsight the best was 370 (gain £9,857); at K=200 realised gain is £9,277

Reading the chart. Under these assumptions the net gain rises quickly with the first calls, flattens, and falls once calls start reaching customers whose expected rescue value is below the £25 cost. The model's own optimum is about 640 calls, in hindsight about 370 would have been best, and our planned 200 calls realised roughly £9,300 (exact figures printed above). The most important feature is that the curve is flat across a wide range: anywhere from about 100 to 650 calls earns within about a tenth of the best, so being in the right region matters more than the exact K.

Notice that the two lines disagree, and not in a simple direction. For small budgets the model expects less than what happened, because a few very large customers it considered safe lapsed (we meet them in section 5). Beyond roughly 300 calls it expects more than happened, because it under-predicts how many customers return, so many of the extra calls go to people who would have bought anyway. Calibration error becomes money error, in both directions.

How much does this depend on the assumptions we invented? Sweep them.

The best number of calls swings from about ten to the whole 1,600-call range of the grid (a value of 1600 means "at least that many"), depending on the cost per call and the rescue rate. The assumptions, not the model, decide the budget. The model supplies the ranking; the business must supply the economics. def slice_table(groups):
    rows = []
    for name, labels in groups.items():
        for g, d in v.groupby(labels, observed=True):
            rows.append({"slice": name, "group": str(g), "customers": len(d), "actually returned": d["y"].mean(), "model predicted": d["p"].mean(),

Reading the table and the chart. Two separate things stand out.

  1. A level shift almost everywhere. In nearly every group more customers returned than the model predicted (the orange dot sits to the right of the blue one), typically by five to nine points; overall the model predicts about 31% against 37% actual. The groups with essentially no gap are the long-silent (180+ days) and the middle-tenure customers. This is mostly a calibration problem rather than a ranking problem: the AUCs are healthy, but the probabilities run low across the board. It is not specific to any kind of customer: UK and non-UK customers show the same gap (about 5.5 points each), so there is no sign of a country-specific failure.
  2. One segment is badly off: new customers. Customers whose first order was under 90 days ago actually returned about 40% of the time, and the model said 22%. That is an 18-point miss on 381 customers, three times the typical gap.

Is the new-customer miss a flaw in the model, or did something change? Compare the same group in the training period and in validation.

In training, new customers came back about a quarter of the time, and the model learned exactly that. In the validation period the same kind of customer came back about 40% of the time. The model is not mis-fitted; behaviour changed. Newly acquired customers in early summer reorder far more often than newly acquired customers in winter. The data cannot tell us why (running up to the autumn peak is one candidate), and with only one winter and one summer in view we should not pretend otherwise. This is our first concrete evidence of drift, a model faithfully describing a world that has moved on. We return to it when we monitor.

The confident misses. Thirty-seven customers the model was at least 70% sure would return did not. They hold about a tenth of all the revenue that lapsed, which is why they matter. They are not obscure: typically about eleven orders in the year, one every month or so, against a population median of two. The most striking, customer 17850, placed 94 orders in the year (about one every two days), had then been silent for six months, and was still scored 91% likely to return. These are regular customers who suddenly stopped.

Two lessons. First, a model built from recency, frequency and spend cannot know why a loyal customer vanished (a competitor, a dispute, a closed business). Second, swapping the algorithm does not fix it: the challenger scores most of the same customers just as confidently. When two quite different models make the same mistake, the missing piece is information, not model power. (One cheap hypothesis for the next page: our champion caps the "overdue" ratio at 50, which treats a customer silent for 50 times their usual gap the same as one silent for 100 times.)

The surprise returners. The 322 customers the model gave 20% or less who came back were mostly one-order customers spending a few hundred pounds. They are the opposite kind of error: numerous but cheap, so they cost little revenue.

The calls we would make. The 200 customers picked by value at risk have a median past-year spend of about £4,700 and a median predicted return chance of about one half, and 44% of them really lapsed. So more than half of the calls reach customers who would have bought anyway. Ranking by value buys revenue protection at the price of precision; whether that is a good trade depends on what a call costs, which is exactly what the profit analysis priced in.

1. The AUC inside several groups is lower than the overall AUC. Is the model worse for each of them?

Not necessarily. AUC measures how well the score separates returners from lapsers. Inside a narrow slice (say, customers who all ordered once) the scores and outcomes are less spread out, so there is less to separate. The overall AUC benefits from the easy contrasts between groups (a heavy buyer versus a one-off). Compare each slice's calibration gap and look at who the model is for, not just a smaller AUC number.

2. In the profit chart, is the model's expected gain above or below what really happened? Why does it matter?

It depends on the budget: below roughly 300 calls the model expects less than happened (a few big, wrongly-trusted customers lapsed), and above that it expects more (it under-predicts returns). The expected-gain calculation multiplies the model's probabilities by money, so any calibration error becomes a money error, and it need not point in one direction. A decision made on expected value is only as good as the probabilities feeding it.

3. Why do we report the sensitivity table instead of just the 'best K' for our assumed numbers?

Because the assumed cost, rescue rate and margin are guesses. If the optimal K swings widely as they change, the recommendation is fragile and the business must pin those numbers down; if it barely moves, we can act with confidence. Showing the dependence is more honest than a single confident number.

A call costs £100, not £25. Predict what happens to the best K and to the realised gain, then check it with profit_curve. 
for cost in (25, 100):
    ks_c, ex, re = profit_curve(cost=cost, save_rate=0.10, margin=0.25)
    print(f"cost £{cost}: expected-best K = {ks_c[ex.argmax()]}, realised gain there = £{re[ex.argmax()]:,.0f}")

At £25 per call the model's best K is about 640 (realised gain about £8,900); at £100 it falls to about 20 (realised gain about £2,900). The economics, not the model, changed the answer: when calls are expensive only the very highest-value customers are worth phoning. This is why the budget is a business decision, and why we show the sweep instead of a single number.

docs.title: Evaluation and Error Analysis¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Report a headline metric with an interval, in the units of the decision.
  • Turn predictions into money using explicit, adjustable assumptions, and test their sensitivity.
  • Slice results to find groups where the model's probabilities cannot be trusted.
  • Read the worst mistakes to form hypotheses about missing information.

Prerequisites: Modelling. Dataset: Online Retail II. Time: about 45 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
We have a champion model (the logistic regression) and a headline number. A headline number is where evaluation starts. A model that scores well on average can still fail for a specific group, mislead the business about money, or make mistakes that point to a missing piece of information. This page asks four questions in turn:

  1. How good is it, with honest uncertainty?
  2. What does it mean in money, under stated assumptions?
  3. For whom does it work, and for whom does it not?
  4. What are its worst mistakes telling us?

docs.title: 1. The headline, with uncertainty¶
docs.text: We report the decision metrics from the baselines page, each with a 90% bootstrap interval. Revenue is ranked by value at risk, the rule that won there.

docs.title: 2. How many calls are worth making?¶
docs.text: Everything so far fixed the call budget at 200, which was an assumption. The capture curve shows what happens as the budget changes: for each number of calls K, the past-year revenue of the lapsers we reach, against what random calling, the earlier no-model rule, and a perfect oracle would reach.

docs.title: 3. From revenue to profit: the decision needs assumptions¶
docs.text:
Revenue reached is not profit. A call costs money, only some at-risk customers are won back, and revenue is not margin. These numbers belong to the business, not to the model, so we make them explicit and adjustable.

These numbers are illustrative assumptions, not data

We assume a call costs £25, a call rescues 10% of the lapsers it reaches, and a rescued customer is worth 25% of their past-year revenue. Replace them with real figures before using the output for anything. The point of the exercise is to see how the answer depends on them.

docs.title: 4. For whom does it work? Slice the results¶
docs.text: An average hides the places where a model is weak. We cut the validation customers into meaningful groups and compare, for each, the share who really returned with what the model predicted (on average), plus the ranking quality (AUC) inside the group. A group where actual and predicted differ a lot is one where the probabilities cannot be trusted.

docs.title: 5. What are the worst mistakes telling us?¶
docs.text: Averages and slices say where the model is off. Reading individual cases says why. Two kinds of mistake matter most to the business.

docs.title: What we would try next¶
docs.text:
These are hypotheses from the evidence, not conclusions:

Finding Hypothesis to test Probabilities low everywhere the training period is not typical; recalibrate on a more recent period, or monitor and refresh regularly New customers badly under-predicted their behaviour is seasonal; needs more than one winter and one summer of history to learn Loyal customers who stop a feature that is not capped, e.g. the full "overdue" ratio, may sharpen the signal; otherwise new information is needed Budget depends on assumptions agree the economics with the business before fixing K

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• A headline metric is the start. Report it with an interval, and in the units of the decision (here, revenue protected within a call budget).
  • A capture curve shows how value grows with the budget and where returns diminish.
  • To turn predictions into money you need assumptions. Make them explicit, label them as assumptions, and sweep them: a fragile recommendation should look fragile.
  • Slice the results. Averages hide groups where the model is badly calibrated; those are where trust breaks down.
  • Read the worst mistakes. They suggest what information is missing, not just that the model is imperfect.

Next: Tuning and experiment tracking, where we try to improve the model systematically and keep a record that makes every result reproducible.

def show4(df):
    """Display a table with four decimals, so small but real differences are visible."""
    with pd.option_context("display.float_format", "{:.4f}".format):
        display(df)

def cv_metrics(make_model, folds=5):
    """Grouped cross-validation on the training data: AUC (ranking) and Brier score (probability quality)."""
    auc, brier = [], []
    for fit_idx, test_idx in GroupKFold(folds).split(train, groups=train["customer_id"]):
        m = make_model().fit(train.iloc[fit_idx][F], train["y"].iloc[fit_idx])
        p = m.predict_proba(train.iloc[test_idx][F])[:, 1]
        auc.append(roc_auc_score(train["y"].iloc[test_idx], p)); brier.append(brier_score_loss(train["y"].iloc[test_idx], p))
    return {"cv_auc": float(np.mean(auc)), "cv_auc_sd": float(np.std(auc)), "cv_brier": float(np.mean(brier))}

def validation_scores(make_model):
    """Fit on all training data and report validation metrics (used to confirm, not to choose)."""
    p = make_model().fit(train[F], train["y"]).predict_proba(valid[F])[:, 1]
    q = at_risk_report(valid["y"], p, valid["monetary"], probabilities=True)
    m = at_risk_report(valid["y"], p, valid["monetary"], risk=(1 - p) * valid["monetary"], probabilities=True)
    return {"val_auc": q["AUC"], "val_brier": q["brier"], "val_revenue_pct_oracle": m["revenue@200 % of oracle"]}, p

Reading the charts.

  • Left: cross-validation ranks settings the way validation does (a correlation near 0.96). Choosing by CV was a sound use of the training data for ranking quality; we never had to spend the validation set on the search. The good settings cluster at the top right with the default among them, and the worst (deep trees fitted for many rounds, which overfit) lose roughly three hundredths of AUC. Search helps most by steering us away from bad regions.
  • Right: but the money metric is a different animal. Across the same twelve settings, neither CV Brier score nor CV AUC predicts how much revenue a setting protects on validation (correlations of about −0.11 and −0.19, i.e. close to nothing). Revenue@200 depends on whether a handful of giant customers land in the top 200, and that swings from setting to setting in ways smooth metrics like AUC cannot see.

So a setting that wins on a proxy can lose on the thing we actually care about. We check the decision metric before adopting anything:

Reading the comparison. This time the two ways of choosing disagree: the best cross-validated AUC points at trial 05, the best cross-validated Brier score at trial 09. Both are worse for money than the default boosting model, by roughly £45,000 and £37,000 of revenue protected, and in both cases the interval stays below zero. Neither is better at ranking (AUC differences of about −0.0005 and −0.0004, intervals around zero). Against the logistic champion, the Brier-picked setting ranks very slightly better (about +0.004, the interval just touching zero) but protects roughly £26,000 less revenue, again with an interval below zero.

Two cautions on how far to trust this.

  • These intervals only know about which customers were in the snapshot. They say nothing about whether a different month would rank the settings the same way. With heavy-tailed revenue and a single snapshot, read the money differences as a warning, not a measurement.
  • The process worked. Because we compared on the decision metric before adopting a tuned model, the proxy-metric winners were caught. Had we shipped on "best CV score" alone, we would have shipped a worse model for the business.

Does the tuned challenger clearly beat the champion on BOTH AUC and revenue? False
Final model: logistic regression (champion)

Decision. No boosting model, tuned or default, is clearly better than the logistic regression on both ranking and money, so by the simplest-within-noise rule the logistic regression is our final model. (The decision is computed from the intervals, so if the data ever changed it would be re-derived, not left to our memory.)

This is the typical shape of tuning on a noisy problem: a lot of compute, a clearer map of which settings to avoid, no real gain over a sensible default, and one cautionary tale about optimising a proxy. None of that is a failure. It is information, and it says the limit sits in the inputs, as the learning curve already suggested.

1. Why choose the winning setting by cross-validation on training data rather than by validation score?

Each setting you score on the validation set uses up a little of its honesty: pick the best of many and its score is optimistically biased. By choosing on training-data CV, the validation set stays an independent check that the choice generalises. Our scatter plot showed the two agree, which is what makes this safe.

2. The overdue-cap experiment found nothing. Was it wasted?

No. It tested a specific, evidence-based hypothesis and refuted it cheaply, and the result is in the log. A project that only records successes cannot tell "we tried and it did not help" from "we never tried".

3. A colleague says: 'We tried 200 settings, and the best has validation AUC 0.805, so the model gets 0.805.' What is wrong?

The 0.805 was selected for being the highest of 200 noisy numbers, so it overstates what a fresh sample would show (the winner's curse). The honest estimate comes from data not used in the selection: choose by CV, and quote the score of the chosen model on an untouched set, with an interval, as we did.

How many of the twelve random-search trials beat the default boosting model's validation AUC by more than 0.003? Guess first, then count from the log. 
t = log.table()
default_auc = t.loc[t["name"] == "boosting, defaults", "metric.val_auc"].iloc[0]
trials_only = t[t["name"].str.contains("trial")]
print((trials_only["metric.val_auc"] > default_auc + 0.003).sum(), "of", len(trials_only))

None of them: the best trial's validation AUC is within about 0.001 of the default's, inside the noise. Random search found no improvement over the defaults, only settings that are worse. That is the usual outcome when the defaults are sensible and the signal is limited.

docs.title: Tuning and Experiment Tracking¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Search for better settings without spending the validation set.
  • Record every run with data fingerprint, seed and versions so results are reproducible.
  • Test a specific hypothesis from error analysis, and keep the negative result.
  • Judge a tuned winner against simpler models with paired evidence.

Prerequisites: Evaluation and Error Analysis. Dataset: Online Retail II. Time: about 45 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
The champion and challenger are in place, and every model has settings: how strongly to regularise, how deep to grow trees, how many to build. Tuning searches for better settings. It is also where a project quietly fools itself, in two ways:

  1. Spending the validation set. Try fifty settings and pick the best by validation score, and you have chosen the one that was luckiest on that data. The winner's score is optimistic, and the more you try, the worse it gets.
  2. Losing the trail. Three weeks later nobody can say which setting produced the number in the report, or whether it can be reproduced.

This page deals with both: a search that does not use the validation set to choose, and a log that makes every run traceable.

docs.title: Where to search¶
docs.text:
We tune with grouped cross-validation on the training data: split the training customers into five groups, train on four, score on the fifth, rotate. Whole customers stay together, so no customer sits on both sides (the leak from the splitting page). The validation snapshot is then held back as an independent check on the winner.

An honest limitation

These folds mix snapshot dates, so they do not enforce the one-horizon time gap of our real split. That would be a flaw if we were reporting the CV score as our result. We are only using it to rank settings against each other, which is far more forgiving, and we will test afterwards whether the ranking it gives agrees with the validation set.

docs.title: A log that makes runs traceable¶
docs.text: Every run records what was tried (name, parameters), what happened (metrics), and where it came from: a fingerprint of the exact data, the random seed, the code version and library versions. The small tracker in mlp_data.tracking does that; industrial tools (MLflow, Weights & Biases) add dashboards and storage, but the habit is the same.

docs.title: Two cheap hypotheses first¶
docs.text: Before a broad search, test the specific ideas the evidence gave us. On the evaluation page we wondered whether the logistic regression was hurt by capping the overdue ratio at 50, and the regularisation strength is its only real dial.

docs.title: A broader search for the challenger¶
docs.text: Boosting has more dials, so we try a random search: draw settings at random from sensible ranges, score each by grouped CV. Random search is, surprisingly, usually as good as a grid with far fewer trials, because most dials barely matter and random draws cover the important ones more evenly.

docs.title: Stop on purpose¶
docs.text:
Tuning has no natural end, so decide the budget before you start: how many trials, how much time, and what improvement would be worth shipping. Here, twelve trials plus two cheap hypotheses was plenty, and the log lets anyone see exactly what was tried.

What the log buys you

  • Reproducibility: data fingerprint + seed + library versions + code commit recreate any run.
  • Honesty about the search: the number of trials is on record, so an "improvement" can be judged against how hard we looked for it.
  • Negative results kept: the refuted overdue-cap idea is documented, so nobody repeats it.

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Tuning is a search, and every look at validation data spends some of its honesty. Choose on training-data cross-validation (grouped by customer), and use validation to confirm.
  • Log every run: parameters, metrics, data fingerprint, seed, code and library versions. Keep negative results.
  • Test specific hypotheses from your error analysis before a broad search. Here they were refuted, which is a result.
  • A winner on a proxy metric can lose on the decision metric. CV AUC and Brier did not predict revenue protected, and the settings it chose were worse for money than the default. Always check the metric you actually care about, and remember a single snapshot makes it noisy.
  • Search steers you away from bad regions far more than it finds big gains. A sensible default is hard to beat on a noisy problem.
  • Decide your tuning budget up front, compare the winner paired, and prefer the simpler model unless the gain is clear.

Next: Interpretation and fairness, where we ask what the final model has actually learned, and whether it treats groups of customers consistently.

A positive weight pushes the probability of returning up; a negative one pushes it down. The strongest are frequency, spend and the recent order counts, as the exploration page predicted.

But look at three of them together:

Input Weight orders in the last 90 days positive orders in the 90 days before that positive orders in the last 180 days negative

The last 180 days is simply the sum of the other two, so these three are almost the same information. The model splits credit among them in a way that is mathematically fine for prediction but meaningless to read one by one: nobody should conclude that ordering more over 180 days makes a customer less likely to return. This is the standard warning about correlated inputs: individual coefficients are unreliable when inputs move together.

Do not read single coefficients of correlated features

Use them to see the rough picture, never to explain one input in isolation. For a trustworthy ranking of what matters, measure the damage when information is removed, in groups.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def permutation_drop(model, cols, repeats=10):
    base = roc_auc_score(valid["y"], model.predict_proba(valid[F])[:, 1])
    drops = []
    for _ in range(repeats):
        shuffled = valid[F].copy()
        shuffled[cols] = shuffled[cols].to_numpy()[rng.permutation(len(shuffled))]      # shuffle the whole group together
        drops.append(base - roc_auc_score(valid["y"], model.predict_proba(shuffled)[:, 1]))
    return np.mean(drops)

Reading the chart. Both very different models say the same thing: recency, frequency and spend carry the signal, far ahead of anything else. The rhythm features (how overdue a customer is relative to their own pattern) come next. After that the two models disagree a little about the order of tenure and country versus the order-count windows, both small. Basket features and returns, which looked sensible, contribute almost nothing. This agrees with the feature page's finding that the extra groups added little, and it is reassuring that two unlike models point the same way.

Reading the chart. The explanation adds up to the model's score exactly, which is the great virtue of a linear model: no approximation. The story is clear. An enormous order frequency pushes the prediction strongly towards "returns", the long silence relative to this customer's rhythm pushes back, and frequency wins. Seeing it laid out, we can see why the model is wrong here: it treats a hundred orders as overwhelming evidence of loyalty and has no way to say "someone who orders every two days and has been silent for six months has almost certainly gone".

Country has a negligible influence on any customer's score: the weight is tiny and forcing everyone to "UK" changes the AUC in the fourth decimal. So the model is not using country to discriminate. It adds essentially nothing, which means we could remove it with no loss and one less thing to defend; we record that as a recommendation for the next model version rather than editing a validated model in passing.

Now the third question, the important one: who gets the calls? For each grouping we compare the group's share of all customers, its share of the customers who really lapsed, its share of the 200 calls, and what fraction of its lapsers the calls actually reach.

v = valid.assign(p=p, lapse=1 - valid["y"], value_at_risk=(1 - p) * valid["monetary"])
calls = v.nlargest(200, "value_at_risk")

def coverage(label, groups):
    tab = pd.DataFrame({
        "share of customers": groups.value_counts(normalize=True),
        "share of lapsers": groups[v["lapse"] == 1].value_counts(normalize=True),
        "share of the 200 calls": groups.loc[calls.index].value_counts(normalize=True),
    }).fillna(0)
    tab["lapsers reached"] = [calls.loc[groups.loc[calls.index] == g, "lapse"].sum() / v.loc[groups == g, "lapse"].sum() for g in tab.index]
    tab.index = [f"{label}: {g}" for g in tab.index]
    return tab

    coverage("spend", pd.qcut(v["monetary"], 4, labels=["lowest quarter", "2nd", "3rd", "highest quarter"])),
    coverage("country", v["is_uk"].map({1: "UK", 0: "outside UK"})),

Reading the table. Three things, in order of importance.

  1. Spend decides everything. All 200 calls go to the highest quarter of customers by spend. The other three quarters hold roughly 88% of all the lapsers and receive none of the calls. This is not a bug: we deliberately ranked by value at risk, which is the right way to protect revenue within a budget. But it means the system, as designed, automates neglect of small customers. Whether that is acceptable is a business and policy decision, and the business must see this table to make it.
  1. Country shows a disparity. Customers outside the UK are under a tenth of customers yet a fifth of the calls. The previous check showed the model does not use country, so it is not favouring a location. But "the model ignores country" and "outcomes are even across countries" are different claims, and we should find out what is really happening.
  2. New customers are nearly invisible. Those under 90 days old are about 9% of customers and get almost no calls (they are small, and the model also under-predicts their return rate, as we found).

Fairness is a design choice with options, not a number to minimise

  • Accept and complement: keep the value-ranked calls for large accounts and run a cheap, automated campaign (an email, say) for the long tail, so no group is simply ignored.
  • Allocate by segment: give each spend tier its own call quota, ranking within the tier.
  • Monitor: track these coverage numbers over time so a drift in who gets served is noticed.

The model cannot choose between these. People can, once it shows them the trade-off.

Reading it. The guess is wrong, or at least incomplete. Even inside the top-spend quarter, overseas customers are called about twice as often as UK customers, and the gap persists within finer spend bands (overseas bands are small, so individual cells are noisy, but the direction is consistent).

The profiles show why. High-spend overseas customers place much larger orders (a median order value roughly double), order less often, and have been silent longer. To the model, those are textbook signs of a large account that may be drifting away, so their value at risk is higher. The model is reacting to behaviour, not to the country label, but because behaviour differs by country, the effect still lands unevenly by country. This is how a variable you remove can still leave its footprint: through the correlated things that remain.

Is that a problem? Maybe not: if overseas wholesalers with big baskets really are the accounts most worth a call, concentrating calls on them is the intended result. But it should be a conscious choice, made by someone who has seen this table, and tracked over time.

1. Why did the weight on 'orders in the last 180 days' come out negative?

Because it is almost exactly the sum of the 90-day and previous-90-day counts, which carry positive weights. With nearly duplicate inputs the model can trade weight between them freely without changing its predictions, so the individual signs and sizes are unstable and carry no standalone meaning. That is why we read groups of related inputs (permutation importance) instead.

2. The model never sees a customer's name or any personal attribute, and country has almost no weight. Does that make it fair?

Not automatically. Fairness is about outcomes, not just inputs. Here, the decision to rank by value means three quarters of customers (and most lapsers) receive no attention at all. A model can be neutral about a variable and still produce an uneven result through correlated quantities like spend. You have to measure who receives the benefit.

3. Overseas customers get a fifth of the calls despite being under a tenth of customers. Is that evidence the model discriminates by country?

Not by country as an input: the model gives the country flag almost no weight, and forcing everyone to 'UK' barely changes any score. But the disparity is real and does not vanish when comparing customers of similar spend. It comes from behaviour that differs by country (bigger orders, less frequent, longer silence), which the model reads as high value at risk. So removing a variable does not remove its footprint: correlated behaviour carries it. Whether that outcome is acceptable is a policy decision; the lever for changing it is the allocation rule, not the scoring model.

What would the group coverage look like if we ranked by the plain probability of lapsing instead of value at risk? Predict who would be called, then check. 
by_probability = v.assign(lapse_probability=1 - v["p"]).nlargest(200, "lapse_probability")
spend_group = pd.qcut(v["monetary"], 4, labels=["lowest quarter", "2nd", "3rd", "highest quarter"])
print(spend_group.loc[by_probability.index].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3).to_dict())
print("past-year spend of those 200 (median):", by_probability["monetary"].median().round(0))

The calls would flip toward the opposite end: the customers most certain to lapse are overwhelmingly small, one-off buyers, so roughly nine in ten of the 200 would come from the lowest spend quarter, with a median past-year spend of about £90 against about £4,900 for the value-ranked list. Coverage across spend groups would look fairer (small customers finally get attention), but the revenue protected would collapse, as the baselines page showed. This is the trade-off in miniature: a different ranking rule moves benefit between groups and the money with it, and choosing between them is a decision about priorities.

docs.title: Interpretation and Fairness¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Explain why single coefficients of correlated inputs mislead, and use grouped permutation importance instead.
  • Give an exact local explanation of one prediction from a linear model.
  • Test whether a group variable drives a model's decisions.
  • Measure who receives the benefit of a model's decisions, and compare like with like before blaming a variable.

Prerequisites: Tuning and Experiment Tracking. Dataset: Online Retail II. Time: about 45 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
The tuning page ended with a decision: the logistic regression is our final model. Before anyone relies on it, two questions need answers.

  1. What has it learned? For debugging (is it using something it should not?), for trust (does the logic make sense to the people who will act on it?), and for insight.
  2. Whom does it serve, and whom does it leave out? A model that ranks people or businesses decides who gets attention. That deserves a deliberate look, even with no demographic data in sight.

docs.title: What has it learned?¶
docs.text: We start with the most direct reading: the logistic regression's coefficients. Because every input was put on a comparable scale inside the pipeline, their sizes can be compared.

docs.title: A more trustworthy view: grouped permutation importance¶
docs.text: Shuffle a group of related inputs across customers (breaking their link to the outcome) and see how much the score falls. A big drop means the model leans on that information. We shuffle groups (all the window counts together, and so on) so correlated inputs cannot cover for one another. We do it for both models, as a cross-check.

docs.title: Why this customer? A local explanation¶
docs.text: A manager looking at a single score will ask "why". For a logistic regression the answer is exact: the score is the intercept plus a sum of one contribution per input. Take the customer from the error analysis who ordered 94 times and then vanished, and who the model still rated as 91% likely to return.

docs.title: Does it treat groups consistently?¶
docs.text:
Our customers are mostly businesses, not people, and we hold no personal attributes. But who the model sends a salesperson to is still a decision with winners and losers, and a score can have uneven effects even when nobody intended it. A fairness review does not require protected characteristics. It requires asking, for the groups we do have, three things:

  1. Is the model equally accurate for them? (We checked calibration by group on the evaluation page.)
  2. Does the input matter? Does the model use a group variable, directly, to decide?
  3. Who actually receives the benefit: the 200 calls?

Start with the second. We carry one variable that distinguishes groups, whether the customer is in the UK. Does it drive any decision?

docs.title: Digging into the country gap¶
docs.text: A natural guess is that overseas customers simply spend more, so the gap is about spend, not country. Test the guess by comparing like with like: only the highest-spend quarter of customers, then even finer bands of spend.

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Read a model at three levels: global (what it relies on), local (why this score), and by group (who it serves).
  • Individual coefficients of correlated inputs are unreliable. Use grouped permutation importance, and cross-check with a very different model.
  • A linear model gives exact local explanations: the score is the sum of the contributions, and it can show why a mistake happened.
  • A fairness review does not need protected attributes. Check whether a group variable drives the score, whether accuracy is equal, and, most importantly, who receives the benefit.
  • Removing or ignoring a variable does not remove its footprint. The model gave country almost no weight, yet outcomes still differed by country through correlated behaviour. Check outcomes, not just inputs, and compare like with like before explaining a disparity away.
  • Disparities in who is served are usually design and policy choices: surface them to the people who can decide.

Next: Packaging and serving, turning the validated model into something other systems can call safely.

    return p, {"AUC": q["AUC"], "Brier score": q["brier"], "average predicted return rate": p.mean(), "actual return rate": frame["y"].mean(),
               "precision@200": m["precision@200"], "revenue@200 protected": m["revenue@200"], "revenue@200 % of the best possible": m["revenue@200 % of oracle"]}

Reading the verdict. The result has two halves, and they tell different stories.

The ranking held up. AUC slipped a little from validation (the interval is below the validation figure but well above chance), and in money the call list still protects several times what random calling would. The thing we use to make the call list, the order of customers, survives. Against the simple no-model rule, though, it is not demonstrably better: it comes out ahead by a few tens of thousands of pounds, in most resamples, but the interval includes zero. On money the two are tied.

The probabilities did not. On validation the model under-predicted the return rate by a few points. On test it predicted about 32% when roughly half of customers came back. Every probability is too low, and the Brier score is far worse than on validation. The reason is the one the exploration page flagged and our evidence kept hinting at: the test window runs from 1 September to the end of November, the autumn peak (Page 4), when almost everyone buys more. We trained on December to May and validated in June to August, quiet seasons, and the model has simply never seen the behaviour of a peak.

Let us look at it by group, as we did on validation.

Reading the group table and the chart. The shortfall is everywhere: every group returned far more than the model predicted, and the orange test curve sits well above the diagonal along its whole length while the blue validation curve hugs it. New customers are the extreme case, predicted at under a quarter and actually returning about half the time.

What this means in practice:

  • Use the model for the order, not the odds. The call list is built from a ranking, and a uniform shift in probabilities mostly preserves rankings. That is why the money held up while calibration broke.
  • Do not quote its probabilities as forecasts in a season it has not seen. Any "expected gain" computed from them (as on the evaluation page) would be too pessimistic about how many customers return.
  • This is drift, and it needs a plan, not a shrug: seasonal features once we have more than one year of history, recalibration on recent data, and monitoring that notices the moment the base rate moves. That is the next page.

The honest summary is the one we would give the business: "It ranks customers about as well as the simple rule and far better than chance, but its probabilities are unreliable in the busy season, and we should not trust its absolute numbers."

Model files are code, in disguise

A saved scikit-learn model is a pickle, and loading a pickle can execute arbitrary code. Never load a model file from a source you do not trust. The hash check catches corruption and a swapped file; it does not defend against someone who can change both the file and its card. In production keep the expected hash somewhere separate, or sign the artifact.

1. The model's probabilities were far too low on test, yet its call list still protected several times the revenue of random calling. How can both be true?

The call list depends on the order of customers by value at risk, not on the absolute probabilities. A season-wide shift that makes every customer more likely to return pushes all probabilities down together and mostly preserves the order. So the ranking (and the money it protects) survives while calibration fails. This is why we say: use the order, not the odds.

2. We refit the final model on training plus validation. Why is that safe for the test set, and what would make it unsafe?

It is safe because the embargo means no label window in the training or validation snapshots reaches the test period, so the refit data contains nothing about September to November. It would be unsafe if the refit data included any test-period information, or if we changed the model after seeing the test score (turning the test set into a second validation set).

3. Why test that serving reproduces the batch scores, when it uses the same model file?

Because the model is only part of the pipeline. The features are computed by code on the serving path, and a small difference in how they are built (a different window, a missing cleaning step, a different column order) changes the scores without any error. This train/serve skew is one of the commonest silent failures, so we assert exact equality on real data.

Try scoring as of 31 December 2011. What happens, and why is refusing the right behaviour? 
serving.score_customers(loaded, sales, returns, "2011-12-31")

It raises a ValueError saying the cutoff is after the last record and the data is stale. The data ends on 9 December 2011, so a score "as of 31 December" would silently ignore three weeks of activity and produce a confident-looking list from an out-of-date picture. A clear refusal beats a plausible wrong answer.

docs.title: Packaging and Serving¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Open the test set once, report the verdict honestly, and separate what held up from what did not.
  • Package a model with a card and a hash, and load it safely.
  • Serve through one validated function that is tested to reproduce the batch scores.
  • Choose the simplest serving style that meets the need.

Prerequisites: Interpretation and Fairness. Dataset: Online Retail II. Time: about 50 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text: The model is chosen, interpreted and checked. Two things remain before anyone can use it: an honest verdict and a form other systems can call. They come in that order, because the model we ship must be the model we tested.

docs.title: The test verdict¶
docs.text:
Everything so far used the training and validation snapshots. The test snapshot (1 September 2011) has been locked away, and we have not looked at its labels once, not even their average. The protocol:

  1. The final model is the logistic regression refit on training and validation together (more data, and it includes the most recent behaviour we can see). The embargo guarantees that no label window in that data reaches September.
  2. We score the test snapshot once, in a single cell, and report whatever comes out.
  3. We do not change the model in response. If we did, the test set would become a second validation set and we would have no honest number left.

Alongside the final model we score the two yardsticks that need no training: random calling and the "silent × valuable" rule.

docs.title: Ship the model, or the simple rule?¶
docs.text:
On the test window the model and the no-model "silent × valuable" rule are tied on money: the model is ahead by a few tens of thousands of pounds, but the interval spans zero. That is the same message as the baselines page, now confirmed on data nobody tuned against: the decision rule matters far more than the model. So it is fair to ask whether we need the model at all.

The rule The model Money protected (test) about the same about the same Cost to run and explain trivial small: a fitted file, a pipeline, a check Gives a probability per customer no yes (unreliable in a busy season, as we just saw) Can improve with better inputs no yes

Neither choice is wrong. We ship the model, because it is already built and tested, scores everyone in a fraction of a second, and gives us something to improve. But we ship it with the rule alongside as a standing benchmark: each month we score both, and if the model stops beating or matching the rule, that is an alarm worth acting on. A model that cannot beat a free rule is not earning its keep. The next page builds that guardrail into the monitoring.

docs.title: From notebook to artifact¶
docs.text: A fitted model in a notebook cannot be called by anyone else. To ship it we save two things side by side: the model file and a card describing it. The card records what it is, how it was trained, how good it was, the exact feature list, and a fingerprint of the file, so we can tell if it is later corrupted or swapped.

docs.title: Serving: one function, tested against the batch results¶
docs.text:
Whoever uses the model should not need to know about snapshots, feature windows or the order of our columns. They hand over the transactions and a date, and receive a ranked list. That is score_customers, which validates its inputs, builds features using only events before the date, and returns the ranking.

The key test is train/serve consistency: scoring through this function must give exactly the numbers we got in the batch evaluation. If they differed, the shipped model would behave differently from the one we validated, a common and very hard-to-spot failure.

docs.title: Choosing how to serve it¶
Make bad input fail loudly¶
docs.text: Production data is messier than anything in a notebook. score_customers checks its inputs and refuses, with a readable message, rather than failing deep inside the features or, worse, returning plausible nonsense. Three of the cases it covers:

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Open the test set once, after every decision is made, and report it whatever it says. Ours showed the ranking surviving and the probabilities failing, because the model had never seen the autumn peak.
  • Use the model for what it still does well (the order) and say plainly what it does not (the odds). When a free rule ties the model on money, ship the model only with the rule as a standing benchmark.
  • Package the model with a card (features, training data, metrics, fingerprint) and verify the hash on load. Model files are pickles: only load files you trust.
  • Serve through one function that validates its inputs, uses only information before the cutoff, and is tested to reproduce the batch scores.
  • Pick the simplest serving style that meets the need (here, a monthly batch job), and make bad input fail with a clear message.

Next: Monitoring and drift, where we build the alarm that would have caught the base-rate shift before anyone relied on the numbers.

def psi(reference, current, bins=10):
    """Population Stability Index of one feature: how far the current distribution has moved from the reference one."""
    reference, current = reference.dropna(), current.dropna()
    if reference.nunique() <= 2:                                    # a binary flag: compare the two categories directly
        edges, a, b = None, reference.value_counts(normalize=True), current.value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(reference.value_counts(normalize=True).index).fillna(0)
        a, b = a.clip(lower=1e-4), b.clip(lower=1e-4)
        return float(((b - a) * np.log(b / a)).sum())
    edges = np.unique(np.quantile(reference, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1))); edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    a = np.clip(np.histogram(reference, edges)[0] / len(reference), 1e-4, None)
    b = np.clip(np.histogram(current, edges)[0] / len(current), 1e-4, None)
    return float(((b - a) * np.log(b / a)).sum())

drift = pd.DataFrame({c.date(): {f: psi(train[f], history[c][0][f]) for f in F} for c in months})

Reading the heatmap. Two things stand out.

  1. Almost everything is stable. Of eighteen features only two ever cross 0.2.
  2. Neither alarm is the story. tenure_days alarms in every month, and that is built in: tenure is the days since a customer's first order, so every customer's tenure grows by a month each month and the distribution has to move. recency_days crosses the line in four months, including the spring months when nothing was wrong, so September does not stand out from April.

PSI is working as designed. It tells us the kinds of customer in front of us have changed, and they have not: the same sorts of customers simply behaved differently. Input drift cannot see a change in behaviour.

Reading the chart and the table. The September cohort's early return rate jumps well outside the normal band and crosses the alarm line (z about +4), and that is known on 1 October. The other months, including a mild bump in May, stay inside it.

Compare when each signal could have fired. The early rate for September arrives on 1 October. The first full outcome to cross the alarm line belongs to the August cohort and arrives on 30 October (z about +4.8, and its window already reached into the September upswing). September's own full outcome, the one the test verdict measured, arrives on 30 November (z about +8.4). So the early partial label gave a warning four weeks before any full outcome showed it, and two months before the full September figure.

The right-hand chart shows the model's side of the story: its average prediction stays near 31% while reality climbs, so the gap is the signal, and the gap can only be measured once outcomes arrive.

Reading the guard. From April to August the model protects far more than the rule (by roughly £110,000 to £190,000 a month, ahead in 99% to 100% of resamples). Then its lead shrinks, and in September it is down to about £32,000, ahead in only about 88% of resamples: no longer distinguishable from the free rule. That matches the test verdict on the previous page.

A policy of "model behind the rule two months running" would not yet have fired, because the model was never behind. But the narrowing margin is itself a trend worth alerting on, and it is one more sign that September was different. (Revenue is noisy, so judge the trend over several months, not one.)

Reading the table. August was flat year on year (about 1,270 orders both times), and then the same climb repeated: September up 30% on August in 2010 and 37% in 2011, October up 65% and 49%. The autumn surge was not a surprise in 2011; it was sitting in the 2010 data. A seasonal expectation ("the base rate rises from September") would have warned us before a single September order arrived, and before any statistical monitor could fire. When the cycle is regular, the calendar is the cheapest and earliest monitor you have.
