from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss, roc_auc_score

shipped = models.make_logistic().fit(pd.concat([train, valid])[F], pd.concat([train, valid])["y"])      # the model we shipped on the last page
p_raw = shipped.predict_proba(test[F])[:, 1]
logit = lambda p: np.log(np.clip(p, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6) / (1 - np.clip(p, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6)))

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
half = rng.random(len(test)) < 0.5                                   # fit the correction on one half ...
fixer = LogisticRegression(C=1e6).fit(logit(p_raw[half]).reshape(-1, 1), test["y"].to_numpy()[half])
p_fixed = fixer.predict_proba(logit(p_raw).reshape(-1, 1))[:, 1]
judge = ~half                                                        # ... and judge it on the other half

before_after = pd.DataFrame({
    "average predicted": [p_raw[judge].mean(), p_fixed[judge].mean()],
    "actually returned": [test["y"].to_numpy()[judge].mean()] * 2,
    "Brier score": [brier_score_loss(test["y"].to_numpy()[judge], p_raw[judge]), brier_score_loss(test["y"].to_numpy()[judge], p_fixed[judge])],
    "AUC (ranking)": [roc_auc_score(test["y"].to_numpy()[judge], p_raw[judge]), roc_auc_score(test["y"].to_numpy()[judge], p_fixed[judge])],
}, index=["as shipped", "recalibrated"])
before_after.assign(**{"average predicted": before_after["average predicted"].map("{:.1%}".format), "actually returned": before_after["actually returned"].map("{:.1%}".format),
                       "Brier score": before_after["Brier score"].map("{:.3f}".format), "AUC (ranking)": before_after["AUC (ranking)"].map("{:.3f}".format)})
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss, roc_auc_score shipped = models.make_logistic().fit(pd.concat([train, valid])[F], pd.concat([train, valid])["y"]) # the model we shipped on the last page p_raw = shipped.predict_proba(test[F])[:, 1] logit = lambda p: np.log(np.clip(p, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6) / (1 - np.clip(p, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6))) rng = np.random.default_rng(0) half = rng.random(len(test)) < 0.5 # fit the correction on one half ... fixer = LogisticRegression(C=1e6).fit(logit(p_raw[half]).reshape(-1, 1), test["y"].to_numpy()[half]) p_fixed = fixer.predict_proba(logit(p_raw).reshape(-1, 1))[:, 1] judge = ~half # ... and judge it on the other half before_after = pd.DataFrame({ "average predicted": [p_raw[judge].mean(), p_fixed[judge].mean()], "actually returned": [test["y"].to_numpy()[judge].mean()] * 2, "Brier score": [brier_score_loss(test["y"].to_numpy()[judge], p_raw[judge]), brier_score_loss(test["y"].to_numpy()[judge], p_fixed[judge])], "AUC (ranking)": [roc_auc_score(test["y"].to_numpy()[judge], p_raw[judge]), roc_auc_score(test["y"].to_numpy()[judge], p_fixed[judge])], }, index=["as shipped", "recalibrated"]) before_after.assign(**{"average predicted": before_after["average predicted"].map("{:.1%}".format), "actually returned": before_after["actually returned"].map("{:.1%}".format), "Brier score": before_after["Brier score"].map("{:.3f}".format), "AUC (ranking)": before_after["AUC (ranking)"].map("{:.3f}".format)}) Out[7]: average predicted actually returned Brier score AUC (ranking) as shipped 31.8% 48.7% 0.225 0.763 recalibrated 49.9% 48.7% 0.195 0.763

Reading the repair. On the half of customers we did not use for fitting, the shipped model predicted about 32% against an actual 49%. After recalibration the average prediction is within about a point of the truth and the Brier score improves from roughly 0.225 to 0.195, while the AUC is identical: the ranking is untouched, which is why the call list was never wrong, only the odds.

But note when this fix becomes possible. It needs to know the new return rate, which the September cohort only revealed on 30 November. For the September calls it comes too late. That is the point of the earlier layers: the early-label monitor and the calendar could have triggered this correction, or a seasonal adjustment, before the calls were made.

1. The input-drift report (PSI) did not single out the September shift. Does that mean PSI is useless?

No, it means PSI answers a different question. It tells you when the customers' features have changed, which catches broken feeds and shifting populations. In September the same kinds of customer behaved differently, so the inputs looked as they did before while the outcomes changed. That is why you need outcome-based monitors (early labels, matured calibration) alongside input monitors, not instead of them.

2. tenure_days shows high drift every single month. Is that a problem?

No, and it is a useful false alarm to learn from. Tenure is the number of days since a customer's first order, so every customer's tenure grows by a month each month: the distribution must move, by construction. A monitor that cries wolf every month teaches people to ignore it. Either exclude features that trend by definition, or compare against the same period last year instead of against a fixed reference.

3. Why not just wait for the full 90-day outcome, which is the most reliable signal?

Because it arrives after a complete cycle of decisions has been made on the wrong probabilities. The early 30-day rate is noisier but arrives two months sooner, and its job is to raise a flag so someone looks, not to prove anything. Good monitoring trades some certainty for time, and uses the slow, reliable signal to confirm.

The early-signal alarm uses z above 3. How many months would have been flagged at z above 2, and what is the cost of the lower threshold? Predict first. 
early_z = z["early return, 30 days"]
for threshold in (2, 3):
    flagged = [str(d)[:7] for d in early_z.index if d in [c.date() for c in months] and early_z[d] > threshold]
    print(f"z > {threshold}: {flagged}")

At z above 2, two months are flagged: May and September. At z above 3, only September. May's early rate ran about 2.2 standard deviations above normal, and its full outcome also ended up elevated (about +2.4), so it was a mild genuine uptick rather than noise, but far too small to act on. The lower threshold buys sensitivity (you would catch a smaller shift sooner) at the cost of more alerts to triage, and with only four reference months the threshold itself is uncertain. Choose it by how costly a missed shift is compared with how costly a false alarm is.

docs.title: Monitoring and Drift¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Name the layers of a monitoring system and what each can and cannot see.
  • Read a drift index and recognise false alarms from features that trend by definition.
  • Build an early partial-label monitor and a benchmark guard.
  • Write an alert policy that links signals to actions.

Prerequisites: Packaging and Serving. Dataset: Online Retail II. Time: about 50 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
The model is shipped, and the world does not hold still. Customers change habits, seasons turn, the business launches a promotion, a data feed quietly changes. A model that was right when it left the building starts to drift, and nothing crashes. It just becomes steadily less right, which is why monitoring is the part of the lifecycle that decides whether a model stays useful.

The previous page showed the problem in miniature: on the test window the model's probabilities were far too low, because the autumn peak had arrived. This page asks the question a monitor must answer: could we have seen that coming, and how soon?

docs.title: What can go wrong¶
docs.text:
What changes Example in this project How you would notice The data pipeline a column renamed, a feed truncated, a sheet duplicated the validation checks from Page 2, run on every new batch The inputs ("data drift") customers get older, order sizes change compare input distributions with training The model's outputs scores shift or collapse compare score distributions over time The behaviour itself ("concept" or "prior" shift) everyone buys more in the autumn the real outcomes, but they arrive 90 days late Value against a benchmark the model stops beating a free rule score both, compare on matured outcomes

The hard one is the fourth. Our label needs 90 days to mature, so by the time we know the base rate moved, a whole cycle of calls has been made on the wrong odds. We will build the monitors layer by layer, and see which ones would have warned us in time.

docs.title: Replaying history as if it were production¶
docs.text: We act as though the model trained on December to March (our training window) went live on 1 April, and visit each month-start after it. At each date we record what a monitor could see then, and, separately, when the real outcome would have been known.

docs.title: Layer 1: have the inputs drifted?¶
docs.text: The standard test is the Population Stability Index (PSI): bin a feature using the training data, then ask how differently customers now fall into those bins. By convention, below 0.1 is stable, 0.1 to 0.2 is a moderate shift, and above 0.2 deserves a look.

docs.title: Layer 2: has the behaviour changed? The early-label monitor¶
docs.text:
Inputs cannot see a change in behaviour: the same customers with the same histories simply buy more. For that we need outcomes, and the full outcome takes 90 days. But we do not have to wait for all of it. The share of the cohort that has already bought again after 30 days is a partial label, available 60 days earlier. We compare it with what that number looked like in the reference months, as a z-score (how many standard deviations from normal).

A small reference sample

We have only four reference months to learn what "normal" is, so the standard deviation below is itself poorly known. Treat the z-scores as a rough guide, not a precise probability. In a real deployment you would build the reference from a longer history.

docs.title: Layer 3: is the model still earning its keep? The benchmark guard¶
docs.text: The previous page ended with a rule: ship the model with the simple rule alongside as a benchmark. Now we use it. Each month, once outcomes mature, score both on the same customers and compare revenue protected within 200 calls. If the model stops matching the rule, it is not earning its keep.

docs.title: The calendar was the earliest warning of all¶
docs.text: One more monitor needs no model at all: last year's pattern. The business has a strong seasonal cycle (Page 4), and we have a full autumn on record from 2010.

docs.title: An alert policy¶
docs.text:
Monitors are only useful if they lead to action. Here is how the signals above combine into a policy a team could run:

Signal Threshold Severity Action Data-quality checks (Page 2) any FAIL Stop do not score; fix the feed Early 30-day return rate z above 3 Warn flag probabilities as unreliable; widen the call list or fall back to the rule's ordering Matured calibration gap actual minus predicted above 10 points Warn recalibrate (below) Benchmark guard model behind the rule two months running Review investigate; consider switching to the rule Seasonal calendar a known peak or event approaching Plan schedule a recalibration or a seasonal adjustment before it Input drift (PSI) above 0.2 on a feature that is not structurally trending Note investigate, but do not page anyone

docs.title: A remedy, and why it comes too late¶
docs.text: When the new return rate is finally known, a small repair fixes the probabilities without touching the ranking: recalibration. Fit a one-line correction (a slope and intercept on the log-odds scale) that maps the model's scores to the observed rate. To keep it honest we fit on a random half of the test customers and judge on the other half.

docs.title: When to retrain¶
docs.text:
Policy Trigger Use when Scheduled every quarter, once the previous quarter's outcomes have matured behaviour changes slowly and predictably Triggered a Warn or Review alert from the table above behaviour can change suddenly Seasonal before a known peak the cycle is regular (ours is)

Whatever the trigger, a retrained model passes through the same gates as the first one: the time-ordered split, the embargo, the baselines, the paired comparison against the incumbent and the rule, and a fresh test on data it has never seen. Keep the previous version, its card and its hash, so a bad release can be rolled back in minutes.

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• A shipped model does not crash when the world changes; it quietly gets worse. Monitoring is how you notice.
  • Watch at several layers: data quality, inputs, outputs, outcomes and a benchmark. No single one is enough.
  • Input drift cannot see a change in behaviour. PSI did not single out the autumn shift, and a structurally trending feature (tenure) raised a false alarm every month.
  • Outcomes arrive late, so build early partial-label monitors that trade certainty for time, and use the calendar and last year's pattern as the earliest warning of all.
  • Keep a free benchmark (here the rule) running alongside the model.
  • Recalibration repairs probabilities without touching the ranking, but it needs outcomes you will only have later. Plan retraining (scheduled, triggered and seasonal) through the same gates as the first release.

Next: Reproducibility and project hygiene, the last page of the lifecycle: making all of this repeatable, testable and handed over cleanly.

Reading it. The forest's seed noise is small but not zero: across six seeds the AUC moves by about two thousandths from best to worst (a standard deviation under a thousandth). The logistic regression has no randomness in its fitting, so it gives the same answer every time.

Two uses. First, it sets a noise floor: a gap of a couple of thousandths between two randomised models is inside the seed noise and means nothing; the gaps between model families on the modelling page were several times larger. Second, it is a reason to prefer a deterministic model where it is good enough, and to record the seed wherever randomness enters.

# Model card: repurchase-risk ranking, version 1

**Purpose.** Rank the customers of a UK gift-ware wholesaler by *value at risk* (the chance they do not buy again in the next 90 days, times their past-year spend), so that account managers can phone the top {first['config']['k']} each month.

**Not for.** Quoting the probability of a customer returning as a forecast, especially in a peak season (see Limitations). Not for any decision about an individual other than prioritising outreach.

**Data.** Online Retail II, UCI Machine Learning Repository (CC BY 4.0): invoices from December 2009 to December 2011. Identified customers only; guest checkouts (about 13% of product revenue) are excluded because repeat behaviour cannot be tracked.

**Training.** Logistic regression on {len(models.FEATURES)} behavioural features, fitted on {len(labelled):,} customer-snapshots (snapshots on 1 Dec 2010 to 1 Mar 2011, and 1 Jun 2011), with a 90-day embargo before the test window.

**Test result (snapshot 1 Sep 2011, {len(sp.test):,} customers; scored once).**
- Ranking quality: AUC **{m['AUC']:.3f}**.
- Revenue protected within {first['config']['k']} calls: **{m[f"revenue@{first['config']['k']}"]:,.0f}** ({m[f"revenue@{first['config']['k']} % of oracle"]:.0%} of the best possible). A free no-model rule achieved about the same: the model is **not demonstrably better** than the rule on money.
- Calibration: the model predicted a **{p_test.mean():.0%}** return rate; **{sp.test['y'].mean():.0%}** actually returned.

**Limitations.**
1. Probabilities were far too low in the autumn peak; it had seen one winter and one early summer. Use the *order*, not the *odds*.
2. New customers (under 90 days) were under-predicted by about 28 points on test.
3. It cannot anticipate regular customers who suddenly stop; a different algorithm did not fix this (the information is missing).
4. One season of history: seasonal effects are not modelled.

**Fairness considerations.** The model ignores country (negligible weight), but value-ranking sends all calls to the top spend quarter, and overseas customers receive about twice the call rate of UK customers at similar spend because of behaviour that differs by country. Customers outside the top spend quarter receive no calls. Whether that is acceptable is a policy decision; a low-touch channel for the remainder is recommended.

**Monitoring.** Early 30-day return rate (alarm at z above 3), matured calibration gap, model-versus-rule benchmark, seasonal calendar. Retrain quarterly and before known peaks, through the same gates.

**Provenance.** Model file hash `{saved['sha256'][:16]}...`; data fingerprints {first['data']['train']} (train), {first['data']['valid']} (validation), {first['data']['test']} (test); predictions fingerprint {first['predictions']}; Python {first['env']['python']}, scikit-learn {first['env']['scikit-learn']}, pandas {first['env']['pandas']}.

Identified customers only; guest checkouts (about 13% of product revenue) are excluded because repeat behaviour cannot be tracked. **Training.** Logistic regression on {len(models.FEATURES)} behavioural features, fitted on {len(labelled):,} customer-snapshots (snapshots on 1 Dec 2010 to 1 Mar 2011, and 1 Jun 2011), with a 90-day embargo before the test window. **Test result (snapshot 1 Sep 2011, {len(sp.test):,} customers; scored once).** - Ranking quality: AUC **{m['AUC']:.3f}**. - Revenue protected within {first['config']['k']} calls: **{m[f"revenue@{first['config']['k']}"]:,.0f}** ({m[f"revenue@{first['config']['k']} % of oracle"]:.0%} of the best possible). A free no-model rule achieved about the same: the model is **not demonstrably better** than the rule on money. - Calibration: the model predicted a **{p_test.mean():.0%}** return rate; **{sp.test['y'].mean():.0%}** actually returned. **Limitations.** 1. Probabilities were far too low in the autumn peak; it had seen one winter and one early summer. Use the *order*, not the *odds*. 2. New customers (under 90 days) were under-predicted by about 28 points on test. 3. It cannot anticipate regular customers who suddenly stop; a different algorithm did not fix this (the information is missing). 4. One season of history: seasonal effects are not modelled. **Fairness considerations.** The model ignores country (negligible weight), but value-ranking sends all calls to the top spend quarter, and overseas customers receive about twice the call rate of UK customers at similar spend because of behaviour that differs by country. Customers outside the top spend quarter receive no calls. Whether that is acceptable is a policy decision; a low-touch channel for the remainder is recommended. **Monitoring.** Early 30-day return rate (alarm at z above 3), matured calibration gap, model-versus-rule benchmark, seasonal calendar. Retrain quarterly and before known peaks, through the same gates. **Provenance.** Model file hash `{saved['sha256'][:16]}...`; data fingerprints {first['data']['train']} (train), {first['data']['valid']} (validation), {first['data']['test']} (test); predictions fingerprint {first['predictions']}; Python {first['env']['python']}, scikit-learn {first['env']['scikit-learn']}, pandas {first['env']['pandas']}. """ display(Markdown(card))

Every number in that card was read from a variable, so if the data or the model changes, the card changes with it. Compare it with a hand-written paragraph that says "the model performs well": the card says what it is for, what it is not for, how it was tested, and what would make you stop trusting it.

1. A fresh Python process gave the same fingerprint as the notebook. What would it have meant if it had not?

That the result depended on something other than the code, config and data: a variable left over from an earlier cell, a package version, a file that differs, or an unseeded random number. Running in a clean process is the cheapest way to flush out hidden state, which is why it belongs in the routine.

2. The random forest's AUC varies a little between seeds. Why record the seed anyway?

Because "a little" is still the difference between reproducing a number and not, and because differences smaller than the seed noise are not evidence of anything. Recording the seed makes a run repeatable; measuring the seed spread tells you how large a difference must be before it means something.

3. Why generate the model card from variables instead of writing it by hand?

A hand-written card is true on the day it is written and drifts afterwards, quietly, as the model and data change. Numbers read from the artifacts cannot disagree with them. The prose (purpose, limitations) still needs a human, but anything checkable should be produced, not typed.

Change one setting (the regularisation strength) and re-run the pipeline. What should happen to the predictions fingerprint, and what should not change? 
changed = run_pipeline(Config(C=0.001))
print("predictions fingerprint changed:", changed["predictions"] != first["predictions"])
print("data fingerprints unchanged:   ", changed["data"] == first["data"])

The predictions fingerprint changes (a different model makes different predictions) while the data fingerprints are identical (you altered the model, not the data). The pair tells you instantly what kind of change a result reflects, which is exactly what a manifest is for.

docs.title: Reproducibility and Project Hygiene¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Prove that a whole project reproduces, including from a fresh process.
  • Record a run so that it can be re-created from its manifest alone.
  • Generate a model card and a decision log from artifacts, not memory.
  • Map every trap you met to a test that guards it.

Prerequisites: Monitoring and Drift. Dataset: Online Retail II. Time: about 45 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
Imagine a colleague opens this project in six months and is asked: "Where did the 340,000 come from, and can you reproduce it?" Or the regulator asks. Or you are that colleague, and you have forgotten everything. A result that cannot be re-created is a rumour.

Reproducibility is not one big feature. It is a habit built from small, boring, checkable things: pinned inputs, one place for settings, controlled randomness, recorded environments, tests that guard the traps we hit, and writing down why. This last page of the lifecycle turns each of those from a good intention into something we can run and check.

docs.title: 1. Can the whole project be re-run, and get the same answer?¶
docs.text: mlp_data.pipeline is the entire project as one function: raw data in, a result out. Everything that can change a number lives in a small Config; everything that identifies what was run goes in a manifest. We run it twice in this notebook, and then once more in a brand-new Python process, to rule out hidden state such as variables left over from earlier cells.

docs.title: 2. What exactly was it run on? The manifest¶
docs.text: A fingerprint is only useful if you can compare it with something. The manifest records the configuration, a fingerprint of each dataset, the results, and the environment, which is everything needed to say "that number came from this".

docs.title: The environment¶
docs.text: "Same library versions" needs checking, not assuming. These are the versions installed right now for the packages this project depends on. In a real project this list is saved next to the results (a lock file, or pip freeze > requirements.lock) so the environment can be rebuilt.

docs.title: 3. Controlled randomness: how much does a seed matter?¶
docs.text: Randomness enters in a few places: tie-breaking in the ranking, the bootstrap intervals, the random search, and (for forests) the trees themselves. Each must have a recorded seed. But it is also worth knowing how large the effect of a seed is, so that you know whether a difference you are chasing is bigger than the noise from randomness alone.

docs.title: 4. A manifest is a recipe¶
docs.text: The proof of a record is being able to follow it. Save a run to a log file, forget the notebook, read the file back, and re-create the result from nothing but what it says.

docs.title: 5. Tests: a guard for every trap we met¶
docs.text:
The course is, among other things, a record of traps. Each deserves a test that fails if it ever comes back. Here is the map of what the project's own test suite guards, and where in the course the trap appeared:

The trap The test that guards it Met on The two Excel sheets overlap and double-count a week a synthetic overlap is removed exactly once Cleaning A cancelled order counts as a purchase a fully reversed pair is netted out; partial and late cancellations are kept Cleaning The ledger stops reconciling to the raw file rows removed plus kept equals rows in Cleaning A feature uses the future features unchanged when future data changes; the label window is half-open Feature engineering Train and validation windows overlap the split checker rejects overlapping label windows Splitting Ties in a ranking decided by file order tie-breaking independent of row order Baselines A metric that is optimistic by construction exact random baseline; paired bootstrap detects a real difference Baselines A model that cannot be saved safely save/load round trip; a tampered file is refused Serving Silent bad input missing columns, bad dates and stale data fail with a clear message Serving Serving differs from the batch evaluation serving reproduces the batch scores; future data cannot change a score Serving The project stops being reproducible same config and data give identical fingerprints this page

If the course repository is present (it is when you run from a clone), the suite can be run right here.

docs.title: 6. Say what it is: a model card generated from the facts¶
docs.text: A model card is a short document that travels with a model: what it is for, what it was built from, how well it works, and where it should not be used. The commonest failure is writing one by hand and letting it drift from the truth. So we generate it from the artifacts we already have: the manifest, the test results and the findings recorded on earlier pages.

docs.title: Model card: repurchase-risk ranking, version 1¶
docs.text:
Purpose. Rank the customers of a UK gift-ware wholesaler by value at risk (the chance they do not buy again in the next 90 days, times their past-year spend), so that account managers can phone the top 200 each month.

Not for. Quoting the probability of a customer returning as a forecast, especially in a peak season (see Limitations). Not for any decision about an individual other than prioritising outreach.

Data. Online Retail II, UCI Machine Learning Repository (CC BY 4.0): invoices from December 2009 to December 2011. Identified customers only; guest checkouts (about 13% of product revenue) are excluded because repeat behaviour cannot be tracked.

Training. Logistic regression on 18 behavioural features, fitted on 21,234 customer-snapshots (snapshots on 1 Dec 2010 to 1 Mar 2011, and 1 Jun 2011), with a 90-day embargo before the test window.

Test result (snapshot 1 Sep 2011, 4,323 customers; scored once).

  • Ranking quality: AUC 0.767.
  • Revenue protected within 200 calls: 340,926 (50% of the best possible). A free no-model rule achieved about the same: the model is not demonstrably better than the rule on money.
  • Calibration: the model predicted a 32% return rate; 50% actually returned.

Limitations.

  1. Probabilities were far too low in the autumn peak; it had seen one winter and one early summer. Use the order, not the odds.
  2. New customers (under 90 days) were under-predicted by about 28 points on test.
  3. It cannot anticipate regular customers who suddenly stop; a different algorithm did not fix this (the information is missing).
  4. One season of history: seasonal effects are not modelled.

Fairness considerations. The model ignores country (negligible weight), but value-ranking sends all calls to the top spend quarter, and overseas customers receive about twice the call rate of UK customers at similar spend because of behaviour that differs by country. Customers outside the top spend quarter receive no calls. Whether that is acceptable is a policy decision; a low-touch channel for the remainder is recommended.

Monitoring. Early 30-day return rate (alarm at z above 3), matured calibration gap, model-versus-rule benchmark, seasonal calendar. Retrain quarterly and before known peaks, through the same gates.

Provenance. Model file hash 139b73b8b494b66f...; data fingerprints de610f93a4c9 (train), e0eb1c938a1c (validation), a9be028b046b (test); predictions fingerprint fe7f3fda68e5; Python 3.14.2, scikit-learn 1.9.1, pandas 3.0.6.

docs.title: 7. The decision log¶
docs.text:
Pages of reasoning are easy to lose. A decision log records each choice with the evidence behind it, in one place a newcomer can scan. The ones this project made:

# Decision Evidence Page 1 Predict "buys again within 90 days" for customers active in the past year 81% of reorder gaps are 90 days or shorter Problem framing 2 Snapshots start 1 Dec 2010 Earlier snapshots are left-censored; the data starts Dec 2009 Problem framing, EDA 3 Chronological split with a 90-day embargo: train Dec to Mar, validate Jun, test Sep A random split flattered a flexible model by about +0.07 AUC Splitting 4 Clean in six accounted steps; exclude guest checkouts; net out orders cancelled within a day Cancelled orders left labels untouched but distorted spend Cleaning 5 Judge by revenue protected within a call budget, alongside AUC Accuracy-optimised rankings protected less than random calling Baselines 6 Rank by value at risk, not probability Same model: ~2% of the best possible revenue vs ~58% Baselines 7 Keep all features Small real AUC gain; no demonstrable money gain Features 8 Logistic regression is the final model Nothing beat it on both ranking and money Modelling, Tuning 9 Ship the model with the simple rule as a benchmark On the test window they were tied on money Packaging 10 Monitor with an early partial-label rate, a benchmark guard and the seasonal calendar PSI did not see the autumn shift; the early rate did, a month before any full outcome Monitoring

docs.title: 8. Handing it over¶
docs.text:
A project is finished when someone else can run it, check it and change it. A last checklist:

  • The repository contains no data and no secrets; data is fetched and checksummed
  • One command re-creates the headline result (python -m mlp_data.pipeline), and its fingerprint is recorded
  • Every setting lives in one Config; every random choice has a recorded seed
  • The environment is captured (versions or a lock file)
  • Tests run in CI on every change, including the leakage and serving-consistency tests
  • The model file is stored with its card and hash, and the previous version is kept for rollback
  • The model card states intended use, limitations, fairness findings and the monitoring plan
  • The decision log is current, and negative results are kept
  • There is a named owner, a retraining schedule and an alert policy

docs.title: What the lifecycle taught¶
docs.text: Follow one project from a vague request to a documented, monitored model and a theme appears again and again. The expensive mistakes were not modelling mistakes. They were a wrong question, a leaky split, an unexamined cleaning choice, a metric that did not match the decision, a headline number that did not survive a fair test, and a world that changed after launch. The modelling itself was, in the end, a small part: a logistic regression was good enough, and a free rule nearly matched it.

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Reproducibility is a handful of checkable habits: pinned inputs, one Config, recorded seeds, a captured environment and a fingerprint that proves two runs agree.
  • Run in a fresh process to rule out hidden state. A manifest should be enough to rebuild a run.
  • Measure the noise from randomness so you know how big a difference has to be to matter.
  • Keep a test for every trap you met, especially leakage and serving consistency.
  • Generate the model card and decision log from facts, and record limitations and fairness findings alongside the numbers.
  • The lesson of the whole lifecycle: the hard, expensive mistakes are upstream and downstream of the model. Spend your care there.

That completes the lifecycle. The next parts take what we built on the retail data and widen it: classical models in more depth, time-series forecasting on taxi demand, and recommender systems on ratings and purchases.

docs.title: Top 10 Common Mistakes & Debugging Guide
docs.text: A rapid diagnostic guide for the most frequent runtime errors and logical bugs students encounter during Machine Learning Practice labs.

docs.title: 1. ValueError: Found input variables with inconsistent numbers of samples
docs.text:
• Symptom: ValueError: Found input variables with inconsistent numbers of samples: [1000, 950]
  • Root Cause: \(X\) and \(y\) have differing numbers of rows (usually caused by filtering or dropping NaN from \(X\) without applying the same filter to \(y\)).
  • Solution: Always drop missing values or filter rows from the combined DataFrame before separating \(X\) and \(y\): 
    # ✅ Fix:
df = df.dropna(subset=["critical_column"])
X = df.drop(columns=["target"])
y = df["target"]

docs.title: 2. ValueError: Expected 2D array, got 1D array instead
docs.text:
• Symptom: Calling .predict() or StandardScaler.fit() on a single 1D feature array crashes.
  • Root Cause: Scikit-Learn estimators expect feature matrices to be 2-dimensional (n_samples, n_features).
  • Solution: Reshape with .reshape(-1, 1) or slice using double brackets df[['feature']]: 
    # ✅ Fix for NumPy:
single_feature_2d = feature_arr.reshape(-1, 1)

# ✅ Fix for Pandas:
single_feature_df = df[["single_col"]]  # Note double brackets!

docs.title: 3. Data Leakage (The "Overly Perfect" Test Score)
docs.text:
• Symptom: Your model gets 99.8% accuracy in cross-validation, but plummets to 65% when tested on new data.
  • Root Cause: Scalers, imputers, or target statistics were computed on the entire dataset prior to train_test_split.
  • Solution: Encapsulate transformers inside a Pipeline: 
    # ✅ Fix:
pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", LogisticRegression())
])
cross_val_score(pipeline, X_train, y_train, cv=5)

docs.title: 4. ConvergenceWarning: lbfgs failed to converge
docs.text:
• Symptom: ConvergenceWarning: lbfgs failed to converge (status=1): STOP: TOTAL NO. of ITERATIONS REACHED LIMIT.
  • Root Cause: Optimization solver did not reach minimum before running out of iterations. Typically happens when features are not scaled or max_iter is too low.
  • Solution: Scale numerical features with StandardScaler and increase max_iter: 
    # ✅ Fix:
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)

docs.title: 5. ValueError: Found unknown categories in column ... during transform
docs.text:
• Symptom: OneHotEncoder crashes when evaluating test data because a new unseen category appeared.
  • Root Cause: Default OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='error') raises an error on new categories.
  • Solution: Set handle_unknown="ignore": 
    # ✅ Fix:
encoder = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False)

docs.title: 6. SettingWithCopyWarning in Pandas
docs.text:
• Symptom: A value is trying to be set on a copy of a slice from a DataFrame.
  • Root Cause: Assigning values to a chained slice (e.g. df[df['a'] > 5]['b'] = 10).
  • Solution: Use .loc[] or explicitly call .copy(): 
    # ✅ Fix:
df.loc[df["a"] > 5, "b"] = 10

docs.title: 7. The Accuracy Paradox on Imbalanced Classes
docs.text:
• Symptom: The model achieves 96% accuracy, but has 0% recall on the positive minority class (e.g. fraud detection).
  • Root Cause: When 96% of labels are negative, predicting negative for all samples yields 96% accuracy.
  • Solution: Use f1_score, roc_auc_score, or classification_report, and enable class_weight='balanced': 
    # ✅ Fix:
model = RandomForestClassifier(class_weight="balanced")
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))

docs.title: 8. Forgetting to Scale Before Distance / Kernel Algorithms
docs.text:
• Symptom: KNN, SVM, or PCA performance is completely dominated by one feature with a huge numerical range (e.g. income 100,000 vs age 25).
  • Root Cause: Euclidean distance gives \((100000)^2\) vastly more weight than \((25)^2\).
  • Solution: Always use StandardScaler or MinMaxScaler prior to distance-based estimators.

docs.title: 9. Dimension Broadcasting Errors in NumPy
docs.text:
• Symptom: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (100, 3) (100,)
  • Root Cause: Subtracting a 1D vector (100,) from a 2D matrix column-wise instead of row-wise.
  • Solution: Ensure correct trailing dimensions with np.newaxis: 
    # ✅ Fix:
diff = matrix_100x3 - vector_100[:, np.newaxis]

docs.title: 10. NotFittedError: This instance is not fitted yet
docs.text:
• Symptom: Calling .predict() or .transform() before .fit().
  • Root Cause: Attempting inference on an uninitialized or newly reinstantiated model.
  • Solution: Verify that .fit(X_train, y_train) has completed before .predict().

Two rhythms are obvious: a daily cycle (quiet at 4am, busy in the evening) and a weekly cycle (the weekend looks different from weekdays). Nearly everything in forecasting is about those repeating patterns and what is left after you account for them.

Out[7]: pickups hour 2023-01-02 65777 2023-01-01 76752 2023-02-20 79583 2023-01-16 80120 2023-01-30 83768

Four of the five quietest days are holidays: New Year's Day, the Monday after it (the observed public holiday), Presidents' Day and Martin Luther King Day. Holidays are information the series itself cannot tell you in advance, so later pages feed them to the model.

Now the trap. Weekly totals look like an easy use of resample("W"), but weeks are cut at Sunday, and our data does not start or end on one.

In [8]: Copied! 
weekly = y.resample("W")
counts = weekly.size()                                # how many hourly rows landed in each bin
print(counts.iloc[[0, 1, -1]].to_string(), sep="")
weekly = y.resample("W") counts = weekly.size() # how many hourly rows landed in each bin print(counts.iloc[[0, 1, -1]].to_string(), sep="") 
hour
2023-01-01     24
2023-01-08    168
2023-04-02    120

The first "week" has just 24 rows (1 January was a Sunday) and the last has 120 (it ends on Friday 31 March). Their totals are far smaller than a full week's, and any chart or model that treats them as comparable is wrong. Always check how many observations fed each bucket.

In [9]: Copied! 
grid = y.asfreq("h")
missing = grid[grid.isna()]
print("expected hours:", len(grid), "| present:", len(y), "| missing:", len(missing))
print(missing.index.tolist())
y["2023-03-12 00:00":"2023-03-12 05:00"].to_frame()
grid = y.asfreq("h") missing = grid[grid.isna()] print("expected hours:", len(grid), "| present:", len(y), "| missing:", len(missing)) print(missing.index.tolist()) y["2023-03-12 00:00":"2023-03-12 05:00"].to_frame() 
expected hours: 2160 | present: 2159 | missing: 1
[Timestamp('2023-03-12 02:00:00')]
Out[9]: pickups hour 2023-03-12 00:00:00 6111 2023-03-12 01:00:00 5231 2023-03-12 03:00:00 4267 2023-03-12 04:00:00 2530 2023-03-12 05:00:00 910

Exactly one hour is missing: 02:00 on Sunday 12 March 2023. It is not that nobody took a taxi. On that date New York moved its clocks forward from 02:00 to 03:00, so 02:00 never happened on the wall clock. The timestamps in the file are local wall-clock time with no time zone attached (naive), so the skipped hour is simply absent. Two consequences:

  • That Sunday has 23 hours, so its daily total is a little lower for a reason that has nothing to do with demand.
  • In November the clocks go back and 01:00 happens twice. A naive timestamp cannot tell the two apart. (Our three months do not contain that date, but a year-long series does.)

pandas can attach the time zone and handle this explicitly:

In [10]: Copied! 
ny = pd.date_range("2023-03-12 00:00", periods=6, freq="h", tz="America/New_York")
print(pd.DataFrame({"wall clock": ny, "UTC": ny.tz_convert("UTC")}).assign(offset=ny.strftime("%z")).to_string(index=False))
ny = pd.date_range("2023-03-12 00:00", periods=6, freq="h", tz="America/New_York") print(pd.DataFrame({"wall clock": ny, "UTC": ny.tz_convert("UTC")}).assign(offset=ny.strftime("%z")).to_string(index=False)) 
               wall clock                       UTC offset
2023-03-12 00:00:00-05:00 2023-03-12 05:00:00+00:00  -0500
2023-03-12 01:00:00-05:00 2023-03-12 06:00:00+00:00  -0500
2023-03-12 03:00:00-04:00 2023-03-12 07:00:00+00:00  -0400
2023-03-12 04:00:00-04:00 2023-03-12 08:00:00+00:00  -0400
2023-03-12 05:00:00-04:00 2023-03-12 09:00:00+00:00  -0400
2023-03-12 06:00:00-04:00 2023-03-12 10:00:00+00:00  -0400

In UTC the six hours are consecutive; on the wall clock one is skipped and the offset changes from -0500 to -0400. A common professional practice is to store and model in UTC and convert to local time only to build calendar features such as "hour of day". Here we keep the local naive clock, because that is what the data gives us and because people's habits follow the wall clock: the morning rush stays at 8am local time on both sides of the change.

For one missing hour out of 2,160 we simply fill the gap by linear interpolation so that the series has a regular grid, which every later page needs.

In [11]: Copied! 
y = taxi_hourly(["2023-01", "2023-02", "2023-03"]).asfreq("h").interpolate()
assert y.notna().all() and len(y) == 90 * 24
print("filled value at 02:00:", round(y["2023-03-12 02:00"]), "(between", y["2023-03-12 01:00"], "and", y["2023-03-12 03:00"], ")")
y = taxi_hourly(["2023-01", "2023-02", "2023-03"]).asfreq("h").interpolate() assert y.notna().all() and len(y) == 90 * 24 print("filled value at 02:00:", round(y["2023-03-12 02:00"]), "(between", y["2023-03-12 01:00"], "and", y["2023-03-12 03:00"], ")") 
filled value at 02:00: 4749 (between 5231.0 and 4267.0 )

Filling is a modelling decision

Interpolating is fine for one hour that does not exist. It would be wrong for a sensor that was switched off for a day (you would be inventing a day of data), and wrong if "missing" really means "zero events", in which case fill with 0. Always ask what a gap means before choosing how to fill it, and keep a record of what you filled.

In [12]: Copied! 
demo = pd.DataFrame({"pickups": y})
demo["same hour yesterday"] = y.shift(24)
demo["same hour last week"] = y.shift(168)
demo["mean of last 24 h"] = y.rolling(24).mean()
print("leading NaNs:", demo.isna().sum().to_dict())
demo["2023-01-09 08:00":"2023-01-09 10:00"]
demo = pd.DataFrame({"pickups": y}) demo["same hour yesterday"] = y.shift(24) demo["same hour last week"] = y.shift(168) demo["mean of last 24 h"] = y.rolling(24).mean() print("leading NaNs:", demo.isna().sum().to_dict()) demo["2023-01-09 08:00":"2023-01-09 10:00"] 
leading NaNs: {'pickups': 0, 'same hour yesterday': 24, 'same hour last week': 168, 'mean of last 24 h': 23}
Out[12]: pickups same hour yesterday same hour last week mean of last 24 h hour 2023-01-09 08:00:00 4,488.00 1,703.00 1,540.00 3,251.12 2023-01-09 09:00:00 4,550.00 2,569.00 2,325.00 3,333.67 2023-01-09 10:00:00 4,422.00 3,905.00 3,134.00 3,355.21

The count above shows the warm-up: shift(24) is NaN for the first 24 rows (there is no yesterday on the first day), shift(168) for the first 168, and the rolling mean needs a full window so it is NaN for its first 23. Dropping or handling these warm-up rows is a routine step.

A subtlety: rolling(168) counts rows, while rolling("7D") counts time. They agree on a complete grid and disagree as soon as rows go missing. Compare them on the raw, un-filled series around the daylight-saving gap:

In [13]: Copied! 
raw = taxi_hourly(["2023-01", "2023-02", "2023-03"])           # the 02:00 hour is absent here
by_rows = raw.rolling(168).mean()
by_time = raw.rolling("7D").mean()
day = "2023-03-14 12:00"
t = pd.Timestamp(day)
first_by_rows = raw.index[raw.index.get_loc(t) - 167]            # the oldest of the last 168 rows
first_by_time = raw.index[raw.index > t - pd.Timedelta("7D")][0]  # the oldest row inside the last 7 days
print(f"oldest value used at {day}: rolling(168) -> {first_by_rows},  rolling('7D') -> {first_by_time}")
print(f"rolling(168) = {by_rows[day]:,.1f}   rolling('7D') = {by_time[day]:,.1f}")
raw = taxi_hourly(["2023-01", "2023-02", "2023-03"]) # the 02:00 hour is absent here by_rows = raw.rolling(168).mean() by_time = raw.rolling("7D").mean() day = "2023-03-14 12:00" t = pd.Timestamp(day) first_by_rows = raw.index[raw.index.get_loc(t) - 167] # the oldest of the last 168 rows first_by_time = raw.index[raw.index > t - pd.Timedelta("7D")][0] # the oldest row inside the last 7 days print(f"oldest value used at {day}: rolling(168) -> {first_by_rows}, rolling('7D') -> {first_by_time}") print(f"rolling(168) = {by_rows[day]:,.1f} rolling('7D') = {by_time[day]:,.1f}") 
oldest value used at 2023-03-14 12:00: rolling(168) -> 2023-03-07 12:00:00,  rolling('7D') -> 2023-03-07 13:00:00
rolling(168) = 4,688.5   rolling('7D') = 4,681.1

With a hole in the data, "the last 168 observations" reach one hour further back in time than "the last seven days". Regularise first (as we did), then both mean the same thing.

1. Why aggregate trips into hourly counts instead of forecasting trip by trip?

A forecast needs a regular series with a fixed grain; individual trips are irregular events. The grain should match the decision: dispatchers plan cabs by the hour, so hourly counts are the natural unit. A coarser grain (daily) would hide the within-day pattern they care about, and a finer one (per minute) would be mostly noise.

2. Sunday 12 March 2023 has a lower total than the Sundays either side of it. Name one reason that is not about demand.

It has only 23 hours: the clocks moved forward and 02:00 never existed. Part of the dip is a calendar artefact, which is why a model fed raw daily totals should know about such dates (or work in UTC).

3. You see a gap of 36 hours in a sensor series. List two quite different things it could mean and how each changes the fix.

(a) The sensor was offline: the true value is unknown, so interpolating invents data. Better to leave it missing, or model the series with the gap, or drop the affected period. (b) Nothing happened, so the value is genuinely zero, such as no sales on a closed day: fill with 0. The same NaN needs a different treatment depending on the meaning, which you must find out from whoever produced the data.

Compute the average number of pickups for each hour of the day on weekdays and on weekends separately. At which hour is the weekend ahead of the weekday? Predict first. 
by = y.groupby([y.index.dayofweek >= 5, y.index.hour]).mean().unstack(0)
by.columns = ["weekday", "weekend"]
ahead = by.index[by["weekend"] > by["weekday"]]
print(list(ahead))

The weekend is ahead at hours 0 to 4 (by a wide margin: about 5,400 against 1,800 pickups at midnight), and also, narrowly, at 1pm and 11pm. At night people are travelling home from an evening out, while weekday daytime is dominated by commuting and business trips. Two groups of days with different daily shapes is exactly why a single "hour of day" feature is not enough and a model also needs the day of week.

Resample to weekly totals but keep only the weeks that have all 168 hours. 
w = y.resample("W")
full_weeks = w.sum()[w.size() == 168]
print(len(full_weeks), "complete weeks")

Of the 14 week-bins, 12 are complete: the first (only 1 January) and the last (27 to 31 March) are partial. Filtering on the bucket size is the safe way to drop them.

Convert the series to UTC. Does the daylight-saving gap disappear? What happens to the hour-of-day feature? 
raw = taxi_hourly(["2023-01", "2023-02", "2023-03"])
utc = raw.tz_localize("America/New_York").tz_convert("UTC")
print(utc.index.to_series().diff().value_counts())  # use the raw series: see text

On the raw series (before filling) the missing hour is a hole on the wall clock but not in UTC: all 2,158 steps are exactly one hour. After our interpolation the series contains an invented 02:00 on 12 March, a time that does not exist locally, so tz_localize raises an error complaining about a nonexistent time. That is a good argument for localising before filling. In UTC you would compute the "hour of day" feature from the local time (tz_convert("America/New_York").hour), not from the UTC hour.

docs.title: Time-Series Data: Index, Resampling and the Calendar¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Turn raw event records into a regular hourly series, filtering to the period first.
  • Resample to a coarser grain and detect partial buckets.
  • Find missing timestamps, explain a daylight-saving gap, and choose how to fill it.
  • Build lag and rolling-window columns and explain what each one looks like to a model.

Prerequisites: pandas basics (index, groupby). Dataset: NYC Taxi (Jan to Mar 2023). Time: about 30 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
A taxi dispatch team wants to know how many pickups to expect in each hour of tomorrow, so it can decide how many cabs to put on the road. The history it has is not a tidy table of hourly counts. It is millions of individual trips, each stamped with a pickup time. Turning that into a series you can forecast is the first job, and it is full of small traps: stray dates, hours that do not exist, and a calendar that is not as regular as it looks.

We use the New York City yellow-cab records (the TLC trip files). First, one month of raw trips.

docs.title: 1. From events to a series¶
docs.text: A time series is a value observed at regular times. Our events are irregular (one per trip), so we choose a grain, here one hour, and count the events in each bucket. floor("h") rounds each timestamp down to the hour, and value_counts counts per hour.

docs.title: 2. Resampling: changing the grain¶
docs.text: resample is groupby for time. Choose a coarser grain and say how to combine the values; for counts that is sum.

docs.title: 3. Missing timestamps and the clock¶
docs.text: A series on a regular grid has an entry for every hour. Does ours? asfreq("h") lays out the full grid and puts NaN wherever an hour is absent.

docs.title: 4. Windows and shifts¶
docs.text: Two operations carry most of the weight in time-series feature work. shift(k) moves the series down by k steps, so each row sees the value from k steps ago. rolling(w) computes a statistic over the last w steps.

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix A plot stretches back to 2008 stray timestamps outside the period filter to the period before aggregating First and last "weeks" look tiny resample("W") cuts at Sundays check .size() per bucket; drop or flag partial buckets A day has 23 or 25 hours daylight-saving change in a naive local clock model in UTC, or know the date and treat it Missing hours break lag features irregular grid asfreq to the regular grid, then fill deliberately rolling(n) and rolling("nD") disagree rows versus time regularise the grid first Slice s["a":"b"] includes b label slicing is inclusive remember it when counting rows

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Turn events into a series by choosing a grain and counting; filter to the intended period first.
  • A DatetimeIndex gives date-string slicing (end inclusive), resample and time-based windows.
  • Check bucket sizes (size()), partial buckets mislead.
  • Naive local timestamps hide daylight-saving gaps and repeats; know them, or model in UTC.
  • A gap is a modelling decision: interpolate, zero-fill or leave missing, depending on what it means.
  • shift and rolling are how history becomes features: the next pages are careful about which history is allowed.

Next: Trend, seasonality and stationarity.

docs.text:

from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf, adfuller, kpss

y = taxi_hourly(["2023-01", "2023-02", "2023-03"]).asfreq("h").interpolate()
daily = y.resample("D").sum()
print(len(y), "hourly values |", len(daily), "daily values")
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import MSTL, STL from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf, adfuller, kpss from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf y = taxi_hourly(["2023-01", "2023-02", "2023-03"]).asfreq("h").interpolate() daily = y.resample("D").sum() print(len(y), "hourly values |", len(daily), "daily values") 
2160 hourly values | 90 daily values
In [3]: Copied! 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.4))
ax.plot(daily.index, daily / 1000, lw=1, label="daily total")
ax.plot(daily.index, daily.rolling(7, center=True).mean() / 1000, lw=2.4, label="7-day centred mean")
ax.set(title="Daily yellow-cab pickups, January to March 2023", ylabel="thousands of pickups"); ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(daily.groupby(daily.index.month).mean().round(0).rename(lambda m: ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"][m - 1]).to_frame("mean pickups per day").T)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.4)) ax.plot(daily.index, daily / 1000, lw=1, label="daily total") ax.plot(daily.index, daily.rolling(7, center=True).mean() / 1000, lw=2.4, label="7-day centred mean") ax.set(title="Daily yellow-cab pickups, January to March 2023", ylabel="thousands of pickups"); ax.legend() plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() print(daily.groupby(daily.index.month).mean().round(0).rename(lambda m: ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"][m - 1]).to_frame("mean pickups per day").T) 
hour                       Jan        Feb        Mar
mean pickups per day 98,926.00 104,068.00 109,946.00

There is a clear upward drift: the average day in March has about 11% more pickups than in January. Over three months we cannot say whether that is a long-run trend, a seasonal recovery from the post-holiday winter lull, or a mix. That is a real limit of short histories: you cannot estimate a yearly seasonal pattern from less than two years of data, so we do not try.

The weekly saw-tooth is the weekly seasonality, and the dips are holidays.

In [4]: Copied! 
fit = MSTL(y, periods=(24, 168)).fit()
parts = pd.DataFrame({"observed": y, "trend": fit.trend,
                      "daily cycle (24 h)": fit.seasonal["seasonal_24"],
                      "weekly cycle (168 h)": fit.seasonal["seasonal_168"],
                      "remainder": fit.resid})

zoom = slice("2023-02-06", "2023-02-19")                 # two ordinary weeks
fig, axes = plt.subplots(5, 1, figsize=(10, 8.5), sharex=True)
for ax, col in zip(axes, parts.columns):
    ax.plot(parts.loc[zoom, col].index, parts.loc[zoom, col].to_numpy(), lw=1.1)
    ax.set_ylabel(col, rotation=0, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_title("MSTL decomposition of hourly pickups, 6 to 19 February 2023")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
fit = MSTL(y, periods=(24, 168)).fit() parts = pd.DataFrame({"observed": y, "trend": fit.trend, "daily cycle (24 h)": fit.seasonal["seasonal_24"], "weekly cycle (168 h)": fit.seasonal["seasonal_168"], "remainder": fit.resid}) zoom = slice("2023-02-06", "2023-02-19") # two ordinary weeks fig, axes = plt.subplots(5, 1, figsize=(10, 8.5), sharex=True) for ax, col in zip(axes, parts.columns): ax.plot(parts.loc[zoom, col].index, parts.loc[zoom, col].to_numpy(), lw=1.1) ax.set_ylabel(col, rotation=0, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9) axes[0].set_title("MSTL decomposition of hourly pickups, 6 to 19 February 2023") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Read the panels top to bottom. The daily cycle repeats identically every day. The weekly cycle is smaller but changes the daily shape between weekdays and weekends. The trend is nearly flat over two weeks. The remainder is what is left, and it is small next to the observed series.

How much of the variation does each part explain? Variances of components do not add up to exactly the total, because the parts are correlated with each other, but the shares are still a good guide.

In [5]: Copied! 
shares = (parts.drop(columns="observed").var() / parts["observed"].var()).round(3)
print(shares.to_string())
print(f"\nstd of the series: {y.std():,.0f} pickups per hour;  std of the remainder: {fit.resid.std():,.0f}")
assert shares["daily cycle (24 h)"] > 0.7 and shares["remainder"] < 0.05
shares = (parts.drop(columns="observed").var() / parts["observed"].var()).round(3) print(shares.to_string()) print(f"\nstd of the series: {y.std():,.0f} pickups per hour; std of the remainder: {fit.resid.std():,.0f}") assert shares["daily cycle (24 h)"] > 0.7 and shares["remainder"] < 0.05 
trend                  0.01
daily cycle (24 h)     0.82
weekly cycle (168 h)   0.15
remainder              0.01

std of the series: 2,431 pickups per hour;  std of the remainder: 252

The daily cycle accounts for roughly four-fifths of the variance, the weekly cycle for about one seventh, the trend and the remainder only about a percent each. After removing the two cycles the typical error is about 250 pickups an hour against a spread of about 2,400 in the raw series: a forecast that gets the cycles right is already close, and almost all of the forecasting skill lies in the seasonal structure. Keep that in mind when the models arrive.

Decomposition is a description, not a forecast

MSTL looks at the whole series, including the future of each point (it is a smoother). That is fine for understanding the data, and wrong for building features that a model will use at prediction time. For forecasting, every number must be computable from the past alone.

In [6]: Copied! 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4))
plot_acf(y, lags=24 * 8, ax=axes[0], zero=False, title="Hourly pickups: autocorrelation up to 8 days")
plot_acf(fit.resid, lags=24 * 3, ax=axes[1], zero=False, title="Remainder after removing both cycles")
for ax in axes: ax.set_xlabel("lag (hours)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

a = acf(y, nlags=168)
r = acf(fit.resid, nlags=48)
print("pickups:   lag 1 = %.2f, lag 12 = %.2f, lag 24 = %.2f, lag 168 = %.2f" % (a[1], a[12], a[24], a[168]))
print("remainder: lag 1 = %.2f, lag 2 = %.2f, lag 24 = %.2f" % (r[1], r[2], r[24]))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4)) plot_acf(y, lags=24 * 8, ax=axes[0], zero=False, title="Hourly pickups: autocorrelation up to 8 days") plot_acf(fit.resid, lags=24 * 3, ax=axes[1], zero=False, title="Remainder after removing both cycles") for ax in axes: ax.set_xlabel("lag (hours)") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() a = acf(y, nlags=168) r = acf(fit.resid, nlags=48) print("pickups: lag 1 = %.2f, lag 12 = %.2f, lag 24 = %.2f, lag 168 = %.2f" % (a[1], a[12], a[24], a[168])) print("remainder: lag 1 = %.2f, lag 2 = %.2f, lag 24 = %.2f" % (r[1], r[2], r[24])) 
pickups:   lag 1 = 0.94, lag 12 = -0.68, lag 24 = 0.89, lag 168 = 0.90
remainder: lag 1 = 0.74, lag 2 = 0.49, lag 24 = -0.17

Left: the correlation swings up and down with a 24-hour rhythm; at 12 hours it is strongly negative (day versus night) and at 24 hours strongly positive. The value at lag 168 is as high as at lag 24, so the same hour last week is as informative as the same hour yesterday, and it also has the right weekday.

Right: the remainder is not white noise. Its lag-1 autocorrelation is about 0.74: if demand is a bit above the pattern this hour, it is probably above it next hour too (a rainy evening, a concert letting out). That short-run momentum is information a model can use, but only when the forecast is made one hour ahead. When forecasting a full day ahead, those recent values are not yet known, a point that returns on the feature-engineering and backtesting pages.

In [7]: Copied! 
def stationarity(name, s):
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")                    # KPSS warns when its p-value is off its lookup table
        adf_p = adfuller(s, autolag="AIC")[1]
        kpss_p = kpss(s, regression="c", nlags="auto")[1]
    verdict = {(True, True): "stationary (both agree)", (False, False): "NOT stationary (both agree)"}.get(
        (adf_p < 0.05, kpss_p >= 0.05), "tests disagree")
    return {"series": name, "ADF p": adf_p, "KPSS p": kpss_p, "verdict": verdict}

table = pd.DataFrame([
    stationarity("daily totals", daily),
    stationarity("daily totals, differenced once", daily.diff().dropna()),
    stationarity("daily totals, seasonal difference (7)", daily.diff(7).dropna()),
    stationarity("hourly pickups", y),
    stationarity("hourly, seasonal difference (24)", y.diff(24).dropna()),
    stationarity("hourly, seasonal difference (168)", y.diff(168).dropna()),
]).set_index("series")
table.style.format({"ADF p": "{:.4f}", "KPSS p": "{:.3f}"})
def stationarity(name, s): with warnings.catch_warnings(): warnings.simplefilter("ignore") # KPSS warns when its p-value is off its lookup table adf_p = adfuller(s, autolag="AIC")[1] kpss_p = kpss(s, regression="c", nlags="auto")[1] verdict = {(True, True): "stationary (both agree)", (False, False): "NOT stationary (both agree)"}.get( (adf_p < 0.05, kpss_p >= 0.05), "tests disagree") return {"series": name, "ADF p": adf_p, "KPSS p": kpss_p, "verdict": verdict} table = pd.DataFrame([ stationarity("daily totals", daily), stationarity("daily totals, differenced once", daily.diff().dropna()), stationarity("daily totals, seasonal difference (7)", daily.diff(7).dropna()), stationarity("hourly pickups", y), stationarity("hourly, seasonal difference (24)", y.diff(24).dropna()), stationarity("hourly, seasonal difference (168)", y.diff(168).dropna()), ]).set_index("series") table.style.format({"ADF p": "{:.4f}", "KPSS p": "{:.3f}"}) Out[7]: ADF p KPSS p verdict series daily totals 0.1206 0.010 NOT stationary (both agree) daily totals, differenced once 0.0000 0.100 stationary (both agree) daily totals, seasonal difference (7) 0.0011 0.100 stationary (both agree) hourly pickups 0.0000 0.010 tests disagree hourly, seasonal difference (24) 0.0000 0.100 stationary (both agree) hourly, seasonal difference (168) 0.0000 0.018 tests disagree

(KPSS reports p-values only between 0.01 and 0.10; a printed 0.010 means "0.01 or smaller" and 0.100 means "0.10 or larger".)

Several lessons are in this table.

  1. Daily totals: ADF cannot reject a unit root and KPSS rejects stationarity. Both say not stationary, as the drift and the weekly cycle suggest.
  2. Differencing fixes it. Replacing each value with its change from the previous one (or from the same weekday last week) gives a series both tests accept as stationary.
  3. The hourly series is a case where the tests disagree. ADF rejects a unit root while KPSS rejects stationarity. A strong deterministic seasonal pattern is not a unit root, so ADF is satisfied, but the mean is certainly not constant over the day, so KPSS objects. When tests disagree, trust the plot and the context, not one p-value.
  4. Subtracting the value 24 hours ago removes the daily cycle and both tests are satisfied. Subtracting the value 168 hours ago, which also removes the weekly cycle, leaves ADF satisfied but KPSS still objecting (p = 0.018): the upward drift is still there. Even a good seasonal difference does not settle the question.

Do not over-trust these tests

With 90 days of data the tests have limited power, p-values are sensitive to the number of lags tried, and "stationary" is a property of a model assumption, not a fact about the world. Use them to guide decisions such as how much to difference, then judge the decision by out-of-sample forecast error (the backtesting page).

1. The autocorrelation of the hourly series at lag 12 is strongly negative. Why?

Twelve hours apart is day versus night: a busy afternoon hour pairs with a quiet small-hours hour, so when one is above the mean the other tends to be below. A negative value at half the period is a typical signature of a strong cycle.

2. The remainder's lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.74. Does this mean you can forecast tomorrow's remainder well?

No. It means the remainder one hour ahead is predictable once you have seen this hour. Forecasting a whole day ahead you do not know today's recent remainders for the hours you are predicting, and the correlation decays with the lag (it was already down to 0.49 at lag 2). Predictability depends on the forecast horizon, not just on the series.

3. A colleague says: ‘ADF p < 0.05 so the series is stationary, no need to difference.’ What do you ask?

Ask what KPSS says, what the plot shows, and what the test was run on. ADF's null is a unit root, so rejecting it does not prove a constant mean: a strongly seasonal series can pass ADF and still have a clearly time-varying mean, as the hourly row above shows. Then check whether differencing improves out-of-sample error rather than relying on the test.

Decompose the daily series with STL(daily, period=7, robust=True) and report the weekly pattern as a table. Which weekday is quietest and which is busiest? Does anything about the answer give you pause? 
stl = STL(daily, period=7, robust=True).fit()
week = stl.seasonal.groupby(stl.seasonal.index.day_name()).mean().round(0)
print(week.sort_values())

The quietest weekday is Monday (about 16,000 pickups below the level, with Sunday next at about 13,000 below) and the busiest is Thursday (about 10,000 above, with Saturday and Friday close behind). Pause: three of the thirteen Mondays in the sample were public holidays (2 January, 16 January, 20 February), which pulls the Monday figure down. The seasonal estimate mixes weekday and holiday effects, which is why holidays become explicit inputs on the last page of this track.

How much does seasonal differencing at lag 168 reduce the standard deviation of the hourly series? What does that say about a forecast that simply repeats last week? 
print(y.std(), y.diff(168).std(), y.diff(168).std() / y.std())

The standard deviation falls from about 2,430 to about 520, roughly a fifth of the original. The differenced series is the error of the forecast "same hour last week" (up to sign), so that trivial forecast already removes about four fifths of the spread. Any model has to beat this very strong baseline, and the next page turns it into a proper benchmark.

Take the logarithm of the hourly series (add 1 to avoid log of zero if needed) and check whether the weekly seasonal amplitude looks more constant across months than in the raw series. 
for name, s in [("raw", y), ("log", np.log(y))]:
    amp = s.groupby(s.index.month).apply(lambda m: m.groupby([m.index.dayofweek, m.index.hour]).mean().std())
    print(name, amp.round(3).to_dict())

The raw weekly-pattern amplitude grows month by month (about 2,320, 2,400, 2,490 pickups, up 7%, tracking the 11% rise in the level), while the logged version is flat (about 0.98 each month). So the seasonal swing scales with the level: the pattern is mildly multiplicative, and modelling the log of demand would remove the interaction. With a difference this small an additive model is still adequate, which is why we keep the raw scale for readability.

docs.title: Trend, Seasonality and Stationarity¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Decompose a series with two seasonal periods and report how much variance each part carries.
  • Read an autocorrelation plot to identify seasonal periods and remaining memory.
  • Run ADF and KPSS together, and explain why they can disagree.
  • Choose between ordinary and seasonal differencing, and say what three months of data can and cannot show.

Prerequisites: Page 1 of this track. Dataset: NYC Taxi (Jan to Mar 2023). Time: about 30 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
Before choosing a forecasting method you need to know what is in the series. Is demand drifting up? Which repeating cycles does it have, and how strong are they? Is what remains after removing them just noise, or does it still have structure a model can use? This page answers those questions for New York taxi demand, and introduces stationarity, a property that several classical models assume.

We use the same January to March 2023 hourly series as before.

docs.title: 1. Trend, seasonality and the rest¶
docs.text:
A common way to think about a series is as a sum of three parts:

$$y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t$$

the trend $T_t$ (slow movement of the level), the seasonality $S_t$ (a pattern that repeats with a fixed period) and the remainder $R_t$ (everything else). If the seasonal swing grows with the level, a multiplicative form $y_t = T_t \times S_t \times R_t$ fits better, and taking logs turns it into the additive one.

Start with the daily totals and a 7-day rolling mean, which averages out the weekly cycle and so reveals the trend by eye.

docs.title: 2. Decomposing hourly demand with two seasons¶
docs.text: Hourly demand has two cycles at once: a daily one (period 24) and a weekly one (period 168). MSTL (multiple seasonal-trend decomposition using Loess) peels off several seasonal periods in turn.

docs.title: 3. Autocorrelation: how much does the past say about now?¶
docs.text: The autocorrelation function gives, for each lag $k$, the correlation between $y_t$ and $y_{t-k}$. It shows both the memory of the series and its seasonal periods.

docs.title: 4. Stationarity¶
docs.text:
A series is (weakly) stationary if its mean and variance are constant over time and the correlation between two points depends only on the gap between them. Classical models such as ARIMA are built for stationary series. Trend and seasonality break stationarity, because the mean moves.

Two standard tests, which ask opposite questions:

  • ADF (augmented Dickey-Fuller): the null hypothesis is a unit root (non-stationary). A small p-value rejects it, which suggests stationarity.
  • KPSS: the null hypothesis is stationary. A small p-value rejects it, which suggests non-stationarity.

Run both on several versions of the series.

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix Trend estimated from 3 months "keeps rising" too short to separate trend from yearly seasonality state the limit; do not extrapolate a trend you cannot tell from a season Decomposition used as a model feature smoothers use the future compute features only from the past (lags, causal rolling windows) ADF and KPSS disagree seasonality is not a unit root; low power look at the plot, difference as needed, judge by forecast error Multiplicative pattern fitted additively seasonal swing grows with the level model the log of the series Autocorrelation plot looks cyclic seasonality read the lag of the peaks: they are the periods

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• A series is trend + seasonality + remainder; here the two seasons (daily, weekly) carry nearly all the variance.
  • MSTL handles several seasonal periods. Decompositions describe; they must not be used as features, because they look at the future.
  • ACF reveals memory and periods. The remainder still has short-run memory, usable only at short horizons.
  • Stationarity: ADF and KPSS ask opposite questions, and can disagree. Differencing (ordinary or seasonal) is the standard remedy.
  • Three months cannot support a trend or a yearly pattern claim.

Next: Baselines: the forecasts to beat.

How to read the metrics. MAE (mean absolute error) is in the units we care about: pickups per hour. RMSE punishes large misses more. sMAPE is a percentage error. MASE divides the MAE by the error that "same hour last week" made on the training period, so 1.0 means "as good as that baseline did historically" and anything below 1 is better. (The next-but-three page explains why percentage errors are risky; here they are a rough guide.)

The ranking is a staircase, and each step teaches something:

  1. Repeating the last value is hopeless for a day-ahead forecast (MASE above 7): the series swings by thousands within a day, so "now" says little about "twelve hours from now". It is the right baseline for series without a cycle, such as a stock price, and the wrong one here.
  2. Same hour yesterday removes the daily cycle, but is still poor.
  3. Same hour last week respects the weekly cycle too and cuts the error roughly in half again.
  4. Averaging the last four weeks is better still: one week's values are noisy (a rainy Tuesday, a holiday), and averaging four of them smooths the noise.

So a four-week seasonal average is the number to beat: roughly 280 pickups an hour of error, about 7% in sMAPE.

On the Tuesday both forecasts have the right shape, but "same hour yesterday" runs low all day, because it copies a Monday and Mondays are quieter. On the Saturday it is wrong in shape: it copies a Friday, which has quiet small hours, while a Saturday starts the day still busy with people coming home from Friday night, and the morning ramp arrives later. The four-week average, which has seen several Saturdays, tracks the curve closely.

Monday (copying a Sunday), Saturday (copying a Friday) and Sunday (copying a Saturday) are the worst, with errors of 900 to 1,250; Wednesday and Thursday, which copy a similar weekday, are the best at about 270 to 360. Forecasting a Monday from a Sunday, or a Saturday from a Friday, copies the wrong kind of day. Errors are not spread evenly: they concentrate at the transitions of the weekly cycle. That is also the best argument for always reporting error broken down by something meaningful (weekday, hour, season) rather than one average.

Out[7]: weeks averaged (k) 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 validation MAE 283 298 311 316 321 329 336 346 test MAE 372 318 296 277 261 262 257 255

The two windows disagree completely. On the validation fortnight, the shortest memory wins (k = 1) and longer averages get steadily worse; on the test fortnight the opposite happens (longer is better, and k = 1 is the worst of all). Demand was drifting upward through March, which rewards recent weeks in one window, while in the other the single week we copy from happens to be an unusual one.

Three lessons:

  1. A choice made on one window may not carry to the next. If we had used k = 1 as chosen on validation we would have scored about 370 on the test, worse than every longer average. This is why a single holdout is fragile, and the backtesting page uses many windows.
  2. Do not pick k on the test window and then quote its score. Here it would have given the flattering figure of about 255, which the validation procedure would never have found.
  3. The curve is flat from k = 4 to 8 on the test window, within about 10%. When the differences are that small compared with the window-to-window noise, choosing a middle value (4) and moving on is the sensible response.
