worst hours: {18: 515.0, 17: 494.0, 15: 443.0} | quietest-hours error: {4: 95.0, 5: 49.0, 6: 105.0}

The absolute error is largest in the evening peak (5 to 7pm, about 430 to 520 pickups) and smallest at 4 to 6am (about 50 to 105). That is natural: more demand means more room to be wrong in absolute terms. But relative to demand the picture flips: at 2 to 4am the error is 13 to 18% of the demand, against about 5% in the middle of the day. That is exactly the trap in percentage errors, discussed on the metrics page.

The baseline is a deliverable, not a formality

Keep the baseline in the project forever. It is the line every later model is measured against, and the fallback when a model breaks. If your model beats it by a little, say so honestly: the cost of running a complex model has to be paid for.

1. What does a MASE of 0.80 for the four-week average tell you, and what would 1.00 mean?

The model's mean absolute error is 80% of the error that the "same hour last week" forecast made on the training data. So it is 20% better than that reference. A value of 1.00 would mean no better than that reference, and a value above 1 would mean worse. MASE is useful because it needs no division by the (possibly near-zero) actual values and it compares series of very different sizes.

2. The seasonal-naive-168 forecast scores MASE 1.08 on the test fortnight although MASE is defined relative to its own training error. Is the test period harder than the training period?

Slightly, or about the same: 1.08 says its test error is 8% larger than its in-sample error scaled the same way. The test fortnight is not much harder than the training period, so differences between models there are not an artefact of an unusually difficult stretch. A value far from 1 for the reference baseline itself would be a warning that the test window is unrepresentative.

3. A teammate reports: ‘I tried 20 smoothing settings and the best one scores 240 on the test fortnight, beating the baseline’s 277.’ What is wrong with that claim?

The best of 20 attempts is selected using the test data, so its score is optimistically biased, as the table above showed (255 chosen on test versus 372 for the value validation picked). The fix is to choose among the 20 settings on a validation window and report the single chosen setting on the test, ideally across several test windows. Even a real improvement of about 13% needs that protocol to be believable.

Replace the mean with the median of the last 4 weeks (statistic='median'). Predict first: better, worse, or the same? Then compare the scores. 
f = lambda hist, idx: fc.seasonal_mean(hist, idx, weeks=4, statistic="median")
print(fc.score(fc.backtest(y, f, origins=test_origins, horizon=HORIZON), train))

On these data the median and the mean give the same score to the nearest pickup (about 277). The median helps when one of the four weeks is badly off (a snowstorm or a holiday); here the test fortnight had no such week, so there is nothing for it to protect against. It would matter for a window containing a public holiday.

Build a profile baseline: forecast each hour with the all-history mean for that weekday and hour. How does it compare with the four-week average? Why might it not do better, given it uses more data? 
def profile(hist, idx):
    g = hist.groupby([hist.index.dayofweek, hist.index.hour]).mean()
    return pd.Series([g[(t.dayofweek, t.hour)] for t in idx], index=idx)
print(fc.score(fc.backtest(y, profile, origins=test_origins, horizon=HORIZON), train)["MAE"])

It scores about 282, practically the same as the four-week average (277). More data does not help much because the level drifts (about 11% higher in March than in January, as the previous page showed), so old weeks are slightly out of date. A real model must be able to follow the level, not just the shape.

For the naive (last value) forecast, how does the average error change with how far ahead we predict (step 1 to 24)? Why is it not a steadily rising line? 
bt = runs["naive: repeat the last value"]
print(bt.assign(e=(bt.actual - bt.forecast).abs()).groupby("step")["e"].mean().round(0).tolist())

The error is about 1,400 at step 1 and rises to nearly 3,900 at steps 5 and 6 (4am and 5am), then falls to about 2,100 to 2,500 across the middle of the day, climbs again to about 3,500 at step 19 (6pm) and ends near 1,200 at step 24. The forecast is stuck at the 11pm level, which is fairly busy, so it overshoots badly when demand bottoms out at 4 to 5am and undershoots in the evening peak; it is nearly right only where the daily curve happens to cross that level. The error follows the daily cycle, not the horizon.

docs.title: Baselines: The Forecasts to Beat¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Set up a rolling-origin test in which a forecaster can only see the past.
  • Compute naive, seasonal-naive and seasonal-average baselines and rank them with MAE, RMSE and MASE.
  • Explain why a baseline tuned on the test window gives an optimistic score.
  • Break forecast error down by weekday and hour to see where a forecast fails.

Prerequisites: Pages 1 and 2 of this track. Dataset: NYC Taxi (Jan to Mar 2023). Time: about 35 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
The dispatch team asks for one thing: at midnight, a forecast of pickups for each of the next 24 hours. Before building anything clever, we need two things. First, a precise protocol for testing a forecast so that nobody, including us, can cheat. Second, a set of baselines: very simple forecasts that any real model has to beat. If a sophisticated model cannot beat "same as last week", it is not worth running.

We use the January to March 2023 hourly series. The last two weeks (18 to 31 March) are held back for testing.

docs.title: 1. The protocol: a rolling-origin test¶
docs.text:
At each origin (a midnight) the forecaster may look at the history strictly before the origin and must predict the next 24 hours. Then the clock moves on one day and we repeat. This mimics how the forecast will really be used: every night, with the data that exists that night. fc.backtest enforces it: it hands the forecaster only the past, and the unit tests in the repository check that.

A forecaster here is any function f(history, target_times) that returns one number per target time. Our baselines are one-liners.

docs.title: 2. Where does "same hour yesterday" go wrong?¶
docs.text: Break its error down by the weekday being forecast. Each forecast copies the day before, so Monday is forecast from Sunday, Saturday from Friday, and so on.

docs.title: 3. Tuning a baseline, honestly¶
docs.text:
"Average of the last k weeks": what should k be? The tempting move is to try every k on the test window and keep the best. That is tuning on the test set, and the number you report is then optimistic. The honest way: pick k on a validation window that comes before the test window, then report the test score once.

The validation window is the two weeks just before the test: 4 to 17 March.

docs.title: 4. When is the baseline wrong?¶
docs.text: A final look at the best baseline: its absolute error by hour of day (averaged over the 14 test days).

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix "Naive" forecast has a huge error wrong baseline for a seasonal series use seasonal naive with the right period Great test score after trying many settings tuned on the test window choose settings on a validation window before the test Best setting differs between windows few windows, drift evaluate on many origins; prefer a flat region of the curve One bad week hurts "last week" forecast a single week is noisy average several weeks (or take the median) One average error hides the pattern errors cluster at weekday and hour transitions always break error down by weekday and hour

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Test forecasts with a rolling origin: at each origin, only the past is visible. Report an average over many origins.
  • Seasonal naive (same hour last week) and a multi-week seasonal average are strong baselines for strongly seasonal series. Plain naive is only right for series without a cycle.
  • Here the four-week average gets about 280 pickups of error (MASE 0.80), the number every model must beat.
  • Do not tune on the test window: choose settings on an earlier validation window. One validation window can still mislead, which motivates backtesting over many windows.
  • Break errors down by weekday and hour: they cluster at the transitions.

Next: Classical models: exponential smoothing and ARIMA.

Read the table in groups.

  • Models with no seasonal part are stuck at the naive forecast's level (MASE 2.0 to 2.1), or barely better. They have no way to represent the weekly cycle, so the best they can do is a flat line. The level-only smoother does exactly what the naive forecast does; look at why:
In [4]: Copied! 
fit = ExponentialSmoothing(train_d, initialization_method="estimated").fit()
print("smoothing weight alpha chosen for the level-only model:", round(fit.params["smoothing_level"], 3))
print("MAE: level-only ETS =", round(table.loc["ETS(A,N,N): level only", "MAE"]), "| naive =", round(table.loc["naive (last value)", "MAE"]))

smoothing weight alpha chosen for the level-only model: 1.0
MAE: level-only ETS = 11267 | naive = 11267

The fitted weight is 1.0: "trust only the latest value", which is the naive forecast. The data told the optimiser that, without a seasonal term, nothing beats the last value.

  • Adding the weekly season is what matters. ETS(A,N,A) cuts the error by about 18% relative to seasonal naive (MASE 0.86 against 1.05). The weekly pattern is learned from all the weeks with smoothing, rather than copied from one week.
  • Multiplicative seasonality is a little worse than additive here, consistent with the mild scaling we saw earlier, and not worth the extra complexity.
  • Ordinary ARIMA(1,1,1) gains almost nothing (MASE 1.98 against 2.11). Seasonal ARIMA is on par with the seasonal naive forecast (MASE about 1.0): it also learns the weekly season, but its estimates from only 62 training days are noisy.

How would you check whether a fitted SARIMA has captured the structure? Look at the residuals. If the model is adequate they should look like noise; the Ljung-Box test checks that formally (null hypothesis: no autocorrelation up to the lag tested).

print(sarima.summary().tables[1].as_text()[:520])
acorr_ljungbox(resid, lags=[7, 14])

The p-values are tiny: the residuals still contain autocorrelation, so this SARIMA has not captured everything. (The usual reaction is to try more terms; with 62 observations that quickly overfits, which is what the backtest is for.) Diagnostics suggest where a model is deficient. The backtest tells you whether the deficiency matters for forecasting.

ETS with 168 seasonal states is sensitive to how much history you give it: even at its best (the last 4 weeks, MAE 331) it is about 20% worse than the baseline's 277, and with 8 weeks (395) it is clearly worse. Having more data makes it worse, because its level and smoothing weights have to adapt to a drifting series. That sensitivity is a warning sign: a model whose quality changes this much with a setting that has no principled value is hard to trust.

The second route is harmonic regression: describe the seasonal shape with a handful of sine and cosine terms (Fourier terms) and let ARIMA model what is left.

In [7]: Copied! 
def fourier(index, k24, k168):
    t = (index - pd.Timestamp("2023-01-01")).total_seconds().to_numpy() / 3600
    cols = {}
    for period, k in ((24, k24), (168, k168)):
        for j in range(1, k + 1):
            cols[f"sin_{period}_{j}"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * j * t / period)
            cols[f"cos_{period}_{j}"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * j * t / period)
    return pd.DataFrame(cols, index=index)

def regression_arma(make_exog, order=(1, 0, 0), weeks=6, method="lbfgs"):
    """Seasonality from a regression on exogenous columns, short-term memory from ARMA errors."""
    counter = {"fits": 0, "not_converged": 0}
    def forecaster(hist, idx):
        hist = hist.iloc[-168 * weeks:]
        with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
            warnings.simplefilter("always")
            model = SARIMAX(hist, exog=make_exog(hist.index), order=order, trend="c").fit(disp=False, maxiter=200, method=method)
        counter["fits"] += 1
        counter["not_converged"] += any(issubclass(w.category, ConvergenceWarning) for w in caught)
        return model.forecast(len(idx), exog=make_exog(idx)).to_numpy()
    forecaster.counter = counter
    return forecaster

harmonic = regression_arma(lambda idx: fourier(idx, 10, 10), order=(1, 0, 0), method="powell")
bt_h = fc.backtest(y, harmonic, origins=test_origins, horizon=H)
print("Fourier terms (10 daily + 10 weekly harmonics) + AR(1) errors:", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in fc.score(bt_h, train).items()})
print("fits that did not converge:", harmonic.counter["not_converged"], "of", harmonic.counter["fits"])
def fourier(index, k24, k168): t = (index - pd.Timestamp("2023-01-01")).total_seconds().to_numpy() / 3600 cols = {} for period, k in ((24, k24), (168, k168)): for j in range(1, k + 1): cols[f"sin_{period}_{j}"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * j * t / period) cols[f"cos_{period}_{j}"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * j * t / period) return pd.DataFrame(cols, index=index) def regression_arma(make_exog, order=(1, 0, 0), weeks=6, method="lbfgs"): """Seasonality from a regression on exogenous columns, short-term memory from ARMA errors.""" counter = {"fits": 0, "not_converged": 0} def forecaster(hist, idx): hist = hist.iloc[-168 * weeks:] with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught: warnings.simplefilter("always") model = SARIMAX(hist, exog=make_exog(hist.index), order=order, trend="c").fit(disp=False, maxiter=200, method=method) counter["fits"] += 1 counter["not_converged"] += any(issubclass(w.category, ConvergenceWarning) for w in caught) return model.forecast(len(idx), exog=make_exog(idx)).to_numpy() forecaster.counter = counter return forecaster harmonic = regression_arma(lambda idx: fourier(idx, 10, 10), order=(1, 0, 0), method="powell") bt_h = fc.backtest(y, harmonic, origins=test_origins, horizon=H) print("Fourier terms (10 daily + 10 weekly harmonics) + AR(1) errors:", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in fc.score(bt_h, train).items()}) print("fits that did not converge:", harmonic.counter["not_converged"], "of", harmonic.counter["fits"]) 
Fourier terms (10 daily + 10 weekly harmonics) + AR(1) errors: {'MAE': 518.497, 'RMSE': 655.478, 'sMAPE': 0.21, 'MASE': 1.501}
fits that did not converge: 0 of 14

The harmonic version is much worse than the baseline (MAE about 520 against 277), and this is not an optimiser failure: we used a method (Powell) that converged on all 14 fits. (With the default optimiser, 14 of 14 fits of this model reported no convergence in my tests, a reminder to count the warnings rather than silence them.) Twenty smooth waves cannot reproduce the sharp edges of the real weekly shape: the sudden morning ramp, the evening peak, the Friday-night surge. Adding harmonics is a bias-variance trade: too few lose the shape, too many chase noise and slow the fit.

When the season is as short as one week, there is an exact alternative: a separate regression coefficient for each of the 168 weekday-hour slots (dummy variables), with AR errors on top.

In [8]: Copied! 
def slot_dummies(index):
    slot = pd.Series(index.dayofweek * 24 + index.hour, index=index).astype("category")
    return pd.get_dummies(slot).astype(float).reindex(columns=range(168), fill_value=0.0)

slots = regression_arma(slot_dummies, order=(1, 0, 0))
bt_s = fc.backtest(y, lambda hist, idx: slots(hist, idx), origins=test_origins, horizon=H)
six_week = fc.backtest(y, lambda hist, idx: fc.seasonal_mean(hist, idx, weeks=6), origins=test_origins, horizon=H)

compare = pd.DataFrame({
    "4-week seasonal average": fc.score(four_week, train),
    "6-week seasonal average": fc.score(six_week, train),
    "168 slot dummies + AR(1) errors (6 weeks)": fc.score(bt_s, train),
}).T
print("fits that did not converge:", slots.counter["not_converged"], "of", slots.counter["fits"])
compare.style.format({"MAE": "{:,.0f}", "RMSE": "{:,.0f}", "sMAPE": "{:.1%}", "MASE": "{:.2f}"})

fits that did not converge: 0 of 14
Out[8]: MAE RMSE sMAPE MASE 4-week seasonal average 277 381 7.1% 0.80 6-week seasonal average 262 375 6.7% 0.76 168 slot dummies + AR(1) errors (6 weeks) 262 364 7.2% 0.76

This is the first model to match the best baseline, and the comparison is instructive. The regression with AR errors scores essentially the same MAE as the plain six-week seasonal average (262 against 262), with a slightly lower RMSE. That is no accident: with a dummy for every weekday-hour slot, the regression's fitted values are seasonal averages over the training weeks. The only thing ARIMA adds is the AR(1) error term. Where does that help?

In [9]: Copied! 
by_step = pd.DataFrame({
    "6-week average": six_week.assign(e=(six_week["actual"] - six_week["forecast"]).abs()).groupby("step")["e"].mean(),
    "slot dummies + AR(1)": bt_s.assign(e=(bt_s["actual"] - bt_s["forecast"]).abs()).groupby("step")["e"].mean(),
})
by_step["gain"] = by_step["6-week average"] - by_step["slot dummies + AR(1)"]
for label, steps in [("steps 1-2", slice(1, 2)), ("steps 3-6", slice(3, 6)), ("steps 7-24", slice(7, 24))]:
    print(f"mean gain from the AR error term, {label:>10}: {by_step.loc[steps, 'gain'].mean():6.1f} pickups per hour")

h = y[:"2023-03-17"].iloc[-168 * 6:]                      # the AR coefficient of one fit, on the last 6 training weeks
phi = SARIMAX(h, exog=slot_dummies(h.index), order=(1, 0, 0), trend="c").fit(disp=False, maxiter=200).params["ar.L1"]
print(f"fitted AR(1) coefficient: {phi:.2f} per hour  ->  after 24 hours: {phi ** 24:.4f} of the initial deviation")
by_step.round(0).astype(int).T.iloc[:, :8]
by_step = pd.DataFrame({ "6-week average": six_week.assign(e=(six_week["actual"] - six_week["forecast"]).abs()).groupby("step")["e"].mean(), "slot dummies + AR(1)": bt_s.assign(e=(bt_s["actual"] - bt_s["forecast"]).abs()).groupby("step")["e"].mean(), }) by_step["gain"] = by_step["6-week average"] - by_step["slot dummies + AR(1)"] for label, steps in [("steps 1-2", slice(1, 2)), ("steps 3-6", slice(3, 6)), ("steps 7-24", slice(7, 24))]: print(f"mean gain from the AR error term, {label:>10}: {by_step.loc[steps, 'gain'].mean():6.1f} pickups per hour") h = y[:"2023-03-17"].iloc[-168 * 6:] # the AR coefficient of one fit, on the last 6 training weeks phi = SARIMAX(h, exog=slot_dummies(h.index), order=(1, 0, 0), trend="c").fit(disp=False, maxiter=200).params["ar.L1"] print(f"fitted AR(1) coefficient: {phi:.2f} per hour -> after 24 hours: {phi ** 24:.4f} of the initial deviation") by_step.round(0).astype(int).T.iloc[:, :8]

Out[9]: step 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 6-week average 209 203 135 127 83 52 95 249 slot dummies + AR(1) 184 189 149 138 101 49 97 252 gain 24 14 -14 -11 -18 2 -2 -3

The AR error term helps only in the first two hours after the origin (about 24 and 14 pickups), where the last observed deviation from the pattern is still fresh. It slightly hurts in steps 3 to 5, and from then on it does nothing, because the fitted coefficient of about 0.77 per hour leaves essentially nothing after a day. That is the same short memory that the autocorrelation plot of the remainder showed, and the net effect on a day-ahead forecast is zero: the MAE is 262 with and without it.

Do not oversell a 5% edge

The AR model scores about 5% better than the four-week average on this fortnight. But the six-week average does exactly as well, and the previous page showed that the best number of weeks flips between windows. Whether the classical model is really better needs many test windows, the job of the backtesting page. Do not conclude anything from 14 days.

1. The level-only exponential smoother chose a weight of exactly 1. What does that mean, and what forecast does it produce?

The level is updated to equal the newest observation each time, so the forecast for every future step is simply the last observed value: the naive forecast. When a series has a strong cycle and the model has no component for it, the optimiser finds that following the latest value is the least bad option.

2. Why can a model with 168 free seasonal coefficients still not beat a plain average of the same weeks?

Because that regression's coefficients are averages of the weeks it was fitted on, up to the weighting that the error model gives. A more flexible model only helps if it captures something the average misses: a trend, short-term momentum, holidays. Here the only extra it has is a momentum term that helps for two hours, so overall there is no gain.

3. A colleague says: ‘I’ll use ETS with a seasonal period of 168 on a year of hourly data.’ Name two practical concerns.

(1) Sensitivity and drift: as the table showed, how much history you give an ETS model changes its quality, and over a year demand levels change. (2) Cost and fragility: 168 seasonal states plus smoothing weights are estimated by an optimiser that can fail to converge or settle on poor values; and the model cannot take holidays or weather as inputs. Alternatives: a regression with calendar and holiday features plus a short-memory error model, or a gradient-boosting model on lag features.

On the daily series, let an automatic search pick the SARIMA order: try p, q in 0 to 2, P, Q in 0 to 1 with d=0, D=1, m=7, choose the lowest AIC on the training data only, and backtest it. Does AIC pick the model that forecasts best? 
import itertools
best = min(((SARIMAX(train_d, order=(p, 0, q), seasonal_order=(P, 1, Q, 7)).fit(disp=False).aic, (p, 0, q), (P, 1, Q, 7))
            for p, q, P, Q in itertools.product([0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2], [0, 1], [0, 1])), key=lambda t: t[0])
print(best)
bt = fc.backtest(daily, arima(best[1], best[2]), origins=origins, horizon=7)
print(fc.score(bt, train_d, m=7))

AIC is computed from the training fit, so it measures how well a model describes the past, not how well it forecasts. AIC picks SARIMA(1,0,1)(0,1,0,7). Its backtest MAE is about 5,470: a little better than the seasonal naive forecast (5,597), but worse than the hand-picked SARIMA(1,0,1)(0,1,1,7) (5,369), so the lower AIC did not buy a better forecast.

Change the training window of the slot-dummy model from 6 weeks to 4 and to 8. What happens, and what does it tell you? 
for weeks in (4, 6, 8):
    f = regression_arma(slot_dummies, order=(1, 0, 0), weeks=weeks)
    print(weeks, fc.score(fc.backtest(y, lambda h, i: f(h, i), origins=test_origins, horizon=24), train)["MAE"])

The error is about 278 with 4 weeks, 262 with 6 and 256 with 8: more history helps this form, the opposite of what happened to ETS with 168 states. Both are small differences next to the window-to-window noise, so treat them as a tendency, not a finding.

Fit the slot-dummy model with an AR(2) error instead of AR(1). Is it worth it? 
f = regression_arma(slot_dummies, order=(2, 0, 0))
print(fc.score(fc.backtest(y, lambda h, i: f(h, i), origins=test_origins, horizon=24), train)["MAE"])

The MAE is about 261 against 262: the extra term changes nothing meaningful. Simpler is better when the extra term does not improve out-of-sample error.

docs.title: Classical Models: ETS, ARIMA and Regression with ARMA Errors¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Fit exponential-smoothing and (S)ARIMA models and read what the fitted parameters mean.
  • Explain why a model without a seasonal component reduces to the naive forecast.
  • Handle a long seasonal period with regression terms plus ARMA errors, and check convergence.
  • Judge a classical model against a strong baseline without over-reading a small edge.

Prerequisites: Pages 1 to 3 of this track. Dataset: NYC Taxi (Jan to Mar 2023). Time: about 40 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
Baselines are set: a four-week same-hour average gets about 280 pickups an hour of error. Now we try the classical statistical models that dominated forecasting before machine learning, and which are still the right tool for many series: exponential smoothing (ETS) and ARIMA with its seasonal and regression extensions.

The aim is not to crown a winner but to learn what each family can and cannot do, and to see how much of the work is choosing a form that matches the seasonality.

docs.title: 1. The models on a simpler series: daily totals¶
docs.text:
Hourly data with a 168-hour season is awkward for these models (we return to that in section 2). So first learn them on daily totals, where the weekly season is just 7 steps. The task: at each midnight, forecast the next 7 days. We test on 21 origins from 4 to 24 March (a stretch with no public holidays), and compare with the same baselines as before.

Maths ↔ code

Exponential smoothing keeps a running level (and optionally a trend and a seasonal pattern) and updates each with a smoothing weight: the level is $\ell_t = \alpha\,(y_t - s_{t-m}) + (1-\alpha)\,\ell_{t-1}$ in the additive-seasonal form. A weight near 1 means "trust the latest value", near 0 means "trust the history". In code: ExponentialSmoothing(y, trend=, seasonal=, seasonal_periods=). The naming ETS(Error, Trend, Seasonal) uses A (additive), M (multiplicative) or N (none).

ARIMA(p, d, q) differences the series d times, then models what is left as p autoregressive terms plus q moving-average terms of past errors. SARIMA adds the same ideas at the seasonal lag: seasonal_order=(P, D, Q, m). SARIMAX also allows regressors X, with ARMA-modelled errors.

docs.title: 2. Back to hourly: the long-season problem¶
docs.text:
On hourly data the weekly season has 168 steps. ETS must estimate a state for each of the 168 positions, and a seasonal ARIMA with $m = 168$ is impractically slow. Two practical routes exist: let ETS keep its 168 seasonal states, or take the seasonality out of the ARIMA by handing it to a regression (the "X" in SARIMAX) and keeping ARMA only for the errors.

We go back to the 24-hour-ahead task and the 14 test origins (18 to 31 March) from the baselines page, and keep the best baseline in view.

docs.title: Which one when?¶
docs.text: Situation Reasonable first choice Why Short season (4, 7, 12), a few hundred points ETS or SARIMA few parameters, well understood, fast Long or several seasons (24 and 168) regression on calendar slots or harmonics + ARMA errors, or a seasonal average ETS/SARIMA states explode or become unstable No seasonality, noisy level ETS(A,N,N) or ARIMA what they were designed for Many related series a global ML model (next page) one model learns from all of them Needs an interpretable decomposition ETS level, trend and season are explicit

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix ETS or ARIMA forecast is a flat line no seasonal component for a seasonal series add the season (ETS seasonal=, SARIMA seasonal_order) or use regression for the season Smoothing weight is exactly 1 or 0 the model has found nothing to smooth read fit.params; it is information about the data Result changes a lot with history length adaptive states chase drift evaluate several training windows; prefer stabler forms ConvergenceWarning optimiser did not finish count them (as above), simplify the model, scale inputs, do not just silence them Residuals still autocorrelated model is missing structure diagnostics guide; the backtest decides if it matters 168 dummies is "too many parameters" it is 168 coefficients for ~1,000 points fine for a regression, but expect noise; compare against the plain seasonal average

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• ETS and ARIMA are fitted by optimisation. Without a seasonal part, neither beats naive on a strongly seasonal series.
  • ETS(A,N,A) with a weekly season beat seasonal naive by about 18% on daily totals; seasonal ARIMA only matched it.
  • With long seasons (24, 168) put the season in a regression and keep ARMA for the errors. Sharp daily shapes need slot dummies; a few harmonics are too smooth.
  • A model with a coefficient per slot is essentially a seasonal average, which is why it ties the equivalent baseline. The AR error term helps the first two hours and nets out to nothing over a day.
  • Diagnostics (residual autocorrelation, convergence counts) tell you what is wrong; the backtest tells you whether it matters.

Next: Machine-learning forecasts with lag and calendar features.

Look at one row in the table: for 08:00 on 1 February, lag_24 is demand at 08:00 on 31 January, lag_168 the same hour a week earlier, mean_24 the average of the 24 hours ending at 08:00 on 31 January (it is computed from the series shifted by 24, so it never touches the target hour, nor anything newer than a day before it), and same_hour_4w the four-week seasonal average, i.e. our best baseline offered to the model as one more column.

Training one model per forecast origin means fitting on rows whose target lies before the origin, then predicting the 24 rows after it. We reuse fc.backtest:

In [4]: Copied! 
def gbm_forecaster(cols=None, weeks=None, **params):
    cols = list(X.columns) if cols is None else cols
    settings = dict(max_iter=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, random_state=0) | params
    def forecaster(hist, idx):
        rows = X.loc[X.index.isin(hist.index), cols]
        if weeks:
            rows = rows.iloc[-168 * weeks:]
        rows = rows.dropna()                                   # the first weeks have no lag_504 yet
        model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(**settings).fit(rows, hist.loc[rows.index])
        return model.predict(X.loc[idx, cols])
    return forecaster

bt_gbm = fc.backtest(y, gbm_forecaster(), origins=test_origins, horizon=H)
pd.DataFrame({"4-week seasonal average": fc.score(four_week, train),

One column dominates: same_hour_4w, the four-week seasonal average we handed the model (shuffling it raises the error by about 1,580 pickups an hour; the next column, lag_336, by about 270). The hour and the weekday barely register, not because they are irrelevant but because same_hour_4w already encodes both: importance is shared out among redundant columns, so read it as "what the model leans on", not "what matters in the world". In effect the model has been given the baseline's answer and mostly echoes it.

To test that reading, drop feature groups and compare the backtest error. If the lag features carry real extra information, removing them should hurt.

    "all features": list(X.columns),

All five versions land in the same band, roughly 320 to 350. A model that sees only the hour and the weekday does as well as one with every lag. So the lag columns add essentially nothing on this data; the tree is learning a seasonal profile, and learning it less efficiently than a plain average does, because each of the 168 weekday-hour slots has only about ten training examples and a tree splits them noisily.

Does the amount of history matter?

In [7]: Copied! 
curve = {}
for weeks in (2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10):
    curve[weeks] = fc.score(fc.backtest(y, gbm_forecaster(weeks=weeks), origins=test_origins, horizon=H), train)["MAE"]
curve = pd.Series(curve, name="MAE")
curve.index.name = "weeks of training history"
curve.round(0).astype(int).to_frame().T
curve = {} for weeks in (2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10): curve[weeks] = fc.score(fc.backtest(y, gbm_forecaster(weeks=weeks), origins=test_origins, horizon=H), train)["MAE"] curve = pd.Series(curve, name="MAE") curve.index.name = "weeks of training history" curve.round(0).astype(int).to_frame().T Out[7]: weeks of training history 2 3 4 6 8 10 MAE 357 376 373 349 332 328

More history helps (about 375 with 3 to 4 weeks, about 330 with 8 to 10), though not smoothly. The learning curve is still falling at the longest window we can give it: with only 11 weeks in total, we cannot tell how far it would go. That is the real limitation here: a flexible model needs data. A seasonal average has one parameter per slot and needs almost none.

In [8]: Copied! 
X_leaky = X.copy()
X_leaky["lag_1"] = y.shift(1)                              # NOT available at forecast time for steps 2 to 24
X_leaky["mean_24_including_now"] = y.rolling(24).mean()    # window includes the target hour itself

def leaky_forecaster(extra):
    cols = list(X.columns) + extra
    def forecaster(hist, idx):
        rows = X_leaky.loc[X_leaky.index.isin(hist.index), cols].dropna()
        model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(rows, hist.loc[rows.index])
        return model.predict(X_leaky.loc[idx, cols])
    return forecaster

    "+ lag_1 (the previous hour)": fc.score(fc.backtest(y, leaky_forecaster(["lag_1"]), origins=test_origins, horizon=H), train),
    "+ 24-hour mean that includes the target hour": fc.score(fc.backtest(y, leaky_forecaster(["mean_24_including_now"]), origins=test_origins, horizon=H), train),
}
leak = pd.DataFrame(leak).T
leak.style.format({"MAE": "{:,.0f}", "RMSE": "{:,.0f}", "sMAPE": "{:.1%}", "MASE": "{:.2f}"})
X_leaky = X.copy() X_leaky["lag_1"] = y.shift(1) # NOT available at forecast time for steps 2 to 24 X_leaky["mean_24_including_now"] = y.rolling(24).mean() # window includes the target hour itself def leaky_forecaster(extra): cols = list(X.columns) + extra def forecaster(hist, idx): rows = X_leaky.loc[X_leaky.index.isin(hist.index), cols].dropna() model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(rows, hist.loc[rows.index]) return model.predict(X_leaky.loc[idx, cols]) return forecaster leak = { "honest (all legal features)": fc.score(bt_gbm, train), "+ lag_1 (the previous hour)": fc.score(fc.backtest(y, leaky_forecaster(["lag_1"]), origins=test_origins, horizon=H), train), "+ 24-hour mean that includes the target hour": fc.score(fc.backtest(y, leaky_forecaster(["mean_24_including_now"]), origins=test_origins, horizon=H), train), } leak = pd.DataFrame(leak).T leak.style.format({"MAE": "{:,.0f}", "RMSE": "{:,.0f}", "sMAPE": "{:.1%}", "MASE": "{:.2f}"}) Out[8]: MAE RMSE sMAPE MASE honest (all legal features) 328 437 9.0% 0.95 + lag_1 (the previous hour) 265 351 7.7% 0.77 + 24-hour mean that includes the target hour 318 424 9.0% 0.92

The lag_1 model looks about 20% better than the honest model, and the model with a window that includes the target hour a few percent better. Both numbers are fiction. In production, when we need the 15:00 forecast at midnight, the 14:00 value does not exist yet; and a window including the target hour contains the answer. The backtest passes the leaky columns because the whole series is in memory, which is why the make_features guard and the "origin sees only the past" rule in fc.backtest exist.

Notice that the second leak is subtle: a 24-hour rolling mean seems harmless, and it improved the score only a little. Small, quiet leaks are the dangerous kind, because they do not look suspicious. The only defence is the question "would this number exist at the moment of the forecast?", asked of every column.

Two ways to leak in time series

Using the future directly (a lag shorter than the horizon, a window that includes the target). Using it indirectly through preprocessing: scaling, imputing or selecting features with statistics computed over the whole series including the test period. Fit every transformation on the training window only, exactly as in the leakage section of the scikit-learn pipelines page.

In [9]: Copied! 
def recursive_forecaster(lags=(1, 2, 24, 168)):
    def forecaster(hist, idx):
        table = pd.DataFrame({"hour": hist.index.hour, "dayofweek": hist.index.dayofweek}, index=hist.index)
        for lag in lags:
            table[f"lag_{lag}"] = hist.shift(lag)
        table = table.dropna()
        model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(table, hist.loc[table.index])
        extended, out = hist.copy(), []
        for t in idx:
            row = {"hour": t.hour, "dayofweek": t.dayofweek} | {f"lag_{lag}": extended[t - pd.Timedelta(hours=lag)] for lag in lags}
            prediction = model.predict(pd.DataFrame([row]))[0]
            extended.loc[t] = prediction                       # the forecast becomes "history" for the next step
            out.append(prediction)
        return np.array(out)
    return forecaster

bt_rec = fc.backtest(y, recursive_forecaster(), origins=test_origins, horizon=H)
pd.DataFrame({"direct (lags >= 24)": fc.score(bt_gbm, train), "recursive (feeds its own predictions back)": fc.score(bt_rec, train)}).T.style.format(
    {"MAE": "{:,.0f}", "RMSE": "{:,.0f}", "sMAPE": "{:.1%}", "MASE": "{:.2f}"})
def recursive_forecaster(lags=(1, 2, 24, 168)): def forecaster(hist, idx): table = pd.DataFrame({"hour": hist.index.hour, "dayofweek": hist.index.dayofweek}, index=hist.index) for lag in lags: table[f"lag_{lag}"] = hist.shift(lag) table = table.dropna() model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(table, hist.loc[table.index]) extended, out = hist.copy(), [] for t in idx: row = {"hour": t.hour, "dayofweek": t.dayofweek} | {f"lag_{lag}": extended[t - pd.Timedelta(hours=lag)] for lag in lags} prediction = model.predict(pd.DataFrame([row]))[0] extended.loc[t] = prediction # the forecast becomes "history" for the next step out.append(prediction) return np.array(out) return forecaster bt_rec = fc.backtest(y, recursive_forecaster(), origins=test_origins, horizon=H) pd.DataFrame({"direct (lags >= 24)": fc.score(bt_gbm, train), "recursive (feeds its own predictions back)": fc.score(bt_rec, train)}).T.style.format( {"MAE": "{:,.0f}", "RMSE": "{:,.0f}", "sMAPE": "{:.1%}", "MASE": "{:.2f}"}) Out[9]: MAE RMSE sMAPE MASE direct (lags >= 24) 328 437 9.0% 0.95 recursive (feeds its own predictions back) 358 480 9.9% 1.04

The recursive version is worse (MAE about 360 against 330). Errors compound: each step's mistake becomes the next step's input. Recursive forecasting is attractive when the horizon is long and training one model per horizon is too expensive, and it is the standard in classical models (ARIMA does it internally). But for tree models with a moderate horizon, the direct approach is the safer default.

1. You want a 48-hour-ahead forecast issued at midnight. What is the smallest lag you may use, and why?

48 hours. The newest value available at the origin is from 23:00 the previous day; for the target hour 47 hours later (23:00 on the second day) a lag of k hours reaches back to a time that is still in the future of the origin unless k ≥ 48. In general the minimum lag equals the horizon (the number of steps ahead of the last observed value), which is what min_lag encodes.

2. A teammate adds a feature mean_7d = y.rolling('7D').mean() and the score improves by 5%. Is it safe?

Not as written. A rolling window ending at each row includes the target value itself (and the hours between the origin and the target, which are unknown). It must be computed on a shifted series, y.shift(24).rolling('7D').mean(), so that the row for time t only uses data from at least 24 hours earlier. Then re-run the backtest: if the improvement shrinks or disappears, it was leakage.

3. The calendar-only model scores about the same as the model with ten features. Should you keep the ten features?

No: keep the simplest model that performs equally well. More features mean more data to maintain, more ways to leak, and more things to break in production, with no measured gain. Revisit when the evidence changes (more history, a new driver such as weather), not before.

Predict the residual of the four-week average instead of demand itself: target = y - same_hour_4w, then add the baseline back. Is boosting from the baseline better than boosting from scratch? 
def residual_forecaster(hist, idx):
    rows = X.loc[X.index.isin(hist.index)].dropna()
    model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=100, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, random_state=0)
    model.fit(rows, hist.loc[rows.index] - rows["same_hour_4w"])
    return model.predict(X.loc[idx]) + X.loc[idx, "same_hour_4w"]
print(fc.score(fc.backtest(y, residual_forecaster, origins=test_origins, horizon=24), train)["MAE"])

It scores about 321: better than boosting from scratch (about 328 to 330), and still clearly worse than the baseline it starts from (277). The correction the model learns is mostly noise, which makes the baseline worse rather than better.

Train the gradient-boosting model with the absolute-error loss (loss='absolute_error'), which matches the MAE metric. Does matching the loss to the metric help? 
print(fc.score(fc.backtest(y, gbm_forecaster(loss="absolute_error"), origins=test_origins, horizon=24), train)["MAE"])

It does not here: MAE is about 341, worse than the squared-error model's 328. Matching the loss to the metric is a good principle in general, but with so few rows per pattern the more robust but less efficient L1 fit has no room to help. Test it rather than assume.

Add a feature for the daily total of yesterday (sum of the 24 hours of the previous day, known at midnight). Is it legal? Does it help? 
daily_before = y.resample("D").sum().shift(1)                       # each day gets the previous day's total
X["yesterday_total"] = daily_before.reindex(y.index, method="ffill")
print(fc.score(fc.backtest(y, gbm_forecaster(), origins=test_origins, horizon=24), train)["MAE"])

It is legal: at midnight the previous day's total is complete, and shifting by one day means the row for any hour of day D only sees days up to D - 1. (Check the shift before trusting it: using the same day's total would leak.) It does not help: the MAE moves from about 328 to about 336, slightly worse, consistent with the lag features adding nothing.

docs.title: Machine-Learning Forecasts: Lag and Calendar Features¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Build lag, rolling and calendar features that respect the forecast horizon.
  • Explain what a model uses with permutation importance and feature-group ablations.
  • Spot and quantify leakage from a too-short lag or a window that includes the target.
  • Compare direct and recursive forecasting strategies.

Prerequisites: Pages 1 to 4 of this track; scikit-learn basics. Dataset: NYC Taxi (Jan to Mar 2023). Time: about 40 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
A very different way to forecast: forget the time-series machinery and treat it as an ordinary supervised-learning table. Each row is one target hour; the columns are things we can know at the moment we forecast (the hour of day, the weekday, what demand was yesterday and a week ago, recent averages); the target is that hour's demand. Then any regressor you already know (gradient boosting, linear models) can be used.

This is how most forecasting is done in industry today, because it scales to thousands of series and accepts any extra column (weather, prices, holidays). It is also the setting in which leakage is easiest to commit and hardest to spot. So this page spends as much time on what you must not use as on what you can.

docs.title: 1. What may a feature use?¶
docs.text:
The forecast is made at midnight for the 24 hours that follow, so the newest value we hold is from 23:00 of the day before. For a target hour t that means a feature can use a value from time $t - k$ only if it already exists at the origin. For the last hour of the day (23:00 tomorrow), the newest available value is 24 hours older. So the rule for a day-ahead forecast is simple: every lag must be at least 24 hours.

fc.make_features(y, min_lag=24, lags=..., windows=...) builds calendar, lag and rolling-mean columns and refuses a lag shorter than the forecast horizon:

docs.title: 2. What did the model actually use?¶
docs.text: Permutation importance shuffles one column at a time and measures how much the error rises: a big rise means the model leaned on that column. We fit on data up to 10 March and measure on the following week, so that the importance is judged on data the model has not seen.

docs.title: 3. Leakage: how to look better than you are¶
docs.text: Now the part of the page that matters most. Suppose we "improve" the features by adding yesterday's last hour, lag_1: the demand in the hour immediately before the target. In the training table it is perfectly legitimate: for every row, the value one hour earlier exists. But at the origin we do not know it, for any target hour after the first.

docs.title: 4. Direct versus recursive forecasting¶
docs.text: The model above is direct: one model, trained with lags of at least 24, predicts any of the 24 hours. The alternative is recursive: train a one-step-ahead model (using lag_1, which is legal for a one-step forecast), predict the next hour, append the prediction to the history, and repeat 24 times, feeding predictions back in as if they were observations.

docs.title: The honest verdict¶
docs.text: On this series, with 11 weeks of history, no learned model has beaten the six-week seasonal average. That is not a failure of the page; it is the finding. Machine-learning forecasts earn their keep when there are many series to learn from, external drivers (weather, promotions, holidays) or long histories. For one series with a strong, stable weekly shape, a seasonal average is hard to beat and costs nothing to run and explain.

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix Spectacular backtest score a feature that does not exist at forecast time (short lag, window including the target) make_features guard; ask "would I have this at the origin?" for each column Rolling mean looks harmless but leaks window ends at the target hour compute windows on the shifted series Model does no better than hour and weekday alone the lag features add nothing, the tree learns a profile ablate feature groups before believing a feature helps Tree model loses to a simple average too few rows per seasonal slot more history or more series; or use the average Recursive forecast worse than direct error compounding train direct models, or accept it for long horizons Scaling or imputing on the whole series test statistics leak into training fit transformers on the training window only

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Forecasting becomes supervised learning once each row uses only information available at the forecast origin: lags and windows must respect the horizon (min_lag).
  • Check what a model uses (permutation importance) and ablate feature groups; here the hour and weekday carried almost everything.
  • Gradient boosting on one short series did not beat a seasonal average: flexible models need data, and the learning curve was still improving.
  • Leakage can be spectacular (lag_1, about 20% better) or quiet (a window including the target hour, a few percent). Ask of every column: would it exist at the origin?
  • Direct forecasting (lags at least the horizon) beat recursive forecasting here, where errors compound.

Next: Backtesting: rolling origins and honest model comparison.

Shuffled cross-validation reports an error of about 260, the honest forward-in-time scheme about 310 to 320, so shuffling flatters the model by roughly 17%. (The two are scored on different rows, since TimeSeriesSplit only tests on the later weeks, but the direction and the size of the gap are the point.) The model was never wrong in code: every row's features are legal. The leak is in the split: the hour either side of a test row is in the training set, and neighbouring hours are nearly identical, so the model can interpolate rather than forecast.

Notice also the spread across folds: the weekly blocks range from about 260 to about 410, so any one holiday-free week can look like a very different model quality from another. That is the case for many origins.

def slot_dummies(index):
    slot = pd.Series(index.dayofweek * 24 + index.hour, index=index).astype("category")
    return pd.get_dummies(slot).astype(float).reindex(columns=range(168), fill_value=0.0)

def slot_ar(hist, idx):                                       # page 4: slot dummies + AR(1) errors, last 6 weeks
    hist = hist.iloc[-168 * 6:]
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        fit = SARIMAX(hist, exog=slot_dummies(hist.index), order=(1, 0, 0), trend="c").fit(disp=False, maxiter=200)
    return fit.forecast(len(idx), exog=slot_dummies(idx)).to_numpy()

def boosting(hist, idx):                                      # page 5: gradient boosting, all legal features
    rows = X.loc[X.index.isin(hist.index)].dropna()
    return model().fit(rows, hist.loc[rows.index]).predict(X.loc[idx])

def paired(a, b):
    d = per_origin[a] - per_origin[b]                      # negative = a is better
    return {"mean difference (pickups/hour)": d.mean(), "standard error": d.std() / np.sqrt(len(d)),
            "days a wins": int((d < 0).sum()), "of": len(d)}

pairs = [("slot dummies + AR(1)", "4-week average"), ("6-week average", "4-week average"),
         ("gradient boosting", "4-week average"), ("same hour last week", "4-week average")]
comparison = pd.DataFrame({f"{a}  minus  {b}": paired(a, b) for a, b in pairs}).T
comparison.style.format({"mean difference (pickups/hour)": "{:+.1f}", "standard error": "{:.1f}", "days a wins": "{:.0f}", "of": "{:.0f}"})
def paired(a, b): d = per_origin[a] - per_origin[b] # negative = a is better return {"mean difference (pickups/hour)": d.mean(), "standard error": d.std() / np.sqrt(len(d)), "days a wins": int((d < 0).sum()), "of": len(d)} pairs = [("slot dummies + AR(1)", "4-week average"), ("6-week average", "4-week average"), ("gradient boosting", "4-week average"), ("same hour last week", "4-week average")] comparison = pd.DataFrame({f"{a} minus {b}": paired(a, b) for a, b in pairs}).T comparison.style.format({"mean difference (pickups/hour)": "{:+.1f}", "standard error": "{:.1f}", "days a wins": "{:.0f}", "of": "{:.0f}"}) Out[7]: mean difference (pickups/hour) standard error days a wins of slot dummies + AR(1) minus 4-week average -1.1 7.5 22 48 6-week average minus 4-week average +0.1 6.7 23 48 gradient boosting minus 4-week average +26.0 13.3 18 48 same hour last week minus 4-week average +56.8 17.2 16 48

Read each row against its own standard error:

  • Slot dummies + AR(1) versus the 4-week average: about −1 ± 7.5, and it wins 22 days of 48. This is a tie, and the regression's apparent 5% edge on the last fortnight was luck.
  • 6-week versus 4-week average: 0 ± 7. Also a tie, and so the "best number of weeks" question from the baselines page has no answer here that the data can support.
  • Boosting versus the 4-week average: about +26 ± 13. Roughly two standard errors worse, and it wins only 18 days: probably genuinely worse on this series.
  • Seasonal naive versus the 4-week average: about +57 ± 17, clearly worse on average, but it still wins 16 of the 48 individual days. Averaging four weeks costs something on days that really are like last week.

A difference smaller than about two standard errors should not be reported as a win. Here the honest summary is: three methods are indistinguishable, boosting is worse, and a plain weekly copy is worst; pick the simplest of the tied ones.

Do the rankings hold when we split the period in half?

In [8]: Copied! 
first_half = per_origin.index < "2023-03-06"
halves = pd.DataFrame({"12 Feb to 5 Mar": per_origin[first_half].mean(), "6 to 31 Mar": per_origin[~first_half].mean()})
halves.round(0).astype(int).T
first_half = per_origin.index < "2023-03-06" halves = pd.DataFrame({"12 Feb to 5 Mar": per_origin[first_half].mean(), "6 to 31 Mar": per_origin[~first_half].mean()}) halves.round(0).astype(int).T Out[8]: same hour last week 4-week average 6-week average slot dummies + AR(1) gradient boosting 12 Feb to 5 Mar 347 270 269 271 309 6 to 31 Mar 330 291 291 288 306

The ordering of the top three swaps from one half to the other (differences of one to three pickups). Boosting and the weekly copy stay behind in both halves, but the gaps change size. Rankings among close models are not stable, which is the same message again.

In [9]: Copied! 
worst = per_origin[["4-week average", "same hour last week"]].assign(weekday=per_origin.index.day_name()).nlargest(6, "4-week average")
print(worst.round(0).to_string())
print("\nThe origin where the weekly copy fails most:")
bad_copy = per_origin["same hour last week"].idxmax()
per_origin.loc[[bad_copy]].round(0).assign(weekday=bad_copy.day_name())
worst = per_origin[["4-week average", "same hour last week"]].assign(weekday=per_origin.index.day_name()).nlargest(6, "4-week average") print(worst.round(0).to_string()) print("\nThe origin where the weekly copy fails most:") bad_copy = per_origin["same hour last week"].idxmax() per_origin.loc[[bad_copy]].round(0).assign(weekday=bad_copy.day_name()) 
            4-week average  same hour last week    weekday
origin                                                    
2023-02-20          594.00               700.00     Monday
2023-03-13          469.00               330.00     Monday
2023-03-18          459.00               447.00   Saturday
2023-03-07          433.00               571.00    Tuesday
2023-03-22          412.00               584.00  Wednesday
2023-03-17          392.00               546.00     Friday

The origin where the weekly copy fails most:
Out[9]: same hour last week 4-week average 6-week average slot dummies + AR(1) gradient boosting weekday origin 2023-02-27 739.00 309.00 356.00 333.00 265.00 Monday

Monday 20 February (Presidents' Day) is the worst day for the four-week average by a wide margin (about 590 against a typical 280), and the model had no way to know it was a holiday. And the second table shows where the weekly copy fails most: Monday 27 February, where its error jumps to about 740 (the four-week average: about 310) because "same hour last week" copied the holiday. A forecaster can be wrong on a normal day because the reference day was abnormal.

Holidays are information that exists in advance and can be given to a model. That is the subject of the last page of this track.

How to report a backtest

State the origins and the horizon before you look at results. Report the average over all origins and the spread (per-origin or per-fold), the worst cases, and paired differences with standard errors against a baseline. A single number such as "MAE 280" hides most of what a reader needs to decide.

1. Why does random K-fold cross-validation look better than the honest scheme on the same data, even though no feature leaks?

The leak is in the split, not the features. A test hour's neighbours (one hour before and after) are in the training folds and look almost the same, so the model can effectively interpolate between known points instead of forecasting the unknown. It also trains on data from the test row's future. Real forecasting has neither advantage, so the shuffled score is optimistic (about 17% here).

2. The difference between two models is −3 pickups per hour with a standard error of 7. What do you conclude?

Nothing: the difference is under half a standard error, so a result of this size appears by chance all the time. The models are indistinguishable on this evidence; choose the simpler or cheaper one. To detect a difference this small you would need many more origins, or a longer history, or to accept that it does not matter.

3. Why compare models pairwise, on the same origins, rather than just comparing their overall averages?

Because most of the variation between days is shared by all models (some days are simply hard). Subtracting one model's error from another's cancels the shared difficulty and leaves only the difference the models make, which has a much smaller standard error than the averages themselves. It is the same logic as a paired t-test.

Compute the standard error and a 95% bootstrap interval for the difference between the slot-dummy model and the 4-week average, by resampling the 48 origins with replacement 5,000 times. Does the interval contain zero? 
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d = (per_origin["slot dummies + AR(1)"] - per_origin["4-week average"]).to_numpy()
boot = [rng.choice(d, size=len(d), replace=True).mean() for _ in range(5000)]
print(np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5]))

The interval is roughly −16 to +14 pickups per hour, which comfortably contains zero. A bootstrap resamples whole days, which respects that each day's forecasts are a unit; resampling individual hours would give an interval that is far too narrow, because errors within a day are strongly correlated.

Break the error down by forecast step (1 to 24) for the 4-week average and for the slot-dummy model over all 48 origins. In which steps does the AR model win? 
by_step = pd.DataFrame({name: (bt["actual"] - bt["forecast"]).abs().groupby(bt["step"]).mean()
                        for name, bt in runs.items() if name in ("4-week average", "slot dummies + AR(1)")})
print((by_step["4-week average"] - by_step["slot dummies + AR(1)"]).round(0).tolist())

The AR model gains in steps 1 and 2 (about 45 and 14 pickups; the memory of the AR(1) term, as on page 4), loses at steps 3 to 5, wins again at steps 8 and 9 (about 40 to 45), and bounces either side of zero for the rest, with no pattern. Over a whole day this nets out to nothing, which is why the overall difference is so small.

Drop the Presidents' Day origin (20 February) and recompute the table. Do the conclusions change? 
print(per_origin.drop(pd.Timestamp("2023-02-20")).mean().round(0))

The averages of the top three fall to about 275 to 277 (they were about 280), the boosting gap shrinks a little, and the ordering of the three leaders is still a tie: dropping one hard day moves all the models together, and the conclusions stand. That is a robustness check worth doing, as long as you report that you did it rather than silently dropping days that look bad.

docs.title: Backtesting: Rolling Origins and Honest Comparison¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Choose between expanding and sliding windows and run a rolling-origin backtest.
  • Show how shuffled cross-validation inflates a time-series score.
  • Compare forecasters pairwise over many origins with a standard error.
  • Use the worst-case days to find what a model cannot see.

Prerequisites: Pages 1 to 5 of this track. Dataset: NYC Taxi (Jan to Mar 2023). Time: about 40 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
We now have several forecasters and some contradictory impressions. On the baselines page, the best number of weeks to average flipped between two fortnights. On the classical-models page, a regression with AR errors looked 5% better than the four-week average on 14 days, and then turned out to equal a six-week average. How would we ever know which forecaster is better?

The answer is backtesting: evaluate over many forecast origins, not one, then ask how much of the difference could be luck. This page also settles the question of how not to cross-validate a time series.

docs.title: 1. How to split a time series¶
docs.text:
Ordinary cross-validation shuffles rows into folds. For a series that is wrong twice over: a fold can train on the future of its test rows, and its neighbouring hours (almost identical to the test hour) sit in the training data. Time-aware schemes always train on the past and test on what follows, either with a window that expands (all history up to the origin) or one that slides (only the most recent w observations).

scikit-learn offers TimeSeriesSplit; our fc.rolling_origins + fc.backtest does the same with real dates, a forecast horizon and one origin per day. First, the picture of a few origins.

docs.title: 2. Why shuffled cross-validation lies¶
docs.text: Take the gradient-boosting features from the last page and score them three ways on the same rows: random 5-fold, TimeSeriesSplit (five consecutive one-week test blocks, each trained only on what precedes it), and the same with a 24-hour gap between train and test.

docs.title: 3. A proper comparison over 48 origins¶
docs.text: Five forecasters from earlier pages, tested on 48 daily origins (12 February to 31 March). The slowest two (the regression with AR errors and boosting) take about a minute in total.

docs.title: 4. Are the differences real?¶
docs.text: Because every forecaster is scored on the same origins, we can compare them pairwise, day by day, which removes the shared difficulty. For each pair: the average daily difference, its standard error, and how many of the 48 days the first one wins.

docs.title: 5. The hardest days¶
docs.text: Which origins hurt the most? A look at the worst days for the four-week average, with the weekly copy alongside.

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix CV score much better than live performance shuffled folds train on the future and on neighbouring hours TimeSeriesSplit or a rolling-origin backtest Ranking changes when the window changes few origins, heavy day-to-day difficulty many origins; paired comparison with standard errors "5% better" disappears on more data luck on a short window look at the standard error before celebrating Seasonal-naive forecast is wrong after a holiday the copied day was abnormal give the model holiday information, or use a robust average Train and test rows overlap in time lags or targets span the boundary use gap= at least the feature or target length Tuning on the backtest, then reporting it selection bias tune on earlier origins, report on later ones, once

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Never shuffle a time series into folds. Use a rolling-origin backtest or TimeSeriesSplit (with gap= when features or targets span the boundary). Shuffling flattered this model by about 17%.
  • Evaluate over many origins; day-to-day difficulty varies fourfold.
  • Compare models pairwise on the same origins and report the standard error. A difference under two standard errors is not a win.
  • Here three methods tied at about 280 pickups of error; boosting was worse, a weekly copy worst. Choose the simplest of the tied.
  • Hard days reveal what the models cannot see (a holiday). Which leads to the final page.

Next: Forecast metrics and prediction intervals.

Three things to read off this table.

Bias. The four-week average has a bias of about −78 pickups an hour: it ran low, on average, by roughly 1.7% of the average hour's demand (about 4,470 pickups). Demand was rising through the period and a four-week average lags it. MAE cannot show this, because it ignores the sign. When a forecaster leans one way, ask whether the decision cares: under-forecasting demand means too few cabs.

RMSE versus MAE. RMSE is about 1.4 times MAE here. Equal values would mean all errors are about the same size; a gap says a few days are much worse. Test how much one day matters by dropping the worst one (Presidents' Day):

This table is the argument for choosing metrics with care.

  • MAPE is undefined (nan or inf) for every forecaster: about half the actual values are zero, and a percentage of zero does not exist. A pipeline that reports MAPE would silently fail here, or, worse, drop the zero hours and report a number for a different, easier problem.
  • sMAPE crowns the nonsense forecast. "Flat at zero", which says no pickups, ever, gets a much better sMAPE than the four-week average, because every zero hour scores as a perfect match and every non-zero hour is capped at the worst value of 2, which it would not exceed anyway.
  • MAE, RMSE and MASE agree: the four-week average is best, and "never any demand" is not. MASE (0.43 for the average) reads as "57% better than last week's copy did in training", comparable with any other series.

The lesson: never evaluate a forecast with a single metric you have not stress-tested on the shape of your data. For counts with zeros use MAE, RMSE or MASE (or a probabilistic metric such as the Poisson deviance).

In [8]: Copied! 
four_week = four_week.assign(hour=four_week["time"].dt.hour)
z80 = 1.2816                                              # standard-normal 90th percentile
rows = []
for origin in [o for o in all_origins if o >= pd.Timestamp("2023-02-19")]:
    known = four_week[four_week["time"] < origin]          # forecast errors that have already been observed
    now = four_week[four_week["origin"] == origin]
    errors = known["actual"] - known["forecast"]
    lo_q, hi_q = errors.quantile([0.1, 0.9])
    relative = (known["actual"] / known["forecast"] - 1).groupby(known["hour"]).quantile([0.1, 0.9]).unstack()
    for _, r in now.iterrows():
        rel_lo, rel_hi = relative.loc[r["hour"]]
        rows.append({"origin": origin, "time": r["time"], "hour": r["hour"], "actual": r["actual"], "forecast": r["forecast"],
                     "gaussian_lo": r["forecast"] - z80 * errors.std(), "gaussian_hi": r["forecast"] + z80 * errors.std(),
                     "empirical_lo": r["forecast"] + lo_q, "empirical_hi": r["forecast"] + hi_q,
                     "by_hour_lo": r["forecast"] * (1 + rel_lo), "by_hour_hi": r["forecast"] * (1 + rel_hi)})
intervals = pd.DataFrame(rows)

def interval_score(df, lo, hi, alpha=0.2):
    """Winkler score: the width, plus a penalty of 2/alpha times how far the actual falls outside. Lower is better."""
    width = df[hi] - df[lo]
    miss = (df[lo] - df["actual"]).clip(lower=0) + (df["actual"] - df[hi]).clip(lower=0)
    return (width + 2 / alpha * miss).mean()

summary = {}
for name, key in [("Gaussian, constant width", "gaussian"), ("empirical quantiles of past errors", "empirical"), ("quantiles by hour, relative", "by_hour")]:
    inside = (intervals["actual"] >= intervals[f"{key}_lo"]) & (intervals["actual"] <= intervals[f"{key}_hi"])
    summary[name] = {"coverage (target 80%)": inside.mean(), "average width": (intervals[f"{key}_hi"] - intervals[f"{key}_lo"]).mean(),
                     "interval score": interval_score(intervals, f"{key}_lo", f"{key}_hi")}
pd.DataFrame(summary).T.style.format({"coverage (target 80%)": "{:.1%}", "average width": "{:,.0f}", "interval score": "{:,.0f}"})

Lower is better.""" width = df[hi] - df[lo] miss = (df[lo] - df["actual"]).clip(lower=0) + (df["actual"] - df[hi]).clip(lower=0) return (width + 2 / alpha * miss).mean() summary = {} for name, key in [("Gaussian, constant width", "gaussian"), ("empirical quantiles of past errors", "empirical"), ("quantiles by hour, relative", "by_hour")]: inside = (intervals["actual"] >= intervals[f"{key}_lo"]) & (intervals["actual"] <= intervals[f"{key}_hi"]) summary[name] = {"coverage (target 80%)": inside.mean(), "average width": (intervals[f"{key}_hi"] - intervals[f"{key}_lo"]).mean(), "interval score": interval_score(intervals, f"{key}_lo", f"{key}_hi")} pd.DataFrame(summary).T.style.format({"coverage (target 80%)": "{:.1%}", "average width": "{:,.0f}", "interval score": "{:,.0f}"}) Out[8]: coverage (target 80%) average width interval score Gaussian, constant width 81.1% 998 1,485 empirical quantiles of past errors 77.5% 851 1,466 quantiles by hour, relative 75.2% 812 1,390

All three cover roughly 75% to 81% of the actuals: broadly in the right area for an "80%" interval, and none exactly right. The Gaussian interval has the best overall coverage and also the widest intervals; the by-hour interval is the narrowest and has the best (lowest) interval score. But overall coverage can hide where the intervals fail. Check coverage by hour, which is what a dispatcher actually relies on:

In [9]: Copied! 
inside = lambda key: (intervals["actual"] >= intervals[f"{key}_lo"]) & (intervals["actual"] <= intervals[f"{key}_hi"])
by_hour_cov = pd.DataFrame({"Gaussian, constant width": inside("gaussian"), "quantiles by hour, relative": inside("by_hour")}).groupby(intervals["hour"]).mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.3))
by_hour_cov.plot(ax=ax, marker="o", ms=4)
ax.axhline(0.8, color="k", ls=":", label="target 80%")
ax.set(xlabel="hour of day", ylabel="share of actuals inside the interval", ylim=(0.3, 1.05), title="Coverage by hour of day"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("range of hourly coverage, Gaussian:", by_hour_cov["Gaussian, constant width"].agg(["min", "max"]).round(2).to_dict())
print("range of hourly coverage, by hour: ", by_hour_cov["quantiles by hour, relative"].agg(["min", "max"]).round(2).to_dict())
inside = lambda key: (intervals["actual"] >= intervals[f"{key}_lo"]) & (intervals["actual"] <= intervals[f"{key}_hi"]) by_hour_cov = pd.DataFrame({"Gaussian, constant width": inside("gaussian"), "quantiles by hour, relative": inside("by_hour")}).groupby(intervals["hour"]).mean() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.3)) by_hour_cov.plot(ax=ax, marker="o", ms=4) ax.axhline(0.8, color="k", ls=":", label="target 80%") ax.set(xlabel="hour of day", ylabel="share of actuals inside the interval", ylim=(0.3, 1.05), title="Coverage by hour of day"); ax.legend(fontsize=8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() print("range of hourly coverage, Gaussian:", by_hour_cov["Gaussian, constant width"].agg(["min", "max"]).round(2).to_dict()) print("range of hourly coverage, by hour: ", by_hour_cov["quantiles by hour, relative"].agg(["min", "max"]).round(2).to_dict()) 
range of hourly coverage, Gaussian: {'min': 0.54, 'max': 1.0}
range of hourly coverage, by hour:  {'min': 0.63, 'max': 0.88}

The constant-width Gaussian interval is a textbook case of good on average, wrong where it matters. At night its coverage is close to 100% (the interval is much wider than needed), and in the evening peak it falls to about 55% to 65% (too narrow, just when the dispatcher most needs it). The by-hour relative intervals are far more even across the day (about 63% to 88% instead of 54% to 100%), even though each hour's quantiles are estimated from only a few weeks of residuals, which is why they under-cover a little overall.

The residuals method has two virtues and one flaw. It works for any forecaster, because it only needs past errors. It is cheap. The flaw is the usual one: it assumes the future errors look like recent errors, so it fails after a regime change or on a holiday, which no interval learned from ordinary days will anticipate.

A different route is a model that predicts the quantiles directly. Gradient boosting supports this with loss="quantile":

In [10]: Copied! 
X = fc.make_features(y, min_lag=24, lags=(24, 48, 168, 336, 504), windows=(24, 168))
X["same_hour_4w"] = pd.concat([y.shift(168 * k) for k in (1, 2, 3, 4)], axis=1).mean(axis=1)

def quantile_interval(origin, quantiles=(0.1, 0.9)):
    hist = y.loc[: origin - pd.Timedelta(1, "ns")]
    target = pd.date_range(origin, periods=H, freq="h")
    target = target[target <= y.index[-1]]
    rows = X.loc[X.index.isin(hist.index)].dropna()
    out = {}
    for q in quantiles:
        m = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss="quantile", quantile=q, max_iter=150, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, random_state=0)
        out[q] = m.fit(rows, hist.loc[rows.index]).predict(X.loc[target])
    return pd.DataFrame({"time": target, "actual": y.loc[target].to_numpy(), "lo": out[quantiles[0]], "hi": out[quantiles[1]]})

gbm_q = pd.concat([quantile_interval(o) for o in sorted(intervals["origin"].unique())], ignore_index=True)
gbm_q["hour"] = gbm_q["time"].dt.hour
covered = (gbm_q["actual"] >= gbm_q["lo"]) & (gbm_q["actual"] <= gbm_q["hi"])
print(f"quantile boosting: coverage {covered.mean():.1%}, average width {(gbm_q['hi'] - gbm_q['lo']).mean():,.0f}, "
      f"interval score {interval_score(gbm_q.assign(), 'lo', 'hi'):,.0f}")
print("hourly coverage range:", covered.groupby(gbm_q["hour"]).mean().agg(["min", "max"]).round(2).to_dict())
X = fc.make_features(y, min_lag=24, lags=(24, 48, 168, 336, 504), windows=(24, 168)) X["same_hour_4w"] = pd.concat([y.shift(168 * k) for k in (1, 2, 3, 4)], axis=1).mean(axis=1) def quantile_interval(origin, quantiles=(0.1, 0.9)): hist = y.loc[: origin - pd.Timedelta(1, "ns")] target = pd.date_range(origin, periods=H, freq="h") target = target[target <= y.index[-1]] rows = X.loc[X.index.isin(hist.index)].dropna() out = {} for q in quantiles: m = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss="quantile", quantile=q, max_iter=150, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, random_state=0) out[q] = m.fit(rows, hist.loc[rows.index]).predict(X.loc[target]) return pd.DataFrame({"time": target, "actual": y.loc[target].to_numpy(), "lo": out[quantiles[0]], "hi": out[quantiles[1]]}) gbm_q = pd.concat([quantile_interval(o) for o in sorted(intervals["origin"].unique())], ignore_index=True) gbm_q["hour"] = gbm_q["time"].dt.hour covered = (gbm_q["actual"] >= gbm_q["lo"]) & (gbm_q["actual"] <= gbm_q["hi"]) print(f"quantile boosting: coverage {covered.mean():.1%}, average width {(gbm_q['hi'] - gbm_q['lo']).mean():,.0f}, " f"interval score {interval_score(gbm_q.assign(), 'lo', 'hi'):,.0f}") print("hourly coverage range:", covered.groupby(gbm_q["hour"]).mean().agg(["min", "max"]).round(2).to_dict())
