hourly coverage range: {'min': 0.63, 'max': 0.85}

Quantile boosting covers about 74%, no better than the simple residual method, and is wider, with a worse interval score than the by-hour intervals. With 11 weeks of data there is little to learn tail behaviour from. The model-free residual method is a good default; a quantile model earns its place when there is a lot of data or when the spread depends on drivers the point forecast does not use.

An interval is a claim you can check

"80%" must mean 80% in a test. Always report coverage on held-out origins, broken down by something that matters (hour, weekday, level of demand), next to the width. A narrow interval that covers 50% is not "sharp", it is wrong.

1. A forecaster has MAPE 5% on city-wide hourly demand. Can you conclude it will do equally well for a single quiet zone?

No. MAPE depends on the size of the denominator: for a series with demand in the thousands, 5% is a meaningful statement, while for counts near zero the same forecaster's percentage error is undefined or huge. The metric itself does not transfer between scales. Use a scale-free measure that survives zeros, such as MASE, to compare across series of different sizes.

2. The 80% interval covers 82% of the test values. Is it well calibrated?

Not necessarily: that is the marginal coverage. Check it in subgroups: by hour of day, weekday, and demand level. A constant-width interval can cover 100% at night and 55% at the evening peak and still average out near 80%. Calibration that matters is conditional on the situation in which the interval will be used.

3. Why must the residuals used for an interval at origin o come only from targets earlier than o?

At the origin the future errors do not exist yet. Using residuals from after the origin would let the interval 'know' how wrong the forecaster is about to be and would produce coverage numbers that cannot be reproduced in production. It is the same rule as for features: if it is not available at the moment of the forecast, it must not be used.

Build 90% intervals (the 5th and 95th percentiles) with the by-hour relative method. What coverage do you get, and what happens to the width?

Repeat the interval cell with quantiles 0.05 and 0.95 (and z = 1.645 for the Gaussian version), then compute the coverage and the average width.

relative = (known["actual"] / known["forecast"] - 1).groupby(known["hour"]).quantile([0.05, 0.95]).unstack()

Coverage rises to about 85%, again a little short of the nominal 90%, and the average width grows by about 37% (from roughly 810 to roughly 1,110 pickups). Wider intervals buy coverage at a steep price; the nominal level is a decision about the cost of being caught out.

Under-forecasting costs three times as much as over-forecasting (a stranded passenger is worse than an idle cab). Which quantile of the error distribution minimises expected cost, and how much better is it than the plain point forecast?

The cost of an error is $3e$ if you under-forecast by $e$ and $e$ if you over-forecast: the pinball loss with $\tau = 0.75$ (under = 3, over = 1 gives $\tau = 3/(3+1)$). It is minimised by the 75th percentile of the demand distribution, not by the mean.

def cost(df, forecast):
    under = (df["actual"] - forecast).clip(lower=0); over = (forecast - df["actual"]).clip(lower=0)
    return (3 * under + over).mean()

relative75 = (known["actual"] / known["forecast"] - 1).groupby(known["hour"]).quantile(0.75)   # per origin, as above

On this data, shifting each forecast up to its 75th percentile cuts the average cost by about 29% (from about 646 to about 458 cost units per hour) compared with using the four-week average as is. The point: the right number to report depends on the cost of the errors, and a point forecast is the answer to only one particular cost structure.

Compute the mean error (bias) of the four-week average for each hour of the day. In which hours does it under-forecast most? 
print((ev["forecast"] - ev["actual"]).groupby(ev["time"].dt.hour).mean().round(0))

The forecaster under-forecasts at almost every hour: the bias is about −110 to −200 pickups in the evening (5 to 11pm), about −130 around 11am and midnight, and only 7am is (slightly) positive. That fits the overall bias of about −78 and a rising level that a four-week average lags. Bias by hour is a cheap check that points at a systematic fix (correct for the trend), whereas MAE alone would not show it.

docs.title: Forecast Metrics and Prediction Intervals¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Choose among MAE, RMSE, MAPE, sMAPE, MASE and bias, and say what each hides.
  • Show how percentage errors fail when demand is near zero.
  • Build prediction intervals from past forecast errors and test their coverage by group.
  • Choose the quantile to report when over- and under-forecasting cost different amounts.

Prerequisites: Pages 1 to 6 of this track. Dataset: NYC Taxi (Jan to Mar 2023). Time: about 40 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
The dispatch team has two questions we have not yet answered well. First, which number tells us a forecaster is good? We have used MAE, RMSE, sMAPE and MASE somewhat casually, and the choice of metric can crown a different winner or even a useless forecast. Second, a single "expected pickups" number is not what a dispatcher needs to decide how many cabs to field: they need how bad could it be, a range.

This page covers both: how forecast metrics behave (and misbehave), and how to attach honest prediction intervals to any forecaster.

docs.title: 1. A scorecard for point forecasts¶
docs.text:
Every metric is a summary of the errors $e_t = y_t - \hat y_t$. They answer different questions:

Metric Formula Question it answers Watch out for MAE mean of $\lvert e_t\rvert$ typical miss, in the units of the data ignores the sign; treats all days alike RMSE $\sqrt{\text{mean of } e_t^2}$ the same, but large misses count more dominated by a few bad days MAPE mean of $\lvert e_t\rvert / y_t$ miss as a share of demand undefined at $y_t = 0$; explodes for small $y_t$ sMAPE mean of $2\lvert e_t\rvert / (\lvert y_t\rvert + \lvert\hat y_t\rvert)$ a bounded percentage error rewards forecasting low; odd near zero MASE MAE divided by the in-sample MAE of the seasonal-naive forecast error relative to a baseline, comparable across series needs a sensible seasonal period Bias mean of $(\hat y_t - y_t)$ does the forecaster lean high or low? cancels positive and negative misses

All on the same forecasts (the four-week average and the weekly copy, over 48 origins):

docs.title: 2. When demand is near zero: count data¶
docs.text: A whole city is smooth. A single pickup zone is not. We take one quiet zone (the one whose average is closest to one pickup an hour, excluding the TLC's two "unknown" codes) and forecast its hourly counts.

docs.title: 3. Prediction intervals¶
docs.text:
A point forecast says "about 5,000 pickups at 6pm". The dispatcher wants "between 4,300 and 5,800, nine times in ten". An 80% prediction interval should contain the actual value about 80% of the time, and we can check that: a property called coverage. Three ways to build one, each usable with any point forecaster:

  1. Gaussian: forecast ± 1.28 standard deviations of past errors.
  2. Empirical quantiles of past errors: forecast plus the 10th and 90th percentiles of recent forecast errors (no bell-curve assumption).
  3. Errors by hour, as a share of the forecast: the same, but computed separately for each hour of the day and expressed relative to the forecast, so that quiet hours get narrow intervals and busy ones wide ones.

The key rule is the same as always: the residuals that build the interval at an origin must be ones already known at that origin. We reuse the four-week-average backtest from 29 January and, for each origin from 19 February, build intervals from the errors of earlier forecasts whose targets have already happened.

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix MAPE is nan/inf or huge actual values at or near zero MAE, RMSE or MASE; check the data's range before choosing A silly forecast wins on sMAPE zeros score as perfect; sMAPE rewards low forecasts never rely on one metric; include a trivial forecast as a sanity check RMSE jumps when one day is added squared errors weight outliers report MAE alongside; look at per-day errors Forecast looks accurate but leans low MAE ignores the sign report bias Intervals cover 80% overall but 55% at the busy hours constant width, varying uncertainty build intervals by hour, or relative to the forecast; check coverage by group Interval built from errors that include the future residuals computed after the origin use only errors already observed at the origin Interval fails on a holiday residual quantiles come from ordinary days add holiday information, widen manually, or flag as out of scope

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Metrics are questions. MAE for typical miss, RMSE when big misses are costly, bias for direction, MASE for comparisons across series.
  • MAPE and sMAPE break near zero; sMAPE can reward a nonsense forecast. Always check metrics on the shape of your data, and include a trivial forecast as a sanity check.
  • A prediction interval is a claim about coverage: test it on held-out origins and by group; marginal coverage hides local failure.
  • Intervals from past errors work with any forecaster. Build them from errors already known at the origin, by hour, relative to the forecast.
  • The number you should report depends on the cost of errors: asymmetric costs call for a quantile, not a mean.

Next: Holidays, outside drivers and regime change.

d = per_origin["masked + holiday profile"] - per_origin["blind"] print(f"mean difference {d.mean():+.1f} pickups/hour, standard error {d.std() / np.sqrt(len(d)):.1f}, better on {(d < 0).sum()} of {len(d)} days") 
mean difference -15.2 pickups/hour, standard error 7.7, better on 6 of 48 days

About −15 ± 8 pickups an hour: roughly two standard errors, with the forecast better on 6 days and identical on the other 42 (it was never worse). That is a plausible improvement, but notice what it rests on: one holiday in the test period, and a holiday profile learned from just two earlier holidays. Treat the 20 February result as an illustration, not proof; over a full year, with eleven federal holidays and the many other unusual days (Christmas Eve, big parades, snowstorms), a holiday feature in a model with real training data is the right tool. The principle is what carries over: give the forecaster the calendar, and keep unusual days out of the averages used for ordinary ones.

In [6]: Copied!

Demand fell by about 96% within weeks. No amount of history from January and February contained any information about this. Three forecasters for the next 7 days, from every origin between 1 February and 25 May:

  • same weekday last week: long-memory-free, adapts after one week;
  • 4-week average: smoother in normal times, but it keeps averaging the old regime for four weeks;
  • weekday shape × latest 7-day level: keeps the day-of-week pattern from the last four weeks but takes the level from the most recent week.
In [7]: Copied! 
def shape_times_level(hist, idx, weeks=4):
    recent = hist.iloc[-7 * weeks:]
    ratio = recent / recent.rolling(7, center=True, min_periods=4).mean()      # each day relative to its own week
    shape = ratio.groupby(recent.index.dayofweek).mean()
    level = hist.iloc[-7:].mean()                                              # the most recent week only
    return pd.Series([shape[t.dayofweek] * level for t in idx], index=idx)

}

This table is percentage error (appropriate here because the level changes by a factor of 25; absolute errors would be dominated by the pre-break days).

  • Calm weeks: the 4-week average is best (about 5% error), the weekly copy worst (about 7%). Averaging reduces noise.
  • During the break every forecaster fails, but by very different amounts. The four-week average over-forecasts by almost nine times on average (a 860% error), because for four weeks it keeps averaging in the old, busy weeks. The weekly copy and the level-adjusted forecaster are wrong by about 150% to 170%, a fifth as badly.
  • In the new normal the average has not recovered (about 18% error, still blending in the collapse) while the other two are back near 11% to 12%.

This is the classic adaptivity versus noise trade-off: a long window is better when the world is stable and much worse when it changes. The week-by-week picture shows how long each takes to recover:

On the log scale the pre-break errors sit near 5% and every curve leaps by roughly two orders of magnitude (100 to 350 times). The weekly copy and the level-adjusted forecaster behave almost identically, and are back below 35% error by the week of 30 March, within about two weeks of their worst week; the four-week average is still at 91% in the week of 13 April, six weeks after the break began. No forecaster saw it coming; they differ in how long they stay wrong.

daily_error = (one_day["actual"] - one_day["forecast"]).abs() / one_day["actual"]
smoothed = daily_error.rolling(3).mean()

baseline = smoothed["2020-02-01":"2020-03-08"]
threshold = 2 * baseline.max()
alarms = smoothed[smoothed > threshold]
print(f"calm-period error: typical {baseline.median():.1%}, largest {baseline.max():.1%}  ->  alarm threshold {threshold:.0%}")

Out[9]: time 2020-03-09 2020-03-10 2020-03-11 2020-03-12 2020-03-13 2020-03-14 2020-03-15 2020-03-16 3-day smoothed error 6% 10% 16% 29% 51% 88% 136% 168%

The alarm fires on 13 March, the first day the collapse is large, and not before. It is not fooled by Presidents' Day (17 February 2020), which lies inside the baseline period: that holiday produces the largest calm-period error (the baseline maximum of about 17.5%), and the threshold is set above it. A threshold chosen from a period with no holiday would have fired a false alarm in February.

Two honest limits. First, the alarm fires after the first bad forecasts: monitoring shortens the damage, it cannot remove it. Second, it only says "the error is abnormal", not why. A holiday, a data outage and a pandemic all look the same to it. The response is a human one: investigate, then choose among widening the intervals, falling back to a more adaptive forecaster, retraining on the new regime only, or switching the forecast off until the world is understood.

A pre-agreed plan beats improvisation

Decide before the alarm what happens when it fires: who is told, which fallback forecaster takes over (here a weekly copy or the level-adjusted one), and how a human signs off the return to the normal model. The lifecycle track's monitoring page covers the same loop for classifiers.

1. A colleague says a calendar feature is leakage because it uses information about the future. What is the answer?

Leakage is information that would not exist at the forecast origin. The date of a public holiday is fixed far in advance, so it is available. A forecast of the weather is available; the observed weather of the target day is not. The test is always whether the value, as it will be known at the origin, is what the model sees.

2. Why did masking holidays from the history improve forecasts for ordinary Mondays weeks after the holiday?

Because the holiday value was entering the four-week average for the same weekday and hour, pulling the forecast below the level of an ordinary Monday for the next four weeks. Removing it from the average means ordinary days are forecast from ordinary days. The fix is cheap and the effect is local: it matters only for the days whose averaging window contained a holiday.

3. The weekly copy and the level-adjusted forecaster recovered about six weeks sooner than the four-week average in 2020. Why might you still not use them in normal operation?

In calm weeks they were less accurate than the four-week average (about 6% to 7% error against 5%): using only the most recent week adds noise. You pay for adaptivity every day to insure against a break that may never come. The sensible design is a stable forecaster in normal times plus a monitor that switches to an adaptive one when the alarm fires.

Apply only the masking step (no holiday profile) and compare with the full version. Which part of the gain does masking explain? 
masked = fc.score(runs["+ holidays masked out of the history"], scale_history)["MAE"]
full = fc.score(runs["+ holiday forecast from earlier holidays"], scale_history)["MAE"]
blind = fc.score(runs["4-week average (blind to holidays)"], scale_history)["MAE"]
print(blind, masked, full)

The MAE goes from about 281 (blind) to about 273 (masked) to about 266 (masked plus holiday profile): masking explains about half of the total gain in MAE, the holiday profile the rest. In RMSE the holiday profile matters most, since the worst day of the period was the holiday.

Change the alarm threshold to 1.5 times the baseline maximum and to 3 times. When does the first alarm fire in each case, and what does it tell you? 
for factor in (1.5, 2, 3):
    print(factor, smoothed[smoothed > factor * baseline.max()].index[0].date())

The first alarm fires on 12 March with 1.5 times, 13 March with 2 times and 14 March with 3 times: each step up in the threshold costs about a day of delay, because the smoothed error roughly doubles every day at the start of the break (16%, 29%, 51%, 88%). Only a threshold below the baseline maximum would have fired in February (a false alarm), which is why the baseline must include an ordinary holiday. The choice of multiplier moves detection by a day or two here because the shock is huge; for a subtle drift it matters far more.

Repeat the 2020 comparison using the average of the last 2 weeks instead of 4. Where does it sit between the weekly copy and the 4-week average? 
runs_2020["2-week average"] = fc.backtest(daily, lambda h, i: fc.seasonal_mean(h, i, weeks=2), origins=origins_2020, horizon=7)

It lands in between on every period: about 6% in calm weeks (4-week: 5%, weekly copy: 7%), about 350% during the break (862% and 152%) and about 13% in the new normal (18% and 12%). The window length is a dial between noise and adaptivity: no setting is best in both regimes.

docs.title: Holidays, Outside Drivers and Regime Change¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Make a forecaster calendar-aware by masking holidays and forecasting them from earlier holidays.
  • Decide whether an outside driver is legal at the forecast origin.
  • Quantify how different windows fail and recover after a regime change.
  • Build and calibrate a simple error-monitoring alarm.

Prerequisites: Pages 1 to 7 of this track. Dataset: NYC Taxi (Jan to Mar 2023; Jan to May 2020). Time: about 40 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
Every model in this track so far shares one hidden assumption: tomorrow behaves like the recent past. This page is about the two ways that assumption fails.

  1. Known unusual days: holidays are on the calendar months ahead, yet the best forecaster on the backtesting page was blind to them.
  2. Unknown breaks: a change in the world that nothing in the history foreshadows. We use the starkest real example in the data: New York taxi demand in spring 2020.

For the first we can fix the forecaster. For the second we cannot predict the break; what we can do is notice it quickly and limit the damage.

docs.title: 1. Holidays¶
docs.text:
The federal calendar gives three dates in our three months: 2 January (New Year's Day, observed on the Monday), 16 January (Martin Luther King Day) and 20 February (Presidents' Day). All three are Mondays, and all three disturb the four-week average in two ways, which we can see in the earlier per-origin errors:

  • on the holiday itself, the forecast is for an ordinary Monday and the day is much quieter;
  • for weeks afterwards, the holiday sits inside the "last four weeks" window and drags the average down for the same weekday. The weekly copy that failed on 27 February did it for exactly this reason.

Two fixes, each using only what is known at the origin (a calendar is not leakage, as long as the dates are known in advance):

  1. Mask holidays out of the history, so an ordinary day is averaged over ordinary days only (holiday_aware_mean(..., holiday_profile=False)).
  2. Forecast a holiday from earlier holidays: for a target on a holiday, average the same hour of the earlier holidays in the history.

fc.holiday_aware_mean implements both.

docs.title: 2. Outside drivers: what may you feed the model?¶
docs.text:
Holidays are the simplest exogenous variable: known long in advance. Other outside drivers (weather, promotions, events, prices) can lift a forecast a lot, but each raises the same question as every feature in this track: would this value be available at the origin?

Driver At forecast time you have Legal input The trap Calendar (holiday, weekday, school term) the schedule yes none: the date is the date Planned events, promotions, price changes the plan yes plans change; use the plan as it stood at the origin Weather a weather forecast the forecast, as issued at the origin training on observed weather and predicting with a forecast gives a model that has never seen forecast error Competitor behaviour, news nothing no cannot be known in advance The target's own recent values lags at least the horizon (page 5) yes lags shorter than the horizon leak

The weather row deserves emphasis. The tempting setup is to merge observed temperature with the demand history, train, backtest, and celebrate. In production the model receives a weather forecast, which is wrong in ways the model never learned. The honest backtest uses the forecast that existed at each origin, or, if archived forecasts are not available, adds noise to the observed values to mimic forecast error. This course does not add a weather dataset: the datasets it uses are audited for licence and stability (data/README.md), and a weather source with archived forecasts is an open item there.

docs.title: 3. Regime change: New York, spring 2020¶
docs.text: Now the break nobody could forecast. We use five months of 2020: January and February, then March to May. (This page downloads these extra monthly files once, about 240 MB in total; they are cached afterwards.) Daily totals first.

docs.title: 4. Noticing the break¶
docs.text: Since nobody can predict a break, the practical defence is monitoring: compare forecasts with actuals as they arrive and raise an alarm when the recent error is far outside its normal range. The rule below uses the four-week average's one-day-ahead percentage error, smoothed over three days, with a threshold set from a calm baseline period (1 February to 8 March) as twice the largest value seen there.

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix Forecast is poor for weeks after a holiday the holiday sits in the averaging window mask known unusual days out of the history Holiday forecast is wrong although the calendar is in the model too few holidays in the training data pool holidays, or share the holiday effect with a larger data set; be honest about the sample size A model trained with observed weather fails in production production uses a forecast of the weather train and test with the forecast available at each origin Long-window model breaks for weeks after a shift the old regime keeps being averaged in shorter windows, level adjustment, or retraining triggers Alarm fires on every holiday threshold set from a period without any build the baseline from a period with ordinary unusual days Same alarm for a pandemic and for a data outage an error monitor says that, not why add data-quality checks and human review

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• A forecaster assumes tomorrow looks like the recent past. Holidays break that on a known date; give the model the calendar, and keep unusual days out of the averages for ordinary ones.
  • A holiday feature learned from two holidays is fragile; the gain here (about −15 ± 8 pickups an hour) is plausible, not proven.
  • Outside drivers are legal only as they will be known at the origin: use weather forecasts, not observed weather.
  • A regime change (here, a 96% fall in demand) cannot be forecast. Long windows fail longest; level-adjusted forecasts recover fastest but cost accuracy in calm times.
  • Monitor forecast error with a threshold built from a calm period that includes ordinary unusual days; plan the response in advance.

Next: the recommender-systems track, or the exercises and projects section.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.6)) ax.plot(monthly.index, monthly["revenue"] / 1e3, color=style.BLUE, marker="o"); ax.set_ylabel("revenue (thousand £)", color=style.BLUE) ax2 = ax.twinx() # a second y-axis sharing the same x-axis ax2.plot(monthly.index, monthly["customers"], color=style.ORANGE, marker="s"); ax2.set_ylabel("customers", color=style.ORANGE); ax2.grid(False) ax.set_title("Two scales on one chart: colour-code each axis to its line") plt.show()

We colour each axis label to match its line, which is the minimum courtesy to the reader. If the point is "these move together", a scatter of one against the other (or the stacked panels above) is more honest than two free-floating scales.

In [6]: Copied! 
from mlp_data import load_airbnb
airbnb = load_airbnb()
price = pd.to_numeric(airbnb["price"].str.replace(r"[$,]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce").dropna()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.4), constrained_layout=True)
axes[0].hist(price, bins=30, color=style.BLUE);                       axes[0].set(title="All prices, 30 bins", xlabel="£ per night", ylabel="listings")
axes[1].hist(price[price < 600], bins=60, color=style.BLUE);          axes[1].set(title="Under £600, 60 bins", xlabel="£ per night")
axes[2].hist(price, bins=np.logspace(np.log10(price.min()), np.log10(price.max()), 50), color=style.GREEN)
axes[2].set_xscale("log");                                            axes[2].set(title="All prices, log-spaced bins", xlabel="£ per night (log scale)")
plt.show()
from mlp_data import load_airbnb airbnb = load_airbnb() price = pd.to_numeric(airbnb["price"].str.replace(r"[$,]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce").dropna() fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.4), constrained_layout=True) axes[0].hist(price, bins=30, color=style.BLUE); axes[0].set(title="All prices, 30 bins", xlabel="£ per night", ylabel="listings") axes[1].hist(price[price < 600], bins=60, color=style.BLUE); axes[1].set(title="Under £600, 60 bins", xlabel="£ per night") axes[2].hist(price, bins=np.logspace(np.log10(price.min()), np.log10(price.max()), 50), color=style.GREEN) axes[2].set_xscale("log"); axes[2].set(title="All prices, log-spaced bins", xlabel="£ per night (log scale)") plt.show()

The first panel is a tall spike against the left wall with an invisible tail (a few extreme prices stretch the axis). Clipping to under £600 (second panel) shows the body of the distribution but hides that the clip happened, so say so in the title. On a log scale with log-spaced bins (third panel) the whole range is visible at once and the shape is a tidy hump. When data spans orders of magnitude, a log axis is usually the honest choice.

both = airbnb.assign(price=pd.to_numeric(airbnb["price"].str.replace(r"[$,]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce"))[["accommodates", "price"]].dropna()

Both views show the same thing: price tends to rise with capacity but with an enormous spread at every size, and most listings cluster at small sizes and modest prices. The transparent scatter shows density as darkness (and faint horizontal lines at round prices such as £400, £450 and £500, because hosts love round numbers); the hexbin gives density a legend.

import tempfile, os
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3)); ax.plot(monthly.index, monthly["revenue"] / 1e3, color=style.BLUE); ax.set(title="Revenue (thousand £)")
out = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "revenue.png")

import tempfile, os fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3)); ax.plot(monthly.index, monthly["revenue"] / 1e3, color=style.BLUE); ax.set(title="Revenue (thousand £)") out = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "revenue.png") fig.savefig(out, dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.close(fig) # close figures you no longer need: they hold memory print(f"saved {os.path.getsize(out) / 1024:.0f} KB PNG at 150 dpi") 
saved 36 KB PNG at 150 dpi
1. What is the practical difference between plt.plot(...) and ax.plot(...)?

plt.plot acts on a hidden "current" axes, which can be a different chart from the one you expect once you have more than one. ax.plot acts on the specific axes object you hold, so there is no ambiguity. Hold the objects (fig, ax = plt.subplots()) and call methods on them.

2. When is a second y-axis (twinx) a bad idea?

When the point is to suggest the two series are related. The visual agreement of two lines on two free scales depends entirely on the ranges you pick, so it can manufacture or hide a correlation. Prefer stacked panels sharing the x-axis, or a scatter of one series against the other.

3. A scatter of 90,000 points is one solid blob. What are two fixes?

Reduce each point's opacity (alpha, so density shows as darkness) and/or aggregate: a hexbin or 2D histogram colours each cell by how many points fall in it. Jittering helps when one axis is a whole number.

Draw a 2×2 grid showing revenue, customers, orders and revenue-per-customer by month. Share the x-axis. Which panel shows the clearest seasonal rhythm? 
monthly["orders"] = sales.groupby(sales["invoice_date"].dt.to_period("M").dt.to_timestamp())["invoice"].nunique().reindex(monthly.index)
monthly["revenue_per_customer"] = monthly["revenue"] / monthly["customers"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 6), sharex=True, constrained_layout=True)
for ax, col, title in zip(axes.ravel(), ["revenue", "customers", "orders", "revenue_per_customer"], ["Revenue", "Customers", "Orders", "Revenue per customer"]):
    ax.plot(monthly.index, monthly[col], marker="o", color=style.BLUE); ax.set(title=title, ylim=(0, None))
plt.show()

Revenue, customers and orders all swell in the autumn. Revenue per customer is far flatter, which tells you the seasonal rise comes mainly from more customers ordering, not from each spending more.

Here is a misleading chart: a bar chart of two bars with the y-axis starting at 4.0 instead of 0, making a small difference look huge. Redraw it honestly. 
values = {"Group A": 4.2, "Group B": 4.4}
fig, (bad, good) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3), constrained_layout=True)
bad.bar(values.keys(), values.values(), color=style.RED); bad.set(ylim=(4.0, 4.5), title="Misleading: axis starts at 4")
good.bar(values.keys(), values.values(), color=style.BLUE); good.set(ylim=(0, 5), title="Honest: axis starts at 0")
plt.show()

Both draw the same numbers, but the truncated axis makes B look about three times A. Bars encode value by length, so their baseline must be zero. (For lines and dots a non-zero baseline can be fine, as long as it is clearly labelled.)

docs.title: Matplotlib: Figures, Axes and Honest Charts¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Build charts with the object-oriented interface and multi-panel layouts.
  • Choose bins and scales so a distribution tells its true story.
  • Fix overplotting with transparency, jitter or hexbin.
  • Apply the basic rules of an honest chart.

Prerequisites: pandas: Grouping, Merging and Reshaping. Dataset: Online Retail II and Inside Airbnb. Time: about 40 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
Matplotlib draws almost every chart in Python, and seaborn, pandas plotting and many others are built on top of it. It has two interfaces, and the choice between them is the single most important thing to learn: the quick "state-machine" style (plt.plot(...)), and the object-oriented style (fig, ax = plt.subplots()), where you hold the figure and axes in variables and call methods on them. Use the second. It scales from one chart to a dashboard without confusion.

We chart real data: a year-and-a-half of retail sales, and the London Airbnb listings.

docs.title: 1. Why the object-oriented interface¶
docs.text:
The state-machine style keeps a hidden "current figure" and "current axes", and every plt.something() call acts on whatever is current. That is fine for one plot and a trap for two: you lose track of which chart you are editing. The object-oriented style names them:

Concept What it is Figure (fig) the whole canvas, which can hold several charts Axes (ax) one chart: the plotting area with its x and y axis, title and labels Artist anything drawn: a line, a bar, a text label

A first chart, built completely from named objects:

docs.title: 2. Several charts at once: subplots¶
docs.text: Ask for a grid and you get an array of axes. sharex=True links the x-axes so the panels line up, and constrained_layout stops labels colliding.

docs.title: 3. Twin axes: use with care¶
docs.text: Sometimes you do want two scales on one chart. ax.twinx() adds a second y-axis. The danger is that two lines on two different scales can be made to look as correlated (or not) simply by choosing the axis ranges.

docs.title: 4. Distributions: the bin choice changes the story¶
docs.text: A histogram's shape depends on its bins, and on the scale of the axis. Airbnb nightly prices are very right-skewed, so the same data tells three different stories:

docs.title: 5. Overplotting: when there are too many points¶
docs.text: A scatter of 90,000 points is a blob. Two cures: make points transparent (alpha), or aggregate the plane into hexagonal bins (hexbin) coloured by count.

docs.title: 6. Saving figures¶
docs.text: fig.savefig writes the file. Choose resolution (dpi) for the destination, and bbox_inches="tight" to trim wasted margin. Vector formats (.svg, .pdf) stay sharp at any size and suit papers; .png suits web pages.

docs.title: Which chart for which question¶
docs.text:
You want to show Use Avoid a trend over time line bars for continuous time (fine for discrete periods) a comparison between categories bar (zero-based baseline) pie charts with many slices the shape of one variable histogram or ECDF a bar chart of raw values the relationship between two numbers scatter (hexbin if dense) a line joining unordered points a part-to-whole split stacked bar or a table 3D anything

Honesty rules: start bar charts at zero; label axes with units; do not truncate an axis to exaggerate a difference; colour for meaning (and use a colourblind-safe palette); say what was filtered.

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Use the object-oriented interface: fig, ax = plt.subplots(...), then call methods on ax.
  • subplots with sharex and constrained_layout makes aligned multi-panel figures; prefer them to twin axes.
  • The bin choice and scale change a histogram's story; use a log axis for data spanning orders of magnitude, and say what you clip.
  • Fight overplotting with alpha, jitter or hexbin.
  • Save with savefig(dpi=..., bbox_inches="tight"); close figures you are done with.
  • Be honest: zero-based bars, labelled units, colour for meaning.

Next: Seaborn, statistical charts with far less code.

taxi = load_taxi("2023-01") distance = taxi["trip_distance"].to_numpy(copy=True) # a pandas column -> an independent, writable NumPy array fare = taxi["fare_amount"].to_numpy(copy=True) print(type(distance), distance.dtype, distance.shape) distance[:5] 
<class 'numpy.ndarray'> float64 (3066766,)
Out[2]: 
array([0.97, 1.1 , 2.51, 1.9 , 1.43])

pandas 3 note

In pandas 3 (copy-on-write), .to_numpy() without copy=True returns a read-only view, so assigning into it raises an error. That protects your DataFrame from accidental edits. Ask for copy=True when you want an array you can change.

In [3]: Copied! 
pd.Series({
    "shape": distance.shape,
    "ndim (number of axes)": distance.ndim,
    "dtype": distance.dtype,
    "itemsize (bytes per value)": distance.itemsize,
    "total size (MB)": round(distance.nbytes / 1e6, 1),
    "as float32 (MB)": round(distance.astype(np.float32).nbytes / 1e6, 1),
}, name="distance").to_frame()
pd.Series({ "shape": distance.shape, "ndim (number of axes)": distance.ndim, "dtype": distance.dtype, "itemsize (bytes per value)": distance.itemsize, "total size (MB)": round(distance.nbytes / 1e6, 1), "as float32 (MB)": round(distance.astype(np.float32).nbytes / 1e6, 1), }, name="distance").to_frame() Out[3]: distance shape (3066766,) ndim (number of axes) 1 dtype float64 itemsize (bytes per value) 8 total size (MB) 24.5 as float32 (MB) 12.3

Every value takes 8 bytes (float64). Switching to float32 halves the memory at the cost of precision, a common choice for deep-learning data. (A Python list of the same numbers would be several times larger, since each element is a full Python object.)

Maths ↔ code

The mean is distance.mean(); the standard deviation is distance.std(). NumPy's std divides by n (ddof=0); pandas divides by n − 1 (the sample estimate). That is the classic reason the two disagree: pass ddof=1 to NumPy to match pandas.

In [4]: Copied! 
n = 300_000
d, f = distance[:n], fare[:n]

t0 = time.perf_counter()
total = 0.0
for i in range(n):                                    # one Python-level step per element
    if d[i] > 0:
        total += f[i] / d[i]
loop_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
moved = d > 0
vector_total = (f[moved] / d[moved]).sum()            # the same thing, in compiled code over the whole array
vector_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0

assert np.isclose(total, vector_total)               # identical answer
print(f"loop: {loop_seconds:.3f} s   vectorised: {vector_seconds:.5f} s   -> about {loop_seconds / vector_seconds:.0f}x faster")
assert loop_seconds / vector_seconds > 10
n = 300_000 d, f = distance[:n], fare[:n] t0 = time.perf_counter() total = 0.0 for i in range(n): # one Python-level step per element if d[i] > 0: total += f[i] / d[i] loop_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0 t0 = time.perf_counter() moved = d > 0 vector_total = (f[moved] / d[moved]).sum() # the same thing, in compiled code over the whole array vector_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0 assert np.isclose(total, vector_total) # identical answer print(f"loop: {loop_seconds:.3f} s vectorised: {vector_seconds:.5f} s -> about {loop_seconds / vector_seconds:.0f}x faster") assert loop_seconds / vector_seconds > 10 
loop: 0.100 s   vectorised: 0.00598 s   -> about 17x faster

The answer is identical and the array version is dramatically faster, because the loop makes 300,000 trips through the Python interpreter while the array expression makes one trip into compiled code. Rule of thumb: if you are writing a for loop over array elements, look for a whole-array way to say it. The exact ratio depends on your machine, but it will be large.

In [5]: Copied! 
first_ten = distance[:10]                              # a slice
print("shares memory with the original:", np.shares_memory(first_ten, distance))

backup = distance[:3].copy()
first_ten[0] = 999.0                                   # change the slice ...
print("original after editing the slice:", distance[0], "(was", backup[0], ")")
first_ten[0] = backup[0]                               # restore it

picked = distance[[0, 2, 4]]                           # fancy indexing (a list of positions) makes a COPY
print("fancy indexing shares memory:", np.shares_memory(picked, distance))
first_ten = distance[:10] # a slice print("shares memory with the original:", np.shares_memory(first_ten, distance)) backup = distance[:3].copy() first_ten[0] = 999.0 # change the slice ... print("original after editing the slice:", distance[0], "(was", backup[0], ")") first_ten[0] = backup[0] # restore it picked = distance[[0, 2, 4]] # fancy indexing (a list of positions) makes a COPY print("fancy indexing shares memory:", np.shares_memory(picked, distance)) 
shares memory with the original: True
original after editing the slice: 999.0 (was 0.97 )
fancy indexing shares memory: False

The rule: basic slices (a[2:9], a[::2]) give views; indexing with a list of positions or a boolean mask gives a copy. When you need an independent array, call .copy() explicitly.

In [6]: Copied! 
negative_fare = fare < 0
zero_distance = distance == 0
absurd_distance = distance > 100                      # no taxi ride in New York is over 100 miles
suspect = negative_fare | zero_distance | absurd_distance

print(f"negative fares:     {negative_fare.sum():>9,}")
print(f"zero distance:      {zero_distance.sum():>9,}")
print(f"over 100 miles:     {absurd_distance.sum():>9,}   (the longest 'trip' is {distance.max():,.0f} miles)")
print(f"any of the above:   {suspect.sum():>9,}  ({suspect.mean():.1%} of all trips)")

good = ~suspect
print(f"\nmean distance, all trips: {distance.mean():.2f} miles;  after removing the suspect ones: {distance[good].mean():.2f} miles")

negative fares:        25,049
zero distance:         45,862
over 100 miles:            88   (the longest 'trip' is 258,928 miles)

Removing just 2.2% of dubious rows shifts the average noticeably, and the longest trip is a quarter of a million miles, roughly the distance to the Moon. This is why you look at the extremes before trusting any average. (.sum() of a mask counts the True values, and .mean() gives their share.)

long               2122403

Name: count, dtype: int64

print("NaN == NaN ?", np.nan == np.nan)

NaN == NaN ? False

One NaN makes the plain mean nan. Use the np.nan* family (nanmean, nansum, nanstd, ...) or filter with ~np.isnan(a). Never test for missing values with == np.nan; use np.isnan.

pickup = taxi["tpep_pickup_datetime"]
in_january = (pickup.dt.to_period("M") == "2023-01").to_numpy()          # drop the few mis-dated trips

counts = np.bincount(weekday * 24 + hour, minlength=7 * 24).reshape(7, 24)   # rows = weekday, columns = hour
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"]
print("shape:", counts.shape, "| total trips:", counts.sum())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.4))
im = ax.imshow(counts / 1000, aspect="auto", cmap="Blues")
ax.set_yticks(range(7), days); ax.set_xticks(range(0, 24, 3), [f"{h:02d}:00" for h in range(0, 24, 3)]); ax.grid(False)
ax.set(title="Yellow-cab trips starting in each weekday-hour, January 2023 (thousands)"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

peak_row, peak_col = np.unravel_index(counts.argmax(), counts.shape)
print(f"busiest slot: {days[peak_row]} at {peak_col:02d}:00 with {counts.max():,} trips")

shape: (7, 24) | total trips: 3066718

busiest slot: Tue at 18:00 with 36,405 trips

axis tells an operation which dimension to collapse. On this (7, 24) grid, counts.sum(axis=0) collapses the weekdays and leaves 24 hourly totals; counts.sum(axis=1) collapses the hours and leaves 7 daily totals. A handy memory: the axis you name disappears.

The picture is a city's rhythm: a morning ramp, an evening peak, and a different shape at weekends. argmax returns a position in the flattened array, and np.unravel_index turns it back into (row, column).

1. Why is the vectorised version so much faster, when both do the same arithmetic?

The loop executes Python bytecode once per element, with all the overhead of looking up types and objects each time. The array expression hands the whole block of same-typed numbers to compiled code, which loops in C (often using vector instructions). Same arithmetic, vastly less overhead per element.

2. You take x = a[:5] and set x[0] = 0. Does a change? What if you had used a[[0, 1, 2]]?

With a basic slice, yes: x is a view of a, so a[0] becomes 0. With a list of positions (fancy indexing) you get a copy, so editing it leaves a alone. When in doubt, check np.shares_memory, or call .copy().

3. What does np.array([1.9, -1.9]).astype(int) return?

array([ 1, -1]): casting to integer truncates toward zero; it does not round. Use np.round(a).astype(int) if you want rounding.

What share of trips have a fare above $50? Then: which weekday-hour slot has the fewest trips? Predict both first. 
print(f"{(fare > 50).mean():.2%} of trips have a fare above $50")

quiet_row, quiet_col = np.unravel_index(counts.argmin(), counts.shape)
print(f"quietest slot: {days[quiet_row]} at {quiet_col:02d}:00 with {counts.min():,} trips")

About 6.6% of trips cost more than $50, and the first is a one-liner because the mean of a boolean mask is the share of True. The second uses argmin instead of argmax: the quietest slot is Wednesday at 03:00 with 973 trips, against 36,405 at the Tuesday 18:00 peak, a ratio of nearly forty to one.

Standardise the distances: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation, but compute the mean and standard deviation only from the good trips. What happens to the absurd 258,928-mile trip? 
mu, sigma = distance[good].mean(), distance[good].std()
z = (distance - mu) / sigma
print("z-score of the longest trip:", round(z.max()))

It becomes a z-score of roughly 59,000, many orders of magnitude beyond anything plausible. Standardising with statistics from the cleaned data makes such rows stand out instead of hiding them, which is a useful trick for spotting data errors.

docs.title: NumPy: Arrays and Indexing¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Read an array's shape, dtype and memory and explain why arrays beat loops.
  • Tell views from copies and avoid the aliasing bug.
  • Use boolean masks and NaN-aware functions to find and handle bad data.
  • Turn raw records into a grid with bincount and reshape, and read axis correctly.

Prerequisites: Python basics. Dataset: NYC Taxi (January 2023). Time: about 35 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
Almost everything in the Python data stack (pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch) is built on one idea: a block of numbers of a single type, stored contiguously, that you operate on all at once. That is the NumPy array. Learn it well and the rest of the ecosystem stops being mysterious.

We use a real table: every yellow-cab trip in New York City in January 2023, about three million rows. That is big enough for the performance points to be real, and messy enough that the indexing and masking techniques are needed, not decorative.

docs.title: 1. What an array is¶
docs.text: Four attributes describe any array. Check them whenever something behaves oddly: most NumPy surprises are a wrong shape or dtype.

docs.title: 2. Why arrays: whole-array operations¶
docs.text: Suppose we want the fare per mile for every trip that went somewhere. Compare a Python loop with the equivalent array expression on 300,000 trips.

docs.title: 3. Indexing, slicing, and the view trap¶
docs.text: Slices of an array are views: they share memory with the original instead of copying it. That is fast, and it is also the source of a classic bug.

docs.title: 4. Boolean masks: selecting by condition¶
docs.text: Real data has junk in it, and masks are how you find it. A mask is an array of True/False, one per element. Combine masks with &, | and ~ (not and/or), and put each comparison in parentheses, because & binds more tightly than >.

docs.title: 5. Missing values: NaN is not equal to anything¶
docs.text: Float arrays mark missing data with NaN ("not a number"). It poisons arithmetic and fails every comparison, including with itself.

docs.title: 6. Reshaping and the meaning of axis¶
docs.text: The most useful trick for tabular counting is to compute a single flat index and reshape the counts into a grid. Here: how many trips start in each (weekday, hour) combination? np.bincount counts occurrences of each integer, and 7 × 24 = 168 cells reshape into a week.

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix Editing a slice changes the original slices are views .copy() a > 1 & a < 5 raises an error & binds tighter than > (a > 1) & (a < 5) Mean is nan a single NaN np.nanmean or filter with np.isnan astype(int) of 1.9 gives 1 casting truncates, it does not round np.round(a).astype(int) Two means disagree between pandas and NumPy ddof differs (n − 1 vs n) ddof=1

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• An array is a typed block of numbers; check shape and dtype first when something is off.
  • Whole-array expressions replace loops and are far faster.
  • Slices are views; fancy and boolean indexing give copies.
  • Boolean masks select by condition; combine with & | ~ and parenthesise comparisons.
  • NaN is never equal to anything; use np.isnan and the np.nan* functions.
  • bincount + reshape turns raw records into a grid; the named axis disappears when you aggregate.

Next: Vectorisation, broadcasting and linear algebra.

The shape error is the one to recognise. Suppose you wanted to subtract each customer's recency (a single value per row) from all three of their columns. The recency column has shape (4324,), which lines up with the wrong end:

In [4]: Copied! 
recency = X[:, 0]
try:
    X - recency
except ValueError as e:
    print("ValueError:", e)

fixed = X - recency[:, None]                             # [:, None] turns (4324,) into (4324, 1): a column
print("fixed shape:", fixed.shape, "| first column is now all zeros:", bool((fixed[:, 0] == 0).all()))
recency = X[:, 0] try: X - recency except ValueError as e: print("ValueError:", e) fixed = X - recency[:, None] # [:, None] turns (4324,) into (4324, 1): a column print("fixed shape:", fixed.shape, "| first column is now all zeros:", bool((fixed[:, 0] == 0).all())) 
ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (4324,3) (4324,) 
fixed shape: (4324, 3) | first column is now all zeros: True

[:, None] (or np.newaxis, or .reshape(-1, 1)) adds a length-1 axis, so the vector stretches across columns instead of down rows. When you see "operands could not be broadcast together", write down both shapes and line them up from the right.

print("intermediate array:", diff.shape, f"= {diff.nbytes / 1e6:.1f} MB;  distances:", sq_dist.shape)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0) # a seeded generator: reproducible centres = Z[rng.choice(len(Z), size=4, replace=False)] # four customers, picked at random, as starting centres diff = Z[:, None, :] - centres[None, :, :] # (4324, 1, 3) - (1, 4, 3) -> (4324, 4, 3) sq_dist = (diff ** 2).sum(axis=2) # squared Euclidean distance: (4324, 4) nearest = sq_dist.argmin(axis=1) # the closest centre for each customer print("intermediate array:", diff.shape, f"= {diff.nbytes / 1e6:.1f} MB; distances:", sq_dist.shape) print("customers per centre:", np.bincount(nearest, minlength=4))

customers per centre: [ 505 2457  651  711]

Notice the cost: the intermediate array is n × k × d, which for millions of rows and many centres becomes large. Libraries use a smarter formula for big problems, but the broadcasting version is how you understand it.

In [7]: Copied! 
y = np.log1p(customers["monetary"].to_numpy())
A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(customers)), np.log1p(customers["frequency"]), np.log1p(customers["recency_days"])])   # design matrix with an intercept column

beta_normal = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, A.T @ y)          # the textbook formula
beta_lstsq = np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)[0]        # a numerically safer routine
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
sk = LinearRegression().fit(A[:, 1:], y)                 # scikit-learn adds its own intercept

print("normal equations:", beta_normal.round(4))
print("lstsq:           ", beta_lstsq.round(4))
print("scikit-learn:    ", np.r_[sk.intercept_, sk.coef_].round(4))
assert np.allclose(beta_normal, beta_lstsq) and np.allclose(beta_normal, np.r_[sk.intercept_, sk.coef_])

residual = y - A @ beta_lstsq
print(f"R-squared: {1 - (residual ** 2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum():.3f}")
y = np.log1p(customers["monetary"].to_numpy()) A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(customers)), np.log1p(customers["frequency"]), np.log1p(customers["recency_days"])]) # design matrix with an intercept column beta_normal = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, A.T @ y) # the textbook formula beta_lstsq = np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)[0] # a numerically safer routine from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression sk = LinearRegression().fit(A[:, 1:], y) # scikit-learn adds its own intercept print("normal equations:", beta_normal.round(4)) print("lstsq: ", beta_lstsq.round(4)) print("scikit-learn: ", np.r_[sk.intercept_, sk.coef_].round(4)) assert np.allclose(beta_normal, beta_lstsq) and np.allclose(beta_normal, np.r_[sk.intercept_, sk.coef_]) residual = y - A @ beta_lstsq print(f"R-squared: {1 - (residual ** 2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum():.3f}") 
normal equations: [ 4.7063  1.484  -0.0281]
lstsq:            [ 4.7063  1.484  -0.0281]
scikit-learn:     [ 4.7063  1.484  -0.0281]
R-squared: 0.659

Three routes, one answer. Why prefer lstsq? Because forming XᵀX squares the condition number, a measure of how sensitive the answer is to small errors:

In [8]: Copied! 
print(f"condition number of A:       {np.linalg.cond(A):8.1f}")
print(f"condition number of A.T @ A:   {np.linalg.cond(A.T @ A):8.1f}   (about the square of the one above)")

A_dup = np.column_stack([A, 2 * A[:, 1]])                # add a column that is exactly twice another: perfect collinearity
try:
    np.linalg.solve(A_dup.T @ A_dup, A_dup.T @ y)
    print("solve: returned an answer")
except np.linalg.LinAlgError as e:
    print("solve fails:", e)
print("lstsq still answers; its rank detection says the matrix has rank", np.linalg.lstsq(A_dup, y, rcond=None)[2], "not", A_dup.shape[1])
print(f"condition number of A: {np.linalg.cond(A):8.1f}") print(f"condition number of A.T @ A: {np.linalg.cond(A.T @ A):8.1f} (about the square of the one above)") A_dup = np.column_stack([A, 2 * A[:, 1]]) # add a column that is exactly twice another: perfect collinearity try: np.linalg.solve(A_dup.T @ A_dup, A_dup.T @ y) print("solve: returned an answer") except np.linalg.LinAlgError as e: print("solve fails:", e) print("lstsq still answers; its rank detection says the matrix has rank", np.linalg.lstsq(A_dup, y, rcond=None)[2], "not", A_dup.shape[1]) 
condition number of A:           30.6
condition number of A.T @ A:      938.6   (about the square of the one above)
solve fails: Singular matrix
lstsq still answers; its rank detection says the matrix has rank 3 not 4

With a perfectly redundant column the normal equations have no unique solution and solve gives up (or, with near-collinearity, silently returns huge unstable numbers), while lstsq reports the true rank and returns a sensible answer. This is the same phenomenon that made single coefficients meaningless on the interpretation page: correlated inputs make least squares ill-conditioned.

In [9]: Copied! 
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
spend = customers["monetary"].to_numpy()
picks = rng.integers(0, len(spend), size=(1000, len(spend)))     # 1000 resamples, each the same size as the data
boot_means = spend[picks].mean(axis=1)                           # the mean of each resample: shape (1000,)

low, high = np.percentile(boot_means, [5, 95])
print(f"mean spend {spend.mean():,.0f}; bootstrap 90% interval {low:,.0f} to {high:,.0f}")

again = np.random.default_rng(42).integers(0, len(spend), size=5)
print("same seed, same numbers:", np.array_equal(again, np.random.default_rng(42).integers(0, len(spend), size=5)))
rng = np.random.default_rng(42) spend = customers["monetary"].to_numpy() picks = rng.integers(0, len(spend), size=(1000, len(spend))) # 1000 resamples, each the same size as the data boot_means = spend[picks].mean(axis=1) # the mean of each resample: shape (1000,) low, high = np.percentile(boot_means, [5, 95]) print(f"mean spend {spend.mean():,.0f}; bootstrap 90% interval {low:,.0f} to {high:,.0f}") again = np.random.default_rng(42).integers(0, len(spend), size=5) print("same seed, same numbers:", np.array_equal(again, np.random.default_rng(42).integers(0, len(spend), size=5))) 
mean spend 1,840; bootstrap 90% interval 1,659 to 2,025
same seed, same numbers: True

That is a thousand resampled means computed without a Python loop. (The interval is about ten percent either side of the mean, which sounds tight, but remember that this mean is dominated by a few very large customers: the median would tell a very different story.)

1. A has shape (5, 4) and b has shape (5,). Why does A - b fail, and how do you subtract b from every column?

Broadcasting matches shapes from the right: (5, 4) against (5,) compares 4 with 5, which do not match. Make b a column, b[:, None] with shape (5, 1), and it stretches across the 4 columns.

2. What are the shapes of Z[:, None, :] and centres[None, :, :], and why does subtracting them give every customer-centre pair?

(4324, 1, 3) and (1, 4, 3). The length-1 axes stretch: the customers' singleton axis grows to 4 and the centres' to 4324, giving (4324, 4, 3), one 3-vector difference for each (customer, centre) pair.

3. Why prefer np.linalg.lstsq to solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)?

Forming XᵀX squares the condition number, magnifying numerical error, and the normal equations fail outright when columns are perfectly redundant. lstsq works on X directly (using orthogonal factorisations) and reports the rank, so it is more accurate and more graceful.

Write a softmax that turns each row of a matrix into probabilities (non-negative, summing to 1). Test it on Z[:5]. What goes wrong if you forget keepdims=True? 
def softmax(M):
    shifted = M - M.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)            # subtract the row max for numerical stability
    e = np.exp(shifted)
    return e / e.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

P = softmax(Z[:5])
print(P.sum(axis=1))                                      # each row sums to 1

Without keepdims=True, M.max(axis=1) has shape (5,), and subtracting it from a (5, 3) matrix raises the broadcast error from section 1. keepdims=True keeps the reduced axis as length 1, giving (5, 1), which stretches correctly.

Reassign every customer to its nearest centre using Manhattan distance (the sum of absolute differences) instead of squared Euclidean. Do the group sizes change? 
manhattan = np.abs(Z[:, None, :] - centres[None, :, :]).sum(axis=2)
print(np.bincount(manhattan.argmin(axis=1), minlength=4))

Only the line that turns differences into a distance changes (np.abs(...) instead of ** 2). The group sizes usually shift somewhat, because a different distance defines "nearest" differently, especially for the heavy-tailed customers far from every centre.

docs.title: NumPy: Vectorisation, Broadcasting and Linear Algebra¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Predict the result of a broadcast and fix a shape error.
  • Aggregate along an axis, with keepdims when you need to broadcast back.
  • Compute all pairwise distances without a loop.
  • Solve least squares robustly and explain why collinearity breaks the textbook formula.

Prerequisites: NumPy: Arrays and Indexing. Dataset: Online Retail II. Time: about 40 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
The previous page was about holding data in arrays. This one is about computing with them: arithmetic between arrays of different shapes (broadcasting), statistics along an axis, distances between every pair of points, and linear algebra. These four ideas underlie nearly every algorithm you will meet: standardisation, k-means, regression, PCA.

We use a real matrix: three behavioural numbers (recency, frequency, spend) for each of the 4,324 active customers in the retail case study.

docs.title: 1. Broadcasting: arithmetic between different shapes¶
docs.text:
When two arrays have different shapes, NumPy tries to stretch the smaller one to fit. The rule is applied from the trailing (rightmost) dimension backwards: two dimensions are compatible if they are equal, or if one of them is 1.

A shape B shape Result Why (4324, 3) (3,) (4324, 3) the row of 3 is repeated down all 4,324 rows (4324, 3) (4324, 1) (4324, 3) the column is repeated across the 3 columns (4324, 3) (4324,) error trailing dimensions 3 and 4,324 do not match

The most common use is standardising each column: subtract that column's mean and divide by its standard deviation. X.mean(axis=0) collapses the rows and leaves one value per column, shape (3,), which broadcasts back across every row.

docs.title: 2. Statistics along an axis¶
docs.text: The same axis rule as before: the axis you name is the one that disappears.

docs.title: 3. Distances between every pair, by broadcasting¶
docs.text: Clustering algorithms like k-means repeatedly ask "which centre is each customer nearest to?" That is a distance between every customer and every centre, with no loop. Give the customers shape (n, 1, 3) and the centres shape (1, k, 3); broadcasting produces all n × k differences at once.

docs.title: 4. Linear algebra: least squares three ways¶
docs.text:
Fit a straight line (a plane, here) predicting log-spend from log-frequency and log-recency.

Maths ↔ code

Ordinary least squares finds the coefficients β minimising the squared error, and the textbook answer is β = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀy. In NumPy: np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y). Note @ is matrix multiplication and .T is the transpose. (We solve the system rather than computing the inverse, which is slower and less accurate.)

docs.title: 5. Random numbers you can reproduce¶
docs.text: Use a seeded generator, np.random.default_rng(seed), and pass it around. The same seed gives the same numbers every time, which is what makes experiments repeatable. A vectorised bootstrap shows the style: draw a thousand resamples of the customers at once as one (1000, n) array of row indices.

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix "operands could not be broadcast together" shapes do not line up from the right print both shapes; add an axis with [:, None] Standardising down the wrong axis axis=0 collapses rows (per-column stats); axis=1 per-row name the axis you want to disappear corrcoef result looks wrong it expects variables in rows rowvar=False Huge memory in a pairwise-distance step the (n, k, d) intermediate chunk the rows, or use a library routine Wild regression coefficients collinear columns make XᵀX ill-conditioned lstsq, regularisation, drop redundant columns Different results every run an unseeded generator np.random.default_rng(seed)

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Broadcasting stretches the smaller array; compare shapes from the right, and use [:, None] to add an axis.
  • axis names the dimension that disappears; keepdims=True keeps it as length 1 so results broadcast back.
  • Pairwise distances come from broadcasting (n, 1, d) against (1, k, d), at the cost of an (n, k, d) intermediate.
  • Least squares: lstsq beats the normal equations, which square the condition number and fail on collinear columns.
  • Seed a generator (default_rng) and vectorise resampling.

Next: the pandas pages, which wrap this machinery in labelled tables.

before = work["accommodates"].sum()

import warnings
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    work[work["room_type"] == "Shared room"]["accommodates"] = 99      # chained: filter first, then assign into the result

print("chained assignment changed the table:", work["accommodates"].sum() != before)

chained assignment changed the table: False
a single .loc call changed it:         True

The first line filtered (producing a temporary copy) and then assigned into the copy, which was thrown away. Older pandas warned about this with a SettingWithCopyWarning; pandas 3's copy-on-write makes the rule absolute: a filtered result is always its own object, so chained assignment never reaches the original. The fix is a single .loc[rows, column] = value, which is also the only form that is guaranteed to work in every version.

1. After df = df.sort_values("price"), df.iloc[0] and df.loc[0] may differ. Why?

Sorting reorders the rows but keeps each row's original index label. .iloc[0] is the first row by position (now the cheapest), while .loc[0] is the row labelled 0 (wherever it ended up). They agree only while the index is still in its original order.

2. Why does df[df.x > 5]["y"] = 0 leave df unchanged?

The first part, df[df.x > 5], builds a new filtered table; the ["y"] = 0 then assigns into that new object, which is discarded. Use df.loc[df.x > 5, "y"] = 0, which selects and assigns on the original in one step.

3. You add two Series of equal length and get all NaN. What is the likely cause?

Their index labels do not match. pandas aligns by label, not position, so with no shared labels every result is missing. Check a.index and b.index, or drop to arrays with to_numpy() if you really want positional pairing.

Among entire homes, which neighbourhood has the most listings, and what share of all entire homes is that? Which neighbourhood has the highest average number of bedrooms? (Hint: groupby arrives on the third pandas page; try value_counts for the first part.) 
homes = small[small["room_type"] == "Entire home/apt"]
counts = homes["neighbourhood_cleansed"].value_counts()
print(counts.index[0], f"{counts.iloc[0]:,} listings = {counts.iloc[0] / len(homes):.1%} of entire homes")

Westminster comes first with about 8,800 listings, roughly one in seven entire homes. For the second part you need homes.groupby("neighbourhood_cleansed")["bedrooms"].mean(), covered next.

Create a boolean column professional that is True for listings whose host has 10 or more listings, then report how many listings it flags. 
small["professional"] = small["host_id"].map(per_host) >= 10
print(small["professional"].sum(), f"({small['professional'].mean():.1%})")

per_host is a Series indexed by host_id, so .map(per_host) looks each listing's host up in it and returns that host's listing count. The result flags about a quarter of all listings, matching the 24.6% computed earlier.

docs.title: pandas: Series, DataFrames and Selection¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Check a table's dtypes and memory and shrink it sensibly.
  • Choose between .loc and .iloc, and filter with boolean conditions.
  • Explain index alignment and why arithmetic can produce NaN.
  • Assign safely and avoid the chained-assignment trap.

Prerequisites: NumPy: Arrays and Indexing. Dataset: Inside Airbnb (London). Time: about 40 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
pandas is the tool you will use most. It wraps NumPy arrays in a labelled table: rows have an index, columns have names and (this matters) types. Almost every pandas confusion comes from one of four things: not knowing the dtypes, mixing up label-based and position-based selection, forgetting that arithmetic aligns on the index, or modifying something that is a copy.

Our data is real and a little unwieldy: every Airbnb listing in London (snapshot of September 2026), about 92,000 rows and 90 columns.

docs.title: 1. Know what you loaded: dtypes and memory¶
docs.text: Before anything else, ask how big the table is and what types its columns are. Wrong dtypes (numbers stored as text, for instance) are the usual root cause of later errors.

docs.title: 2. Selecting: columns, .loc and .iloc¶
docs.text:
• df["a"] gives a Series (one column); df[["a", "b"]] gives a DataFrame.
  • .loc[rows, cols] selects by label; the end of a label slice is included.
  • .iloc[rows, cols] selects by position; the end is excluded, like Python lists.

The difference only shows when the index is not simply 0, 1, 2, ...: so let us give the table a meaningful index.

docs.title: 3. Filtering rows with boolean conditions¶
docs.text: Build a True/False Series and use it to select rows. Combine conditions with &, |, ~, with parentheses around each condition.

docs.title: 4. Counting and ranking¶
docs.text: value_counts is the workhorse. Combined with a little arithmetic it answers real questions. Airbnb listings are supposed to be people renting out their home, but who actually owns them?

docs.title: 5. Alignment: pandas matches on labels, not positions¶
docs.text: When you do arithmetic between two Series, pandas lines them up by index label. Labels present in only one side give NaN. This is powerful and a classic source of surprise.

docs.title: 6. Copies, views and the chained-assignment trap¶
docs.text: Assigning into the result of a filter usually does nothing to the original table:

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix .loc[2:4] returns one more row than expected label slices include the end use .iloc[2:4] for positions ValueError on a > 1 & a < 5 operator precedence (a > 1) & (a < 5) Arithmetic gives lots of NaN labels do not match align deliberately, or to_numpy() Assignment "did nothing" chained assignment on a copy df.loc[mask, "col"] = value Table uses far too much memory text columns and wide dtypes select columns; category; smaller dtypes

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Check dtypes and memory first. Select needed columns and use category for low-cardinality text.
  • .loc = labels (end included); .iloc = positions (end excluded).
  • Filter with boolean masks (&, |, ~, parenthesised), isin, between or query.
  • Arithmetic aligns on index labels: no shared labels means NaN.
  • Assign with a single .loc[mask, column] = value; chained assignment writes into a discarded copy.

Next: Cleaning and types, where these tools meet genuinely messy columns.

There it is: almost every listing without availability has no price, and almost every listing with availability has one. The price is missing because the listing is not currently for rent: the gap is structural, not random. Consequences:

  • Dropping rows with missing prices quietly removes almost all of the unavailable listings (they account for the large majority of the gaps), so any "typical London listing" you describe now means "typical currently-bookable listing".
  • Filling the gaps with a median would invent prices for listings that are not on the market.

The right choice depends on the question. For "what do available listings cost?" dropping is correct, provided you say so. For "describe all listings" keep the missing values and report them.

The price distribution is strongly right-skewed: the mean sits well above the median, and the largest value is absurdly high (a nightly price of £75,000 is almost certainly a data entry error or a placeholder). On a log scale the shape becomes a tidy hump, which is why prices are almost always modelled in logs. Common treatments for extremes: winsorise (clip to a percentile), filter with a documented rule, or transform (log). Whichever you pick, record it.

Imputation belongs inside the model pipeline

Filling with a group median computed on the whole table uses information from rows you will later test on. That is harmless for exploration but a leak if the table feeds a model. In a modelling workflow use scikit-learn's imputers inside a Pipeline, so medians are learned from training rows only (see the scikit-learn pipelines page).

In [12]: Copied! 
def clean_airbnb(raw):
    out = raw.drop(columns=raw.columns[raw.isna().all()]).copy()
    out["price"] = pd.to_numeric(out["price"].str.replace(r"[$,]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce")
    out["host_is_superhost"] = out["host_is_superhost"].map({"t": True, "f": False}).astype("boolean")
    out["last_review"] = pd.to_datetime(out["last_review"])
    t = out["bathrooms_text"]
    n = t.str.extract(r"(\d+\.?\d*)", expand=False).astype(float)
    n = n.where(~(t.str.contains("half", case=False, na=False) & n.isna()), 0.5).where(~t.str.contains("no bathroom", case=False, na=False), 0.0)
    out["bathrooms"], out["shared_bathroom"] = n, t.str.contains("shared", case=False, na=False)
    out["neighbourhood_cleansed"] = out["neighbourhood_cleansed"].astype("category")
    out["room_type"] = out["room_type"].astype("category")
    assert out["id"].is_unique
    return out

90 columns -> 77
Out[12]: before after price str float64 host_is_superhost str boolean last_review str datetime64[us] bathrooms float64 float64 room_type str category 1. Why pass errors="coerce" to to_numeric, and what must you do right after?

Without it, a single unparseable value raises an error and stops the conversion. With "coerce" unparseable values become NaN instead. That is convenient but silent, so you must count the new NaNs (compare with the count before) to be sure you did not quietly destroy data.

2. Prices are missing for almost exactly the listings with no availability. Should you fill them with the median price?

Not without thought. They are missing because the listing is not on the market, so a filled-in price would be invented. For analyses of current prices, drop them and say so; for describing all listings, keep them as missing and report how many. The missingness carries information; filling erases it.

3. Why must 'Half-bath' be handled separately from the digit-extracting regex?

It contains no digit, so str.extract(r"(\d+\.?\d*)") returns NaN for it, silently converting a real value (half a bathroom) into "missing". Looking at the non-matching values before trusting the regex is how you find such edge cases.

How many listings cost more than £1,000 a night, and what share of those are private rooms? Does that match your expectation? 
expensive = clean[clean["price"] > 1000]
print(len(expensive), "listings above £1,000")
print((expensive["room_type"].value_counts(normalize=True) * 100).round(1).to_dict())

About 980 listings, and roughly 93% of them are entire homes, with about 7% private rooms. A private room at over £1,000 a night is a much stronger sign of a data error than an entire home at that price, so that small group is where to look first.

Add a column pets_allowed that is True when the amenities mention pets, then compare its median price with the rest. 
clean["pets_allowed"] = clean["amenities"].str.contains("pets allowed", case=False, na=False)
print(clean.groupby("pets_allowed")["price"].median())

About 13% of listings allow pets, and their median price is higher (roughly £210 against £168). That is an association, not an effect: it plausibly reflects which kinds of listing allow pets rather than pets raising the price. str.contains(..., na=False) guards against missing amenity strings, and both medians are computed only over listings that have a price.

docs.title: pandas: Cleaning and Types¶
docs.text:
What you will be able to do after this page

  • Audit missingness and find out why values are missing before filling them.
  • Convert text columns to numbers, booleans and dates without silently losing data.
  • Parse numbers out of text, handling the edge cases first.
  • Package cleaning as a repeatable, tested function.

Prerequisites: pandas: Series, DataFrames and Selection. Dataset: Inside Airbnb (London). Time: about 45 minutes.

docs.title: The situation¶
docs.text:
Raw data arrives with numbers stored as text, dates as strings, categories spelled as 't' and 'f', whole columns that are empty, and gaps that are not what they seem. Cleaning is mostly converting types correctly and understanding why values are missing. pandas has a method for each job.

We work on the London Airbnb listings again, with a goal in mind: a tidy table in which price can be analysed. Right now it cannot even be averaged.

docs.title: 1. Audit what is missing¶
docs.text: Start with the shape of the missingness: which columns are completely empty, and which are partly empty?

docs.title: 2. Converting text to numbers¶
docs.text: To convert '$1,234.50' to 1234.5: strip the currency symbol and the thousands comma with .str.replace, then convert with pd.to_numeric. Always pass errors="coerce" so anything unparseable becomes NaN and then count how many that was, because silent coercion is how data gets lost.

docs.title: 3. Why is price missing?¶
docs.text: Before filling or dropping, ask whether the missingness is random. If it is related to something, treating it as random will bias every later result. A good first test is to compare the share missing across a plausible driver. Listings with no availability in the coming year seem a candidate:

docs.title: 4. Outliers: look at the extremes before summarising¶
docs.text: A mean is only as good as its worst value.

docs.title: 5. Booleans and dates¶
docs.text: 't'/'f' strings become real booleans with a mapping; date strings become datetimes with pd.to_datetime, which unlocks the .dt accessor.

docs.title: 6. Parsing numbers out of text¶
docs.text: bathrooms_text holds values like '1 shared bath' and 'Half-bath'. A regex pulls out the number and a second test gets the flag. Real data has edge cases, so look at the oddities first:

docs.title: 7. Keys, duplicates and imputation¶
docs.text: Check that the identifier really is unique, then decide how to treat the small remaining gaps. A defensible, simple choice is the median within a group: for a missing bed count, the typical value for listings that sleep the same number of guests. groupby(...).transform(...) returns a column aligned with the original rows, ready to fill from.

docs.title: 8. Put it all in one function¶
docs.text: Everything above, as a single repeatable function: the cleaning you did by hand becomes code you can re-run on next quarter's snapshot, and test.

docs.title: Pitfalls at a glance¶
docs.text: Surprise Cause Fix mean() fails or concatenates text numbers stored as strings strip symbols, pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce"), then count new NaN Dropping NaN rows changes who is in the data missingness is not random find the driver before dropping or filling A regex silently returns NaN edge cases with no digit list the oddities first; assert no new gaps bool column cannot hold a gap plain bool has no missing value the nullable "boolean" dtype Imputed values leak into the test set statistics computed on all rows impute inside a Pipeline

docs.title: Recap¶
docs.text:
• Audit missingness first: which columns are empty, which are partly empty, and why. Structural gaps (price missing because the listing is unavailable) should not be filled blindly.
  • Convert text to numbers with str.replace + pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce"), and count the new NaNs.
  • Look at extremes before summarising; consider winsorising, filtering or a log transform.
  • Use map for coded categories, pd.to_datetime and .dt for dates, the nullable "boolean" dtype when gaps matter, and str.extract with edge cases checked first.
  • Wrap the steps in a function you can re-run and test; impute inside a Pipeline when a model is involved.

Next: Grouping and merging, combining tables and summarising by group.

The classic disaster is joining on a key that is not unique on either side. Suppose we want to attach user tags to ratings, matching on movie alone:

Each rating was paired with every tag on its movie, so the table more than doubled and any later total or average is wrong. The cure is to make the right-hand key unique first, by aggregating the tags per movie, and then validate:
